A 26-year-old woman presented at week 20 of pregnancy with a 3-month history of fever, cough, and breathlessness. She had hearing loss, epistaxis, nasal crusting, haemoptysis, and a purpuric rash over her legs. No significant weight loss was reported. Chest x-ray (with abdominal shield) showed bilateral cannonball opacities, and contrast-enhanced chest CT (with abdominal shield) revealed multiple nodules, without pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy (figure). Ultrasound of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed a single live fetus and no abnormalities. Her haemoglobin concentration was 8·3 g/dL, total leucocyte count was 8·6 × 109/L, platelet count was 600 × 109/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm/h, and C-reactive protein concentration was 186 mg/L. The patient's serum anti-proteinase 3 antibody concentration was 102 U/mL. Sputum acid-fast bacilli and fungal smear, serum β-D-glucan and galactomannan, and Mantoux test results were all negative. A diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis was made.
The patient commenced remission induction therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once daily for 3 days) and rituximab (1000 mg, two doses 2 weeks apart). She showed substantial improvement over the next 2–3 days and delivered a healthy baby girl at term. The patient commenced oral prednisolone immediately after induction therapy, starting at 60 mg/day for 1 month followed by taper every two weeks. She has received remission maintenance therapy with oral prednisolone (5 mg/day) and intravenous rituximab (500 mg every 6 months) for 1 year, and is planned to continue this treatment for at least 2 years total duration. A follow-up chest x-ray 6 months after the initial treatment showed complete resolution of lung nodules.
Cannonball opacities on chest x-ray usually suggest metastatic malignancies such as choriocarcinoma, lung carcinoma, renal cell cancer, or endometrial carcinoma, but, less frequently, can be due to other conditions, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, fungal infections, and tuberculosis. The most common chest radiological finding at presentation in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is bilateral nodules or masses (reported in up to 90% of patients in case series). In the current case, hearing loss, purpuric rash, and upper respiratory symptoms led us to suspect granulomatosis with polyangiitis. The absence of pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy on chest radiology made a diagnosis of malignancy or infection less likely, the normal pelvic ultrasound helped to rule out choriocarcinoma, and the negative Mantoux test, sputum workup, and fungal serology helped to rule out infection. Elevated concentrations of anti-proteinase 3 antibodies and the patient's rapid response to immunosuppression contributed to confirmation of the diagnosis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis that can mimic malignancy and infections. This diagnosis should be suspected in patients with lung nodules when there are accompanying upper respiratory tract symptoms, rash, neuropathy, or eye, ear, or renal involvement.

An 80-year-old man with a 6-month-history of shortness of breath on minimal exertion and fatigue was admitted to our unit for a planned operation to replace his stenotic aortic valve. The surgery was uneventful and a temporary ventricular epicardial pacing lead was placed on the free wall of the right ventricle. The patient remained haemodynamically stable in sinus rhythm post-surgery and was extubated 8 h later. The following day he was transferred from intensive care to our high dependency unit with the temporary epicardial pacemaker in VVI mode: stimulation amplitude 10 V, sensitivity 1 mV, and back-up pacing rate of 44 beats per min. A pacing check at that time showed no problems.2 days after the operation the patient had a cardiac arrest during mobilisation and physiotherapy; chest compressions were started, and the patient was re-intubated. The defibrillator showed ventricular fibrillation and he was shocked into sinus rhythm using 200 joules biphasic.
A telemetry review showed a spike on a T wave as a possible cause of the cardiac arrest: sinus rhythm was present during the first two cardiac cycles—heart rate 76 beats per min—followed by a premature pacing spike which produced a paced cardiac cycle. Another intrinsic cardiac cycle then followed. However, during the repolarisation phase of this cycle, a second pacing spike was seen falling on the T wave; this spike triggered polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that apparently degenerated into ventricular fibrillation (figure).
The patient was stabilised post-resuscitation and extubated 4 h later; he recovered well and was allowed home 12 days later. 1 month later he was well and asymptomatic when reviewed in our outpatient clinic.
Indications for temporary cardiac pacing include the management of bradyarrhythmias—specifically atrioventricular block—and both atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In cardiac surgery, insertion of temporary epicardial pacing wires is common practice; it both optimises myocardial function in patients, who postoperatively develop haemodynamically significant arrhythmias, and helps maintain a stable cardiac rhythm.
However, placement of epicardial pacing leads is not without risk. In the short term, function deteriorates mainly due to the inflammation around the surfaces of the myocardium and the leads. Daily checking of the pacemaker's pacing (the depolarisation of the atria or ventricles resulting from an impulse delivered from the generator down a lead to the heart) and sensing (the detection by the generator of intrinsic atrial or ventricular depolarisation signals) parameters after cardiac surgery is therefore paramount.
Pacemaker under-sensing occurs when the pacemaker fails to detect spontaneous myocardial depolarisation—as probably happened in our patient—and is a common reason for the appearance of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes. When the spikes fall on the T wave, then the patient may develop a tachyarrhythmia—including polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Increasing the pacemaker rate above that of the intrinsic heart rate may reduce the possibility of production of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes.

input: A51-year-old man presented with acute visual floaters and blurry vision in his left eye for 1 week. The patient had been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis with positive HLA-B27 in his early 20s and had been treated with 40 mg adalimumab every 2 weeks for 1 year. A tuberculin skin test, interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON), and chest radiograph were checked before the initiation of adalimumab therapy, none of which revealed signs of tuberculosis. A hepatitis panel was also negative. His visual symptoms developed 5 days after the latest subcutaneous injection of adalimumab. At presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells; however, 11–20 inflammatory vitreous cells were observed within 1 mm × 3 mm slit beam in the anterior vitreous, snowballs in vitreous, and multiple whitish retinal chorioretinitis lesions were seen in the left eye (figure A). Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from a local chorioretinitis lesion with segmental vascular leakage peripherally (figure B). The patient did not have any symptoms of chronic cough, fever, headache, or bodyweight loss. The cause of uveitis was then re-evaluated. CT of the chest revealed multiple tree-in-bud infiltrations in both right and left upper lobes (figure C). Positive T-spot test, acid-fast bacilli sputum smears, PCR (9·50 × 104 colony forming units per mL), and sputum culture confirmed pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Adalimumab therapy was stopped, and the patient was treated with a full-dose anti-tuberculosis regimen. The patient achieved complete remission with no sign of recurrence after 1 year of follow-up.Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease with systemic involvement, and given that ankylosing spondylitis is commonly associated with anterior uveitis, an underlying infection could easily be missed and eventually lead to irreversible vision loss. In this unique case with posterior uveitis, the absence of respiratory symptoms posed a diagnostic challenge. Our case suggested that ocular manifestations with posterior uveitis could be the first sign of undiscovered newly developed pulmonary tuberculosis in patients with ankylosing spondylitis receiving anti-TNF therapy. The treatment strategy for typical acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis usually involves intensive topical or systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive medications, which is divergent to that of tuberculous uveitis, and thus, an accurate diagnosis is imperative.

input: A man aged 65 years presented to the otorhinolaryngology outpatient clinic at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (India), in January, 2018, with a 1-year history of progressive dysphagia to solids, cervical borborygmi (see video appendix 1), sensation of lump in throat, occasional regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis. He denied any history of weight loss, recurrent cough, hoarseness, or pain. On physical examination a gurgling sound was elicited on pressing the neck (see video appendix 1). Video fluoroscopy revealed stasis of barium in the dilated upper oesophagus extending from C6 to T1 vertebrae (figure and video appendix 2). Trans-nasal oesophagoscopy revealed a large Zenker's diverticulum containing food residue (video appendix 3). The patient underwent endoscopic diverticulectomy. On the day after surgery, the dysphagia and gurgling sounds to liquids disappeared; the patient remained asymptomatic at 12-month follow-up visit.Zenker's diverticulum is an acquired pulsion pseudo-diverticulum originating in Killian's dehiscence, an area bounded by the oblique fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It occurs because of increased intraluminal pressure in the hypopharynx during swallowing, caused by an inadequately relaxed cricopharyngeal upper oesophageal sphincter. Boyce's sign, a gurgling sound due to noise of splashing fluid accumulated in a large Zenker's diverticulum, can be heard on palpation. Although small diverticula might not cause symptoms, larger diverticula are usually symptomatic and surgery could be warranted.

input: A 69-year-old woman with a 27-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented to the rheumatology clinic at Kochi Medical School hospital, Japan, with polyarthralgia of both hands and painless subcutaneous nodules on her right hand that had slowly grown over a year. Physical examination revealed arthritis mutilans with ulnar deviation and yellow masses on the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fingers of the right hand (figure A). There were no abnormal findings in any part of the body other than the joints, such as the eyelids and trunk. Laboratory investigations revealed that the levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor were 1·78 mg/dL (normal range <0·15 mg/dL) and 1 096·0 IU/mL (<15 IU/mL), respectively. Hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins were not detected. We performed a bone marrow biopsy, which was normocellular. An x-ray revealed severe erosion and deformities of the hand bones and punched-out bony radiolucencies associated with the subcutaneous nodular lesions (figure B). A skin biopsy specimen of the subcutaneous mass showed areas of cholesterol clefts and necrobiosis surrounded by foamy histiocytes, lymphocytes, Touton giant cells, and foreign body-type multinucleated giant cells (figure C–F). These findings confirmed a diagnosis of pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are an unusual form of rheumatoid nodule resembling tendon xanthomas, are often mistakenly diagnosed as xanthomatosis, and have been previously regarded by investigators as subcutaneous xanthogranuloma, observed in the juxta-articular sites of the hand, wrist, elbow, knee, foot, and acromioclavicular joints. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are distinguished from xanthomatosis by x-ray findings of demonstrable punched-out bony radiolucencies, which are not present in xanthomatosis. Cholesterol clefts surrounded by granulomatous reactions can also be observed in rheumatoid synovial fluid and bursitis, sometimes presenting as migrating chylous cysts. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule and xanthomatosis are easily misdiagnosed because their histopathological findings are similar. However, xanthomatosis is often associated with hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins, whereas pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule is not accompanied by these diseases and is found in the juxta-articular sites with punched-out bony radiolucencies. After initiating treatment with 6 mg oral methotrexate per week, the concentrations of CRP reduced to 0·63 mg/dL, polyarthralgia improved, and the pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules shrank.

*   **Associated Chest Wall Features:** Other ipsilateral findings can include absence or hypoplasia of the pectoralis minor muscle (common), serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi, and external oblique muscles. Hypoplasia or aplasia of the breast and/or nipple-areola complex is also common. Skeletal defects like hypoplasia or absence of ribs (typically 2nd to 5th) can occur.
*   **Hand and Arm Anomalies:** Ipsilateral upper limb abnormalities are present in the majority of cases and are key to confirming the full syndrome. The most common pattern is **symbrachydactyly**, which is a combination of brachydactyly (short fingers) and syndactyly (cutaneous webbing or fusion of fingers). Other hand anomalies include:
    *   Simple brachydactyly (as in this patient's case).
    *   Hypoplasia of the hand (smaller hand).
    *   Absence of digits (oligodactyly or ectrodactyly).
    *   Hypoplasia or aplasia of the middle phalanges is a frequent finding.

### **2. Etiology of Poland Syndrome (Vascular Disruption Hypothesis)**

**Retrieved Knowledge:**
The etiology of Poland syndrome is not fully understood, but it is generally considered a sporadic developmental field defect rather than a classic inherited genetic disorder. The leading hypothesis is the **Subclavian Artery Supply Disruption Sequence (SASDS)**.

*   **Mechanism:** It is proposed that around the 6th week of embryonic development, there is a temporary interruption or reduction of blood flow in the subclavian artery or its branches (e.g., axillary artery).
*   **Consequences:** This vascular insult leads to hypoxia and subsequent malformation of the tissues supplied by these vessels. The developing pectoralis muscle, overlying soft tissues, ribs, and the apical ectodermal ridge of the growing limb bud are all vulnerable.
*   **Unified Explanation:** This single vascular event provides a compelling explanation for the seemingly disparate combination of unilateral chest wall and ipsilateral limb defects, as both regions share a common embryonic blood supply.

A 70-year-old man presented to our department reporting fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss of 18 kg over the previous 3 months. He said he had been taking numerous nutritional supplements and vitamins daily.On examination, the patient had large, painful lymph nodes in his neck and axilla, and splenomegaly. Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 916 000 × 109 per L.
He was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and started on fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. After four courses, the patient's alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level increased to 326 U/L; he was asymptomatic with a normal bilirubin. After stopping the supplements and vitamins, the ALT normalised. Approximately 18 months later, the patient's ALT increased again to 290 U/L. Further investigations found the patient to be positive for HBsAg and anti-HBc, and his blood concentration of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA was greater than 170 000 000 IU/mL. Entecavir 0·5 mg daily was started; his HBV DNA and ALT levels rapidly improved (figure).
Immunosuppressive therapy can cause reactivation of HBV replication, manifesting as an increase in serum HBV DNA levels, with or without increase in ALT level. Severe cases may lead to liver failure and death. HBV reactivation is more common in patients who are HBsAg-positive—chronic HBV—but it can also occur in those who are HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc IgG positive, indicating a past HBV infection. The latter usually occurs in the setting of potent immunosuppressive therapies such as rituximab and may be accompanied by reappearance of HBsAg. The presence of anti-HBs decreases but does not eliminate the risk of HBV reactivation.
The risk of HBV reactivation in patients who received rituximab without antiviral prophylaxis has been reported to be 33–65% in patients who are HBsAg-positive and 6–24% in those who are HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc IgG positive. Prophylactic antiviral therapy has been shown to be 80–100% effective in preventing HBV reactivation; notably, it is more effective than starting antiviral therapy at or after the onset of HBV reactivation.
Current oncology and hepatology society guidelines recommend patients anticipating rituximab or other anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy should be screened for HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG—which was not done in this patient who received rituximab years before the national recommendations. If either test is positive, then prophylactic antiviral therapy with entecavir or tenofovir should be started to prevent HBV reactivation (video).
HBV DNA testing prior to anticancer therapy can help stratify the risk of HBV reactivation, and HBV DNA monitoring may lead to earlier detection of HBV reactivation. Antiviral therapy should be continued for at least 12 months after the last dose of rituximab.
It is also important to bear in mind that elevated ALT levels in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia receiving treatment may also result from liver injury caused by the chemotherapeutic agents, some nutritional supplements, and other viral hepatitis—including A, C, or E.

A 33-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, reporting 2 months of increasing discomfort and swelling in her upper abdomen, attended a routine antenatal appointment with her midwife. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and had no previous medical problems; she had stopped using combined oral contraceptives several years earlier.On examination, the woman was well; vital signs were within normal limits and her BMI was 27·3 kg/m2. She was not jaundiced and had no features of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, or infection.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, C-reactive protein concentration, urea, creatinine, albumin, electrolytes, and liver function tests—showed no abnormalities.
The findings of an abdominal ultrasound were confirmed by an MRI which showed a 13 cm heterogeneous mass in the left lateral liver segments (figure); no features of liver cirrhosis or vascular malformations were seen.
The patient was referred to our hepatobiliary surgical unit for further investigations—at this stage we were unable to conclude if the mass in the liver was either benign or malignant.
Following the recommendation of our multidisciplinary tumour board, the lesion was biopsied. Histopathological examination of a sample of the biopsy showed hepatocytes without atypia, arranged in two-cell thick trabecular and bland hepatocytes surrounded by fibrous septa containing artery branches; inflammatory infiltrate; and features of chronic cholestasis. Immunohistochemistry showed patchy staining of hepatocytes for glutamine synthetase; CD34 showed patchy sinusoidal staining; glypican 3 and heat shock protein 70 were negative; and staining for oestrogen receptors was positive, and negative for progesterone receptors. The morphology and immune profile were indicative of focal nodular hyperplasia, and we concluded no further intervention was needed. The patient delivered, by caesarean section, a healthy baby girl at gestational age 39 weeks and 6 days.
A CT will be done 6 months after the delivery to check on the liver mass, which we anticipate will reduce in size. For the longer term, the patient will require an ultrasound examination if she becomes pregnant again to ascertain if it has grown further. Additionally, if the mass continues to cause symptoms, and does not reduce in size, there is the option of a laparoscopic resection.
Regarding benign liver tumours, haemangiomas are the most prevalent. They occur more frequently in woman; and are often diagnosed in young women in the third, fourth, and fifth decades of life. Focal nodular hyperplasia is the second most common benign liver lesion—predominantly occurring in women aged 20–40 years; it rarely bleeds and carries no risk of malignant transition. Hepatocellular adenomas are more common in women and may grow under oestrogen stimulation in pregnancy or oral contraceptive use; large or growing hepatocellular adenomas are at risk of malignant transformation and bleeding.
Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma—which was a possible differential diagnosis in our case considering the patient's age, gender, and clinical presentation—characteristically appears as a lobulated heterogeneous mass with a central scar in an otherwise normal, non-cirrhotic liver; it is a rare, but highly aggressive liver cancer that demands urgent treatment.
Pregnancy necessitates a different diagnostic evaluation approach of large liver lesions; radiological investigation with gadolinium-enhanced MRI has shown toxicity to the fetus in animal studies. CT scans are associated with radiation issues. And abdominal ultrasounds are not diagnostic—although a contrast-enhanced ultrasound may suggest the diagnosis. Therefore, the three principles of assessing liver masses in pregnancy are: multimodal imaging, multidisciplinary evaluation, and morphologic assessment by histology.

A 51-year-old man was referred to our department because of reduced exercise tolerance and breathlessness on exertion. He had a medical history of obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS), which was being treated with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). He had complained of snoring and a loss of concentration when he was first diagnosed with OSAS, in 2012.The referring pulmonologist said that the patient's Apnoea–Hypopnea Index had improved from 36 events per h to 0·3 events per h after the positive pressure was increased from 4 to 8 cm water (H2O), and for a short period there had been an improvement in the patient's problems, but then the CPAP seemed to make the situation worse—his exercise tolerance decreased further, and he reported insomnia and pronounced morning fatigue.
When we examined the patient, his oxygen saturation was 94%. On auscultation of his chest, we heard a systolic murmur at the left, second intercostal space. An echocardiogram showed a large ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) and an enlarged right ventricle with preserved systolic function (figure). The patient's mean pulmonary artery pressure was 18 mm Hg (normal <25) with no CPAP, indicating no pulmonary hypertension. However, there was evidence of shunting: the pulmonary to systemic output ratio was 2·8:1 (normal 1:1; greater than 1 indicates left-to-right shunting). We therefore concluded that the augmented CPAP had led to the development of his symptoms.
As proof of concept, we took arterial blood samples both at rest and at a positive pressure of 8 cm H2O: these showed that his arterial partial pressure of oxygen reduced from 15 to 11 kPa. We also did an echocardiogram with agitated saline while gradually increasing the positive pressure (0 cm H2O, 8 cm H2O, and 12 cm H2O; appendix). The echocardiogram with the agitated saline clearly showed that the right-to-left shunting increased concomitantly with the CPAP increases: causing a reduction in arterial oxygen saturation. The patient had surgery to close the ASD and his difficulties resolved. The size of his right ventricle reduced and he was able to use his CPAP without any problems. Interestingly, at the time of the initial diagnosis of OSAS, the patient was found to have some dilatation of the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. An echocardiogram at that time might have resulted in earlier diagnosis of the ASD and earlier surgery.
Around 10% of congenital heart defects are ASDs. Clinically, a fixed, split second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur over the pulmonary valve can be heard; there may also be signs of right-sided heart failure. An electrocardiogram might show arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation and incomplete right bundle branch block with right—in the ostium secundum—or left—in the ostium primum—axis deviation. Late diagnosis of an ASD might lead to the development of Eisenmenger syndrome when surgery would be contraindicated (video).

input: A 61-year-old man presented with bilateral, asymptomatic, indurated non-pitting verrucous plaques and nodules on his extremities and buttocks. He was diagnosed with Graves' disease 20 years ago. The patient developed hypothyroidism secondary to radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid 4 years prior to presenting to us and received levothyroxine replacement therapy, after which he attained a sustained euthyroid state. However, he developed an asymptomatic rash over his extremities and buttock, which worsened gradually. On physical examination, several plaques that were leathery in texture and nodules were observed on his extremities and buttock (figure A–D). The results of thyroid-function tests were normal (free tri-iodothyronine [T3] 3·83 pg/mL, local reference 1·80–4·10; free thyroxine [T4] 1·23 ng/dL, local reference 0·81–1·89) except for a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 0·094 μIU/mL (local reference 0·38–4·34) and thyrotrophin receptor antibody concentration of 280·51 IU/L (local reference <13). Results of liver and kidney function tests were normal, and concentrations of calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, parathyroid hormone, urinary calcium, and urine phosphorus were within normal limits. On histological examination of skin lesion biopsy specimens stained with haematoxylin and eosin and alcian blue, abundant deposition of mucin was seen in the dermis (figure E, F). The final diagnosis according to the pathology report was myxedema. Despite application of potent topical corticosteroids, occlusive or compressive therapy, and multipoint subcutaneous injection of long-acting glucocorticoid, the skin lesions showed no obvious signs of remission after 6 months of treatment.Myxedema results from the accumulation in the dermis of glycosaminoglycan secreted by fibroblasts. The pathogenesis of the extrathyroidal manifestations of myxedema involves fibroblast activation and increased glycosaminoglycan production. Some studies postulate that the destruction of the thyroid gland by therapeutic drugs (especially iodine-131) results in the release of an antigen from thyroid cells that then stimulates the production of the thyrotrophin receptor antibody. The fibroblast in the orbital area and pretibial dermis share antigenic sites that underlie the autoimmune process that causes Graves' disease. Thereby crossreaction contributes to the development of myxedema occurring long after euthyroid status is achieved through treatment. Although myxedema does not seem to be related to the concentrations of T3 and T4, only four cases of euthyroid patients being diagnosed with myxedema have been reported in the literature.

A 58-year-old man attended our hospital with a 3-month history of bloody diarrhoea, proctalgia, arthralgia, and weight loss. The patient said that when his symptoms began, he had noticed a rash that had recently become more conspicuous. Accompanying the change in the rash, he said he had developed a high fever.3 weeks before we saw him, the patient had been admitted to the surgical ward for treatment of an anal fistula; he was given oral antibiotics and the fistula was surgically debrided.
Additionally, in his medical history, he had type 2 diabetes, arterial hypertension, and dyslipidaemia: he was prescribed metformin, gliclazide, enalapril, a thiazide diuretic, and simvastatin.
On examination, the patient looked unwell: he had pale mucous membranes and a temperature of 37·5°C. He had extensive, well-delineated, erythematous, and mildly tender plaques on the upper part of his back, arms, and hands (figure); he had multiple non-tender mouth ulcers. His abdomen was generally mildly tender with no specific area of localisation. We found no other atypicalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 7·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5), white blood cell count of 7·6 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0), neutrophil count of 6·0 × 109 per L (normal 2·0–7·0), and elevated acute phase reactants: ferritin concentration was 533 ng/mL (normal 25–400), erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 120 mm/h (normal 1–10), and C-reactive protein concentration was 15 mg/dL (normal <5).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed a rich, diffuse, predominantly neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate (figure). At colonoscopy we found multiple star-shaped ulcers scattered throughout the colon with areas of preserved mucosa between them (figure); histological analysis showed active chronic colitis with crypt inflammatory destruction and abscesses.
Considering the myriad of clinical and histopathological findings, we concluded that the patient had Crohn's disease with an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis—also known as Sweet's syndrome. The patient was given systemic corticosteroids and his gastrointestinal symptoms improved. His skin lesions significantly improved over the next 14 days, at which point he was started on adalimumab and allowed to go home.
Bloody stools and significant unintentional weight loss should raise the possibility of a serious systemic disease. The presence of a fever and skin lesions suggests an inflammatory, infectious, or paraneoplastic disorder. Mouth ulcers and a recent history of a perianal pathology—as seen in our patient—would suggest an inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's disease. Sweet's syndrome should be considered in the case of a fever and neutrophilic dermal nodular plaques with a neutrophilia.
Sweet's syndrome represents a group of autoinflammatory skin lesions or neutrophilic dermatoses, associated with a wide variety of infections, haematological malignancies, and autoimmune and inflammatory disorders. The concurrence of Sweet's syndrome and Crohn's disease is rare. And in reality, Sweet's syndrome should be considered as an extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease. Differentiation from the other inflammatory diseases accompanying Crohn's disease—including erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum—is key.

An 18-year-old man was referred to our hospital for a planned total hip replacement. He had a long history of reduced mobility and pain in his left hip because of a developmental bone disorder, dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica (DEH). The teenager was first suspected of having DEH following a consultation when he was 10 years old, but because of his young age, the medical team at the time decided to manage his condition conservatively. They were concerned a more interventionist approach was inappropriate at a young age as he had manageable symptoms and delaying hip replacement surgery would allow him to reach skeletal maturity.We recommended that he have the surgery because he had stopped growing and he had reached his maximum height. Also, investigations of his hip had shown that the joint had become progressively more damaged with the result that both his pain and mobility had become significantly worse. During the surgery, the head of the patient's femur was found to be extremely enlarged with concomitant stretching of the joint capsule and surrounding muscles. The implant required appropriate increased offset to avoid instability of the joint. Postoperatively, he was given analgesia and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis. He was also given information on precautions to take to minimise the risk of dislocating the hip joint while the capsule healed. Pleasingly, at follow-up, the patient reported an improvement in both his quality of life and mobility.
DEH is a rare childhood osteochondroma characterised by asymmetrical enlargement of the epiphyseal cartilage of the long bones, usually involving the lower limbs and most commonly occurring in the ankle region. Patients present with painless swelling on one side of the joint, a limitation of movement, angular deformity, regional muscle wasting, and occasionally recurrent locking of the joint.
When assessing any child presenting with chronic hip pain, a careful examination is mandatory with attention being paid to any deformity, asymmetry, and discrepancy between the length of the affected and unaffected limbs. It is also crucial to obtain images of the affected area. Even though it is rare—DEH, must be considered as a differential diagnosis in anyone presenting with chronic hip pain. Other important conditions to consider include Perthes disease, skeletal dysplasias, tumours, and septic and inflammatory disorders.
Assessment of the extent of a patient's pain and the need to wait until skeletal maturity is necessary as often the only feasible long-term solution is total hip replacement. In our case, the patient's pain leading up to surgery was still manageable conservatively and rushing to surgery would not have been beneficial in the long term.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of episodic pain, swelling, and redness of her left ear. She said the problem had re-occurred three to four times each year and had either resolved spontaneously or after she took non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which she had bought over the counter. She also reported infrequent episodes of redness of her eyes.In the 2 months before we saw her, she said she had been increasingly fatigued and that she had lost her appetite; in the week before presenting, she said she believed she had been passing less urine compared to before—though, of course, we could not verify this.
On examination, the patient had a raised blood pressure of 160/90 mm Hg. She had a markedly tender and inflamed left ear pinna—sparing the ear lobe, the auditory canal, and tympanic membrane, which were all normal (figure). No discharge or cervical lymphadenopathy was found, and the right ear, both eyes, and nose were unremarkable. She had 1+ bilateral pitting oedema in her legs: barely detectable impression when finger is pressed into the skin. A chest x-ray was normal.
Urinalysis showed ten to 20 dysmorphic erythrocytes per high power field and 1+ proteinuria. Laboratory investigations showed a serum creatinine concentration of 4·2 mg/dL (normal 0·51–0·95), which had increased from 0·9 mg/dL 1 year earlier. The patient's complement levels were normal, and an anti-nuclear antibody test was negative. However, she tested positive for both anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. A random plasma glucose concentration was 99 mg/dL (normal 70–140), and the patient's serum albumin concentration was 4·1 mg/dL (normal 3·4–5·4).
Histopathological examination of a sample taken from a biopsy of the patient's kidney showed active cellular crescents (figure) with a ruptured glomerular basement membrane (figure) and marked tubulointerstitial inflammation; no endocapillary proliferation or duplication of the glomerular basement membrane was found, and immunofluorescence staining was negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, and kappa and lambda light chains.
We diagnosed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with relapsing polychondritis.
2 days after admission, the patient's serum creatinine concentration rose to 5·6 mg/dL, which required seven sessions of plasmapheresis. She was given both oral cyclophosphamide at a dose of 2 mg per kg per day and intravenous methylprednisolone at a dose of 500 mg a day for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day, which induced clinical remission of the polychondritis and reduced the serum creatinine concentration to 2·4 mg/dL at day 25. After 4 months, the oral cyclophosphamide was replaced with azathioprine and the patient has not had any recurrence of the problems during 2 years of follow-up.
The differential diagnosis of a patient positive for anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and crescentic glomerulonephritis are microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis—the former was more likely in our patient because of the absence of asthma, peripheral neuropathy, and eosinophilia.
Relapsing polychondritis is a rare condition; renal involvement is unusual but has been reported in association with crescentic glomerulonephritis. Unlike isolated relapsing polychondritis—which may resolve either spontaneously or with steroids or NSAID monotherapy—renal involvement needs prompt investigation and immunosuppression to halt illness progression and prevent end-stage kidney disease (video).

A 37-year-old hairdresser presented to our hospital with pain and swelling in her left leg and pain in her lower back. The pain in her back, which she thought was muscular, began as an ache, at the same time as the pain started in her leg, 5 days before. On the day of admission, over a period of 3 h, the back pain had become much worse and her leg had rapidly become swollen and more painful. As a hairdresser, she said she was on her feet for several hours every working day. She had no medical history of note: she did not smoke and was otherwise fit and well. The woman took no medication except for a combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone and estradiol. On examination, the left leg—from the hip to the calf—was markedly swollen, painful, and cyanotic, consistent with a diagnosis of phlegmasia cerulea dolens. All pulses were palpable, and a sensory examination was normal; the lower part of her leg had a mottled, dusky appearance and a prolonged capillary refill time, and was cold to the touch.A full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 10·8 × 109 per L, and a thrombocyte count of 235 × 109 per L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 32 mm/h (normal 0–27). The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 29 mg/L (normal 0–1) and D-dimer concentration was 4·13 μg/mL (normal <0·5). Her international normalised ratio (INR) was 1·0, activated partial thromboplastin time was 25 s (normal 23–36), and fibrinogen concentration was 4·54 g/L (normal 2·0–4·3). Her serum electrolyte, urea, creatinine, and creatine kinase concentrations were all within the normal range.
An ultrasound scan of the patient's pelvis and upper leg showed deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the left common iliac vein that extended into the left common femoral vein. Other investigations including anti-thrombin, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin variant, and factor V Leiden were negative.
Using catheter-directed thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator the DVT was dissolved. However, conventional angiography to confirm that the clot had dissolved showed a persistent narrowing of the left common iliac vein at the level of the right common iliac artery (figure). We decided against stenting the stenotic iliac vein because her signs and symptoms had resolved and there was angiographic evidence of good collateral venous circulation (figure). The patient was started on warfarin with a target INR of 2·0–3·0.
Some degree of compression of the left common iliac vein between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the right common iliac artery is found in 22% of cadavers. Despite this, less than 5% of all left leg venous congestive disorders are attributable to severe compression of the left common iliac vein. May–Thurner syndrome—also known as iliac vein compression syndrome, a condition which gives patients discomfort and swelling of the left leg due to venous congestion—typically manifests in women in their thirties and forties with signs and symptoms of acute or chronic (or both) left leg venous congestion and DVT. Rarely—as may have happened in our patient—engorged epidural veins, acting as collaterals, can cause low lumbar nerve root compression and back pain. Interestingly, the compressed left common iliac vein forms a barrier against clot passage, thereby affording the patient some protection against pulmonary embolism. Risk of a DVT is further increased by conditions that raise intra-abdominal or thoracic pressures, pregnancy, pelvic obstruction, right heart failure, prolonged periods of bed rest, standing or sitting, hypercoagulable states, injection of irritating drugs via a left leg cannula, and the presence of a foreign body (eg, a left femoral vein catheter).
With regards to use of a stent to prevent narrowing of the iliac vein in patients with May–Thurner syndrome, the jury is still out; long-term anticoagulation is necessary even with stenting.

A 67-year-old woman, who had a 4-month history of a sudden onset of intermittent jerking movements with contortions of her head and right arm, attended our specialist unit. She had been seen earlier at another hospital where neuroimaging and electroencephalography were reported as normal. And after the patient was told the diagnosis was probably “psychogenic spells”, she sought a further consultation.She had no notable medical history; she was previously fit and well.
On examination, we found the patient to have paroxysmal retrocollis with rotational head movements accompanied by intermittent contractions of the platysma muscle. The movements were variable in amplitude and frequency, and briefly suppressed while she tried to perform complex finger tapping tasks; they occasionally synchronised to the frequency of finger tapping (video). During walking, the patient had a variable step length and width—astasia-abasia—and additional variations to her head movements (figure). She had an exaggerated response to the pull test. The patient's neurological examination was otherwise normal.
We did no laboratory investigations or imaging since the clinical presentation met the pillars of inconsistence and incongruence, rendering a definitive diagnosis of functional movement disorder (FMD). With explanation and reassurance that unrecognised maladaptive thoughts and beliefs can predispose to the development of FMD, the patient relayed to us that she had a diminished sense of self-worth; she was eager to address this issue with a cognitive behavioural therapist.
After 2 months of therapy, the patient's atypical movements ceased (video).
FMD is not a diagnosis of exclusion and can be established by clearly demonstrating the two clinical pillars of the disorder: inconsistency (or variability or distractibility) of the amplitude, distribution, and severity of the phenotype; and incongruence with the wide spectrum of manifestations of other neurological disorders.
Features suggestive of psychological difficulties are neither necessary nor sufficient to make the diagnosis. Historical details (eg, the way the condition started) are also unnecessary in concluding that the patient has FMD. Additionally, laboratory or neuroimaging investigations are not needed.
Finally, delivering and explaining the diagnosis to the patient is a critical step in the care pathway.
Patients receiving reassurance and a clear appreciation and understanding of FMD increases the possibility of successful resolution of symptoms and concordance with cognitive, physical, and occupational therapies.

Monozygotic twins, aged 2 years, were referred to our outpatient clinic because of a hairless area 2 cm ×  2 cm in a similar point on their occipital vertices (figure). The twin boys were born prematurely after 33 weeks and 3 days of gestation and it was initially thought that the hairless regions, which also had no skin cover, were caused by a fetal scalp electrode. The twins had otherwise developed normally, with no associated anomalies or syndromes, and the defects on their scalps had healed over with scar tissue. A detailed history was taken from the children's mother, who said that the pregnancy had been uncomplicated and that there was no history of skin conditions in the family. Notably, an ultrasound scan done at gestational week 8 showed an empty yolk sac which suggested that a third fetus had been present and was reabsorbed in utero.After considering the history and examining the lesions, we made a diagnosis of aplasia cutis congenita (ACC)—simply a condition with a congenital absence of skin. Vanishing twin syndrome, which perhaps in our case ought to be described as vanishing triplet syndrome—where usually twin fetuses convert to a singleton—is a rare but well recognised phenomenon that is associated with widespread and predominantly truncal ACC. Non-syndromic ACC of the scalp has been associated with a mutation in the ribosome biogenesis factor (BMS1) gene. The suspected mechanism by which this mutation produces ACC is through an increase in the p21 level, which has been linked to an inhibition of cell proliferation and the formation of scar tissue. Scalp ACC in twins is very rare and we found only two other reported cases after a literature search.
At first glance, the scalp defect is easily confused with other conditions causing areas of hair loss, such as alopecia areata or naevoid conditions. The absence of skin poses a slight risk of CNS infection or of sagittal sinus haemorrhage before the healing occurs. Otherwise, ACC is considered benign once the scalp defect has healed and as such does not require further treatment. Therapeutic options include conservative management or surgery for aesthetic purposes, larger defects, or underlying bone defects. Since this condition is very rare, physicians outside of the dermatological arena should not be chastised for missing this spot diagnosis.

A 45-year-old man was diagnosed with asymptomatic Wilson's disease at age 9 years after family screening due to a sibling with acute liver failure. He started on penicillamine and remained asymptomatic; however, he developed skin changes after 21 years of treatment (figure A, B), and his treatment was switched to zinc acetate as a precaution, since penicillamine can be linked to dermatological issues. The man later had a skin punch biopsy of his neck to confirm these changes as acquired cutis laxa (figure C). Despite the appearance of disease stability, with no apparent worsening of his skin changes and good adherence to zinc, he presented with liver decompensation within 4 years and restarted penicillamine. His liver synthetic function normalised after 12 months. During this period of treatment changes, there was no clear improvement or deterioration in his skin condition.10 years after restarting penicillamine, during regular surveillance with echocardiogram (as per our local protocol), mild aortic root dilatation—a complication that can occur with elastin-related or collagen-related conditions—was detected (figure D) and the patient was switched to trientine as a second-line treatment. He has only been on trientine for 6 months and we have not yet observed any visual improvement in his skin, worsening of his aortic root dilatation, or new cardiac issues.
Treatment for Wilson's disease has become more standardised since the introduction of international guidelines, with an increase in the number of patients on long-term treatment with penicillamine. The complications related to this treatment, such as proteinuria, are therefore going to be more commonly seen by clinicians. The most common side-effects of penicillamine are thrombocytopenia (usually seen soon after initiation) and proteinuria (a longer-term complication), with rashes being the most common dermatological side-effect.
A suggested mechanism for the development of cutis laxa is a shortage of copper for lysyl oxidase, which is a copper-dependent enzyme necessary for collagen crosslinking. This potential mechanism stresses the need to avoid overtreatment (which could lead to copper depletion) and the importance of regular treatment monitoring.
We highlight this case to draw attention to the complications of long-term penicillamine administration and the need for appropriate cardiac surveillance, early consideration of switching therapy if side-effects occur, and a better understanding of the mechanism behind these dermatological changes.

A 20-year-old man presented at our emergency department with a progressive painless paralysis of his right arm and right leg. The patient reported that difficulties began approximately 48 h before, while he was sleeping. He had no medical history.On examination, we found the patient to be well apart from a partial amnesic aphasia with hemiparesis on the right side.
MRI brain T2-weighted sequences showed a left periventricular tumefactive lesion without gadolinium (Gd) enhancement, one further periventricular lesion, three subcortical, and one in the medulla oblongata (figure). A patchy heterogeneous apparent diffusion coefficient restriction was found on diffusion-weighted imaging. MRI of the patient's spinal cord showed a non-enhancing lesion at C2 (figure).
Cerebrospinal fluid analyses reported mild pleocytosis with 12 cells (typical range 0–4) and positive unmatched oligoclonal bands.
Considering the findings together, we suspected a clinically isolated demyelinating syndrome and started intravenous high-dose (1000 mg) methylprednisolone for 5 days. However, as the patient's symptoms did not improve within 14 days, we carried out five cycles of plasmapheresis. Again, because of no improvement, another MRI brain was done, which showed an enlargement of the left periventricular lesion, but now, with marked Gd enhancement (figure). We then carried out a stereotactic brain biopsy—to exclude other causes, such as lymphoma—which showed inflammatory demyelination, compatible with multiple sclerosis (MS) (figure; appendix). The patient was given further intravenous high-dose (2000 mg) methylprednisolone for 5 days, which was then tapered off with oral methylprednisolone over the following 3 weeks. His condition improved within 14 days, and 2 months later, he was able to walk alone for a minimum of 500 m and had begun to write again. Notably, his aphasia had resolved completely. Finally, having excluded progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from samples obtained at biopsy, and having obtained a negative anti-JCV antibody result, we started the patient on natalizumab as maintenance therapy for tumefactive MS. He was allowed home after 3 months. At follow-up 2 years later, the patient was able to walk alone for a minimum of 3000 m and he had experienced no relapses.
Tumefactive lesions may be found in MS and acute disseminate encephalomyelitis; in MS, if present, both the initial presentation and radiological findings can lead to uncertainty of diagnosis, often requiring brain biopsy for confirmation.

The investigations showed a raised serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (406 U/L; normal <60) and a raised serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 99·20 μIU/mL (normal 0·27–4·20). The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0·67 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·70) and 1·5 pg/mL (normal 2·0–4·4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies—including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies—were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism—specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes—without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative—without detectable autoantibodies—and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1·5 μg/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone—posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges—the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).

input: A 15-year-old girl presented to our outpatient clinic with a 10-year history of two band-like atrophic grooves located on the left part of the forehead (figure A, B). Within the previous 2 years, the lesions had considerably progressed and resulted in a marked atrophy of subcutaneous tissue and bone structures on the left side of the face (figure C). There was no history of preceding trauma, but the patient had experienced several episodes of focal seizures and recurrent hemiplegic migraine in the past 6 months. Cerebral MRI showed a dense area of gliosis in the ipsilateral frontal region (figure D). Further physical examination showed no pathological findings. Laboratory tests, including screening for auto-antibodies, showed increased antinuclear antibody titres (1:2560 [normal value <1:160]) and a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 24 mg/L (normal value <5 mg/L). Extractable nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and Borrelia-specific antibodies were negative. On the basis of these findings, a diagnosis of bilateral linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” with transition into progressive facial hemiatrophy was made. We initiated a combination of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg for 3 consecutive days monthly) and low-dose methotrexate (10 mg per m2, resulting in 15 mg cumulative dose weekly) for a total of 6 months, followed by methotrexate monotherapy (15 mg weekly) for a further 6 months. Additionally, focal seizures were treated with carbamazepine (200 mg daily). This combination therapy prevented further progression of facial hemiatrophy. At age 22 years, the patient underwent autologous fat transplantation to correct her facial atrophy, with good cosmetic outcome (figure E).Progressive facial hemiatrophy, also known as Parry Romberg syndrome, is a rare craniofacial disease characterised by a slowly progressive atrophy of the facial skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and bone. Disease onset is typically within the first two decades of life, and it affects females more often than males. Progressive facial hemiatrophy might be associated with ipsilateral brain lesions, various neurological symptoms, and ophthalmological or oral complications. Linear scleroderma “en coup de sabre” and progressive facial hemiatrophy are considered to be two variants of localised scleroderma involving the frontoparietal face and skull. The prevalence of localised scleroderma ranges from 0·4 to 2·7 cases per 100 000 people and occurs 2–6 times more frequently in femals than in males. Linear subtypes, as shown here, mostly affect children aged between 2 and 14 years.

A 51-year-old woman with a 3-year history of painful hips presented to our mineral metabolism service having been referred by her general practitioner. The pain was present at rest and made worse by more vigorous movement; she used crutches to walk.Regarding her medical history, the patient had transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia intermedia and had been having regular red blood cell transfusions since she was 40 days old; she had a splenectomy aged 29 years. She reported that she was currently receiving two units of filtered red blood cells every 15 days; her mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin concentration for the past 12 months was between 9·5 and 10·0 g/dL. Genotypically, she had compound heterozygous mutations: intervening segments (IVS)-I–110 (G>A) and IVS-I–6 (T>C). Additionally, she had diabetes mellitus. Both the patient's parents had microcytic anaemia. She was being prescribed deferasirox, cholecalciferol, proton pump inhibitors, and ultralong acting insulin.
On examination we found her to be generally well; she had pain on flexion, internal rotation, and adduction of both hips that limited her range of movements.
Laboratory investigations done prior to our consultation showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·5 g/dL, haematocrit 27·5%, red blood cell count 3·26 × 1012 per L, serum iron concentration 208 μg/dL (normal range 60–170), and ferritin concentration 590 μg/L (normal range 24–336).
An x-ray of the patient's hips showed flattening of both the femoral heads—particularly apparent on the left hip—and a T2-weighted MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity with geodic cavities and marrow oedema, findings indicative of bilateral avascular necrosis of both hips. We recommended the patient have bilateral hip replacement but she did not want to have any surgical intervention. The patient continues to manage her pain with analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories.
Several skeletal abnormalities have been documented in β-thalassaemia and avascular necrosis of the head of the femur is quite rare. It is more commonly seen in patients with sickle cell disease—where the prevalence may be up to 22%. Even rarer is the finding—as seen in our patient—of bilateral osteonecrosis. Multiple microfractures, local hypoxia, and medullary expansion with possible arterial compression represent the most important pathophysiological mechanisms underlying skeletal necrosis.

A 61-year-old Japanese man with a history of cord-blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia 15 years previously, and chronic graft-versus-host disease of the skin, was admitted for bleeding due to a duodenal ulcer. A maintenance dose of 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. The patient was successfully treated with a combination of endoscopic clipping and proton-pump inhibitor. 7 days after the episode of gastrointestinal bleeding, the patient underwent repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopies, which showed multiple, newly developed, shallow ulcers in the oesophagus. Some of the lesions were circumscribed and discrete (figure).An oesophageal biopsy of the lesions was done, and histopathology of the oesophagus showed ballooning degeneration and multinucleated epithelial giant cells with eosinophilic intracellular inclusion bodies (figure). The biopsy samples showed neither malignancy nor graft-versus-host disease. Immunohistochemical staining of the specimens was also positive for herpes simplex virus, but negative for cytomegalovirus. On the basis of the gross and histopathological findings, herpes simplex oesophagitis was diagnosed. A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease presented with fatigue, malaise, dizziness, difficulty ambulating, diarrhoea, easy bruising, and a diffuse rash involving her extremities and trunk that had been present for several days. She explained that she had limited her diet to consist mostly of bread, rice, dumplings, and the occasional egg white to reduce the symptoms she suffered from her gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin—although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). Her laboratory results showed haemoglobin 8·3 mg/dL, haematocrit 25·2%, and a plasma vitamin C concentration of <5 μmol/L (normal range 23–50 μmol/L). Endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract and colonoscopy of the lower bowel did not find a source of bleeding.
A biopsy of the skin from her right lower leg showed a corkscrew shaped profile of the hair follicle, and histopathological examination showed follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging (figure). Taken together, the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings were consistent with a diagnosis of scurvy. Vitamin C must be obtained from dietary sources and it is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues for the synthesis of collagen. It is also important for immune system function and iron absorption. Scurvy rarely affects adults but may be seen in some individuals with malnutrition or malabsorption. Signs and symptoms usually occur by the third month of inadequate consumption, and treatment is with vitamin C supplementation. Early diagnosis and treatment of scurvy can be life-saving, so recognition of the physical findings is important. This patient was given intravenous vitamin C followed by daily oral supplementation and her symptoms resolved within a few weeks.

An 80-year-old man with a 1-week history of a red, swollen, and painful right leg presented to our emergency department. Additionally, he had reported long-term fatigue. A deep vein thrombosis was excluded after an ultrasound of his leg and he was found to have an infected ulcer caused by chronic venous insufficiency and an iron deficiency anaemia. The patient was referred to our clinic for further exploration of his anaemia and painful leg.He had previously had a coronary artery bypass graft; he had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; atherosclerosis with peripheral arterial occlusive disease and coronary artery disease; recurrent deep venous thromboses; and alcohol misuse.
Laboratory investigations had previously found a low haemoglobin concentration of 9·8 g/dL (typical range 13·7–17·7), a mean corpuscular volume of 91 fL (typical range 80–100), and a serum ferritin concentration of 17 μg/L (typical range 22–320).
On examination we found the patient to be pale but not acute unwell. He had ulcers and pitting oedema of both shins and soft respiratory sounds in both lung bases.
Ordinarily, we would have done a routine colonoscopy to investigate possible causes of the patient's anaemia. However, considering the patient's general health and the likelihood of proceeding to surgery being low, we decided to manage the case conservatively.
An abdominal CT showed an unexplained lesion about 6·1 cm in length, located near the xiphoid, ventral to the liver (figure). No other atypical findings were seen. On review of a previous scan, done 4 years earlier, we found that the lesion had been present for some time and that it had increased in size.
Histopathological examination of a sample from a biopsy of the lesion showed lipocytes, megakaryocytes, erythroid precursors, and myeloid precursors: indicative of extramedullary haematopoiesis (EMH; figure).
Additional laboratory investigations ruled out monoclonal proliferation of plasma cells—no M-protein was detectable and no JAK2 gene mutation was found. We did not do a bone marrow aspiration, for the reason stated above regarding the colonoscopy.
After 2 weeks of treating his ulcers with clindamycin and 2 months of ferrous fumarate, his haemoglobin concentration was 17·7 g/dL and his shins had improved.
Considering all the patient's pathologies, we believe that the cause of the EMH was likely to be multifactorial: the chronic ulcers and atherosclerosis, and the iron deficiency anaemia.
EMH is the expansion and differentiation of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells outside the bone marrow as a compensatory mechanism for ineffective haematopoiesis. In adults, EMH typically occurs in the presence of myeloproliferative malignancies. That it is also associated with other conditions—including thalassemia—is well appreciated.
Sites commonly affected are the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes; paravertebral areas, heart, chest, thymus, kidney, adrenal gland, prostate, pleura, nerves in the skin and spinal canal may be involved, but less frequently. On discovering a site of EMH, extensive investigations should be made to find the cause; appropriate treatment can then be started.
EMH in unusual locations—as seen in our patient—needs regular monitoring, and in selected cases where the lesion is causing local symptoms, surgical resection might be considered; not a realistic possibility in this case.

A 47-year-old woman presented to our institution with a 1-month history of swelling and a painless skin plaque on her left breast. 6 years earlier, the patient had been treated for luminal A invasive ductal carcinoma in the superomedial quadrant of the left breast; she had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation therapy—a whole breast dose of 50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed—and oral tamoxifen. The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.
On physical examination, we found the patient was generally well; she had a 1 cm purple plaque on the inferolateral quadrant of her left breast, approximately 1·5 cm from the areola (figure).Breast ultrasound examination showed skin thickening, subcutaneous oedema, and a predominantly hypoechoic nonmass finding in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast with irregular borders, regional distribution, and central hypervascularity on power Doppler (figure). Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia—initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up—54 days after the first ultrasound examination—the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy—60 days after the first ultrasound examination—additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of the surgical specimen, which measured 9·0 cm × 7·0 cm X 6·0 cm and invaded the nipple, dermis, and parenchymal breast tissue, confirmed the diagnosis of post-radiation angiosarcoma. CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the operation and was allowed home 24 h later. At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5–6 years. About one in every 1000 patients treated with radiotherapy for breast cancer may be at risk of developing the condition, and global incidence is expected to rise as the number of patients undergoing breast-preserving surgery plus radiotherapy increases. Typically, the tumour arises within the skin and subcutaneous tissues previously included in the irradiation field—this is unlike primary breast angiosarcomas which usually originate deep within the breast parenchyma. Patients with post-radiation angiosarcomas may develop breast swelling, erythema, skin thickening, and painless erythematous patches or plaques in previously irradiated areas, as well as areas of yellowish discoloration on circumjacent skin which is related to haemoglobin degradation products. Lymph node involvement is uncommon. Imaging findings, when present, are often non-specific and include skin and trabecular thickening, developing asymmetry on mammogram, and solid, irregular masses on breast ultrasound examination.
Surgical excision with negative margins is considered the standard treatment; prognosis is poor even with complete tumour resection, with 5-year survival rates of about 40%.

A 64-year-old woman was referred to our department because of weakness and dizziness that had been troubling her for 3 weeks. She had a microcytic anaemia as noted by her primary care physician: her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·6 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 62·4 fL (normal range 77–95). She said she had never had a period and she did not know why; she had never received any treatment for this problem.Physical examination showed that the patient was short in stature (1·54 m), and that the fourth digit—ring finger—on her left hand (figure) and the fourth digits on both her feet were also noticeably short (figure). She was also partly deaf. According to her medical history, she had hypertension, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, scoliosis, and osteoporosis, and had a recent compression fracture of her L2 vertebra; she had been taking diclofenac 75 mg once or twice a day for several weeks, depending on the intensity of the pain in her back.
We confirmed the patient was iron deficient: her serum iron concentration was 3·4 μmol/L (normal range 10·7–32·2), transferrin saturation was 3% (normal range 16–45), and faecal occult blood (FOB) tests were positive. We did a gastroscopy, which showed an ulcer in the gastric antrum and erosions in the fornix; a colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. We started her on treatment with pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and 10 days later FOB tests were negative. Serology testing for coeliac disease was negative and there were no signs of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) at endoscopy.
Considering the patient's physical signs and medical history, we suspected that she had Turner syndrome. An x-ray of her hands clearly showed a shortened left fourth metacarpal (figure) and Madelung deformity—an abnormality arising from premature arrest of growth along the medial volar aspect of the distal radius—of her left wrist, both characteristic of Turner syndrome. The diagnosis was confirmed by karyotyping, which showed the patient to have a 45,X karyotype (figure). Interestingly, 2 weeks after admission, the patient's relatives presented us with a karyotyping report dated 1980, which also showed X monosomy. We believe that the endoscopic findings and improvement after treatment with the proton pump inhibitor indicate that gastric mucosa damage was responsible for our patient's anaemia. Further, we surmise chronic low levels of oestrogen—the result of many years of no treatment—resulted in her severe osteoporosis and back pains, and prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat the pain then caused the gastropathy and blood loss (video).
Turner syndrome is a rare condition in women and is characterised by complete or partial loss of one X chromosome. Patients are short in stature and have ovarian dysgenesis which leads to sexual infantilism, amenorrhoea, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and endocrine and metabolic disorders. They are at increased risk of autoimmune disorders. With regards to gastrointestinal diseases, the syndrome is associated with coeliac disease, IBD, and intestinal angiodysplasia—all of which can cause iron deficiency anaemia.
Best practice and care for Turner syndrome require a multidisciplinary approach and seeing the patient regularly throughout her life.

A 51-year-old woman attended our emergency department with a 3-day history of dyspnoea, fatigue, and cough; 11 days earlier she had the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination. On examination she was afebrile, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 98% (fraction of inspired O2 21%), blood pressure was 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate was 98 beats per min, and body-mass index was 31 kg/m2.Laboratory investigations showed a severe thrombocytopenia of 37 × 109 platelets per L; 3 days earlier it had been 178 × 109 per L (normal 140–440). Serum concentrations of D-dimer (>34 mg/dL; normal <0·5) and C-reactive protein were increased (42 mg/L; normal <0·5); prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen, creatinine, electrolytes, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and high-sensitivity troponin T were within normal range. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab was negative.
CT pulmonary angiography showed a central pulmonary embolism without right ventricular dysfunction (figure). Magnetic resonance venography showed venous thrombus formation in the left internal iliac vein—including the common iliac vein—with extension into the inferior vena cava (figure; appendix).
We started low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH) at half the therapeutic dose. The patient was admitted and empirically treated with dexamethasone 40 mg orally—we assumed an autoimmune process was responsible for the rapid platelet reduction. Other causes of thrombocytopenia were excluded (appendix).
After 3 days of glucocorticoid therapy, the patient's platelet concentration remained low and the fibrinogen levels dropped rapidly to below 50 mg/dL; factor XIII also dropped to 32% activity (normal >70%); the prothrombin time became unmeasurable. Plasma coagulation factor activities were normal for all other extrinsic and intrinsic coagulation factors—including von Willebrand factor.
Mixing the patient's plasma in a 1:1 ratio with standard human plasma showed a deficiency of fibrinogen and factor XIII; thrombelastography confirmed the result (for details see appendix).
LMWH was increased to a therapeutic dose leading to an anti-factor Xa activity of 0·5–1·0 IU/mL (therapeutic range 0·5–1·0).
On day 5, the patient developed pain in the left lower back and left gluteal region; CT venography showed an increase in the thrombus in the inferior vena cava. The LMWH dose was increased to obtain supratherapeutic anti-factor Xa activity (1·0–1·5 U/mL). On the following day, the pain had reduced.
Over the next 7 days, the platelet count and factor XIII activity increased; fibrinogen levels also started to increase after the platelet count reached 100 × 109 per L. 11 days after admission the platelet count was 173 × 109 per L, fibrinogen concentration was 228 mg/L, and factor XIII activity was 78% (appendix). Anticoagulation therapy was switched from LMWH to oral dabigatran 150 mg twice a day and on day 15 the patient was well and allowed home.
Activation of the coagulation system producing thromboses in the context of thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenaemia—as occurred in our patient—is similar to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and to that seen in critically ill COVID-19 patients (video).

A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with fevers and chills in December, 2014, and was admitted with a diagnosis of pneumonia. CT to exclude pulmonary embolus showed diffuse osseous lytic lesions, and he was also found to have anaemia and an IgG kappa monoclonal protein of 55·8 g/L on protein electrophoresis (a single band). After a bone marrow biopsy he was given a diagnosis of plasma cell myeloma and was treated with four cycles of CyBorD chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone) in preparation for an autologous stem cell transplantation.
The aspirate from the bone marrow sampling showed a substantial increase in plasma cells (figure). The bone marrow core biopsy sample showed a hypercellular marrow with increased plasma cells, estimated to occupy 80% of marrow cellularity by CD138 immunohistochemistry. We saw that the neoplastic plasma cells had two distinct immunophenotypes: one population expressed CD138, kappa, and CD56; the other expressed CD138, kappa, CD20, and CD79a. Morphological differences were visible on routine haematoxylin and eosin staining, with prominent nucleoli in the CD56 area (figure). We could not create a more extensive immunophenotype because of tissue limitations, and too few events were captured by flow cytometry to allow characterisation using this technique.

On examination, the patient had a distended jugular vein, a pulsatile liver, and prominent, pulsating facial veins (figure, video 1). An echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation that was caused by annular dilatation and this, in turn, had resulted in malcoaptation of the valve leaflets (video 2). The patient was also noted to have significant enlargement and dysfunction of the right ventricle, as well as diastolic septal shift, indicating volume overload of the right ventricle (video 2). Ventricularisation of the right atrial pressure tracing—with C-V waves that indicated severe tricuspid regurgitation—was seen during cardiac catheterisation. Despite treatment with intravenous ionotropes, the patient's right ventricular failure worsened and, sadly, he died in a hospice, 6 weeks after he first came to see us.Right ventricular failure after left ventricular assist device implantation is unfortunately common and results in significant morbidity and mortality. Renowned Scottish cardiologist Sir James Mackenzie was one of the first physicians to publish a detailed description of pulsation of the facial vein associated with tricuspid regurgitation, in 1892, and the phenomenon has been the subject of much debate since then. Transmission of atrial pulsations to the facial vein are usually prevented by venous valves present around the lower border of the mandible and in the jugular venous system.
