Her medical history was unremarkable apart from her reporting that she had recurrent tonsillitis as a child. Corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed no abnormalities, with normal pupillary reactions. However, slit lamp biomicroscopy and fundus examination in the right eye showed intra-retinal oedema with retinal whitening in the superior area (figure). Fluorescein angiography showed an arterial filling defect along the superotemporal arcade (figure). A diagnosis of right eye superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) was made. A cardiology review was sought as part of the mandatory systemic investigations required in such cases. Our cardiology colleagues reported that the patient's electrocardiogram was normal but that her echocardiogram showed moderate mitral stenosis. An analysis of her urine found no abnormalities. Her fasting blood glucose, blood cholesterol, and serum triglyceride concentrations were normal, and a full blood count showed values within the normal range. Also, both her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C-reactive protein concentration were normal. The patient was treated with acetyl salicylate 75 mg once a day and spironolactone 25 mg once a day. She was seen again 12 months later, and her visual fields had improved and she had no further problems.The incidence of retinal arterial obstruction in patients under the age of 30 years has been estimated at less than one in 50 000 outpatients. The causes of retinal arterial occlusion in young adults—different from those in older individuals—include systemic vasculitis, migraine, sickle-cell haemoglobinopathy, myeloproliferative disorders, hypercoagulable states, use of oral contraceptives, and intravenous drug abuse. Valvular heart disease—originating from rheumatic fever—remains an important cause of BRAO that should be borne in mind, although rates are declining in developed countries.

A 50-year-old man attended our specialised clinic reporting swelling, paraesthesia, discolouration, and fatigue in both arms while doing physical activity. The patient said the problem was particularly bad when lifting objects above his shoulders; his right side was worse than his left.Notably in his medical history, the patient, aged 32 years, was diagnosed with deep venous thrombosis in his left arm which developed after a period of strenuous physical activity; lifelong anticoagulant treatment was initiated at that time and he was switched to apixaban 3 months before we saw him. Also, aged 46 years, he had a further thrombosis in his right subclavian vein; it was successfully treated with thrombolysis followed by 2 years of fenprocoumon. Thrombophilia screening was negative, and a CT scan found no predisposing factors for thrombosis and no skeletal anomalies—including cervical ribs or anomalies of the clavicular bones. Additionally, no soft tissue abnormalities were identified. After the second episode, the treating physicians felt that both thromboses were primary—or spontaneous—since no trauma had been involved and the first episode had developed after vigorous activity.
Examination of the patient at our specialist centre found him to be fit and healthy looking; his heart rate was 81 beats per min and regular, and his blood pressure was 127/72 mm Hg. A cardiovascular examination found no murmurs or gallops and intact radial and ulnar pulses. Neurological examination was normal; we found no swelling, skin discolouration, or other evidence of venous obstruction at rest. The Eden test—or military brace test—provoked his complaints and both cephalic veins became distended.
An x-ray of the thoracic aperture showed no cervical ribs or bony anomalies of the first rib; venography in four positions showed no abnormalities at the costoclavicular junctions in the neutral position, abduction, or adduction. In a military attitude position, significant effacement of the veins was seen at the site of the pectoralis minor on both sides—indicating thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS; figure).
A 2-stage trans-axillary pectoral minor tenectomy was done and the patient immediately reported relief of his symptoms. Postoperative venography showed no further compression (appendix) and the anticoagulation was stopped. 1 year after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic—even during strenuous activities.
TOS disorders result from compression of either nerves, veins, or arteries in the thoracic outlet. Venous TOS is caused by repetitive extrinsic compression and resultant injury to the subclavian vein at the bony thoracic outlet. Symptoms in the arms are caused by intermittent positional obstruction without thrombosis—known as McCleery syndrome—or with acute or chronic thrombosis—known as effort thrombosis or Paget-von Schröetter syndrome. Compression of the subclavian vein usually occurs at the junction of the first rib and the clavicle: costoclavicular junction. Obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle at the retropectoralis space—as seen in our patient—is relatively rare.
Patients with positional intermittent subclavian vein obstruction will present with episodic arm discolouration and swelling, usually elicited by either exercise or arm elevation; venograms can be normal at rest. Investigation using venography—rather than CT or MRI—we believe, is preferable since it facilitates communication between the radiologist and patient making it easier to elicit symptoms, and at the same time, observing the compression. If dynamic positioning shows no compression at the costoclavicular junction, the possibility of obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle must be considered (video).

A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20·0 g/dL; normal 13·2–16·6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38–48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8–25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12–16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20·1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1–3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.
During follow-up over the past 10 years, the patient presented on two occasions reporting blurred vision, tinnitus, and tingling in his hands and feet—symptoms of hyperviscosity. He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.
Clubbing usually involves both the upper and lower limbs in congenital heart diseases. Differential clubbing, characterised by the involvement of the toes with sparing of the fingers, is a distinctive feature of PDA with reversed shunt from right to left: Eisenmenger syndrome.
Cyanosis and clubbing may also involve the left upper limb if the left subclavian artery arises distal to the PDA. The treatment of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, and bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, has been shown to have some beneficial effects: offering hope to patients—like ours—whose PDAs are inoperable (video).

A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea was referred to our lung disease clinic. The patient—who was originally from Turkey—had a significant cigarette smoking history but no relevant occupational exposures.Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest x-ray was normal and lung function testing showed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide: 72% predicted. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest demonstrated extensive septal thickening and ground glass abnormalities in a crazy-paving pattern (figure; appendix).
Differential diagnoses we considered at this stage included organising pneumonia, lymphangitic spread of a tumour, lipoid pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and atypical infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsies were performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was normal in appearance and no pathogens were identified. Transbronchial biopsy showed architecturally preserved alveoli filled with amorphous material positive for periodic acid-Schiff, granular material, and foamy alveolar macrophages (figure).
Immunohistochemistry showed surfactant protein B proprotein in the intra-alveolar material and cytoplasmic staining in the adjacent alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes (appendix). Surfactant protein C proprotein was also expressed in alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes but absent in the intra-alveolar material (appendix).
Taken together, the findings were consistent with a diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) syndrome. Serum concentration of antibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was raised at 33 μg/mL (normal <5), confirming the diagnosis. Over the subsequent 12 months, the patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and his pulmonary function tests declined. He is under consideration for whole lung lavage or inhaled recombinant GM-CSF therapy.
PAP is a rare syndrome characterised by alveolar surfactant accumulation resulting in progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Autoimmune PAP accounts for 90–95% of cases; notably dust exposure, infection, and myelodysplastic syndrome are among several secondary causes of PAP.
An important clinical feature of PAP is a discrepancy between the severity of chest CT findings and patients' symptoms—as seen in our patient whose symptoms were mild despite a markedly abnormal chest CT. input: In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per μL). White blood cell count and concentrations of creatine kinase were normal (52 units per L; reference range: 34–171 units per L). Nasopharyngeal exudate was negative for influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Symptomatic treatment with oral analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol 650 mg every 8 h, alternating every 4 h with dipyrone 575 mg every 8 h) was initiated, and the patient showed clinical improvement 4 days after admission. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient did not seek medical attention and was not evaluated by a physician until the 3-week follow-up. During this follow-up, the patient reported the fever and headache recurrence, and analysis indicated increased concentrations of inflammatory markers (14 mg/dL of C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm per h). The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A subsequent visceral arteriography showed multiple microaneurysms in the small arteries of the digestive visceral territory and both renal arteries, which suggested polyarteritis nodosa vasculitis (figure). Tests for antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV serological tests were negative. There was no evidence to suggest the involvement of other organs (five factor score=0). The patient received treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone bolus for 2 days (120 mg daily). The patient was discharged and received oral azathioprine (100 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 150 mg daily indefinitely) and a tapering regimen of oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 20 mg daily for 1 week, 1 week off, 10 mg daily for 2 weeks, alternate daily doses of 10 mg and 7·5 mg for 2 weeks, and 7·5 mg daily indefinitely). At the 3-week follow-up, fever, headache, and myalgia had resolved.Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare necrotising vasculitis of medium and small arteries, with substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Clinical features are highly variable; symptoms at onset are usually unspecific, and the differential diagnosis is often broad. Because the patient was admitted during the COVID-19 pandemic, the possibility of an infection with SARS-CoV-2 was initially considered; however, the poor clinical and analytical improvement prompted us to look for other causes of the symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Accurate diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa allowed for early initiation of immunosuppressive treatment.

An 18-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of repeated episodes of rectal bleeding. Over the preceding 5 months the patient had made 4 visits to our emergency room reporting bleeding from the rectum. The problem was not associated with any other symptoms and was self-limiting. Previously, fresh red blood had been found on digital rectal examination, with no other abnormalities; no haemorrhoids, fistulous tracts, or abscesses had been found, and the patient had normal tone of her anal sphincter.Laboratory tests found a typical haemoglobin concentration (14·6 g/dL) with no iron deficiency (82 μg/dL), and a normal ferritin concentration (87 ng/mL).
We carried out an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, to investigate possible causes of the patient's low vitamin B12, which showed no abnormalities. However, at colonoscopy—40 cm from the anal margin at the junction between the sigmoid colon and rectum—we found a large lesion with vascular malformations. Further examination was not possible because, we considered, the risk of bleeding was too high. Therefore, to accurately categorise the lesion, we did a CT angiogram, which showed a vascular abnormality in the wall of the sigmoid colon with vascular ectasia and phleboliths—indicative of a haemangioma-type lesion that would account for the patient's repeated, self-limiting history of bleeding (figure).
Following discussion with the patient about the pros and cons of surgery, we carried out a laparoscopic investigation which showed a large vascular lesion extending from the middle to the proximal part of the sigmoid colon. We proceeded to open surgical resection of the mass and completing a lateral terminal colorectal anastomosis. Notably during the operation, we found the haemangioma was 10·0 cm × 7·0 cm × 20·5 cm; the serosa was dilated, and multiple raised white congestive protuberances were seen.
Histopathological examination of a sample of a biopsy of the excised lesion confirmed it to be a cavernous haemangioma—present in the submucosa, muscularis propria, and subserous fat. No signs of malignancy were observed.
Haemangiomas are classified as capillary, cavernous, arteriovenous, venous, intramuscular, and synovial. They usually occur on the skin in infants but may infrequently develop in internal organs including the liver, brain, and—as in our patient—in the gut; approximately 80% of colonic haemangiomas are cavernous in type and capillary account for less than 10% of cases. Cavernous haemangiomas are most frequently accompanied by bleeding and anaemia. Rarely, they may cause obstruction, intussusception, and platelet sequestration.
Rectal bleeding may be caused by a wide range of pathologies including colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticular disease, haemorrhoids, and anal fissures. Rectal bleeding as a solitary symptom has a positive predictive value for colon cancer of 8% in patients aged over 50 years. Age may be a valuable clue in deciding upon the diagnosis, but it would be wise not to dismiss the possibility of colorectal malignancy in a young person.

On admission, a 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischaemia. Biomarkers of myocardial necrosis were negative. A portable chest radiograph and a bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed pathognomonic findings of acute type A aortic dissection (figure; videos). The patient underwent urgent repair of the aortic root. The patient survived the immediate postoperative course despite complications of haemodynamic instability, hypotension, and acute renal failure, but later succumbed to multiorgan failure.
Delayed presentation of acute aortic syndrome is plagued by high mortality and morbidity. The location of the intimal tear in acute type A aortic dissection is in the immediate vicinity of the sinuses of Valsalva 65% of the time. Transthoracic echocardiography is a valuable diagnostic tool in cases when more sensitive techniques (transoesophageal echocardiography, CT, magnetic resonance angiography) are not readily available or are impractical.

A 6-month-old infant was brought to our hospital by his parents because they were concerned that the child's head had been getting progressively larger and that he had been refusing feeds. The parents also said that their child had a fever and was vomiting; his problems had been getting worse over the previous 2 months. The infant had no history suggestive of congenital heart disease or immunosuppression, and he had not received any vaccinations. He was born by normal vaginal delivery, and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. The child had reached all the normal developmental milestones for age until the current problems began. On examination he was conscious but moderately malnourished and healed boils were seen over his scalp. His anterior fontanelle was tense and full, and his occipitofrontal circumference was 47 cm—between the 98th and the 99th percentiles. He was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38·9°C. Examination of his eyes found them to have a persistent downward gaze—known as the sun-setting sign—and his pupils were 4 mm in diameter and sluggishly reactive to light (figure). He had muscle weakness in his left arm and left leg, with power recorded as 1/5.A full blood count found a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL and a leucocytosis (12×109per μ per L). Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea, and creatine were normal. HIV testing with rapid diagnostic kits was negative. A CT of the infant's brain showed a huge right frontoparietal lesion and a smaller right parieto-occipital lesion: a ring around the outside of both hypodense lesions was enhanced by contrast. There was substantial midline shift and effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and compensatory dilatation of the contralateral occipital horn (figure).
We made a diagnosis of cerebral abscesses causing macrocephaly; the anaemia was corrected by a blood transfusion and the child's haemoglobin concentration was 12 g/dL when he went to the theatre.
During the operation we made burr holes in the right frontoparietal and parieto-occipital regions and drained 250 mL of purulent, yellowish fluid from both lesions; we irrigated the brain with normal saline and did intraoperative barbotage with ceftriaxone solution.
Microbiological cultures of the fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus that was sensitive to ceftriaxone: the infant was therefore commenced on ceftriaxone at a dose of 100 mg/kg per day, divided into two and given intravenously every 12 h for 6 weeks. We then changed the antibiotic to oral cefuroxime, which was given for a further 2 weeks. The infant remained in hospital during the entire time, firstly, to ensure compliance and, secondly, to reduce the possibility of recurrence. He made a very good recovery—the left hemiparesis resolved completely and all the features of raised intracranial pressure resolved. An ultrasound scan of the brain showed no residual abscess collection.
Brain abscesses in children are rare. Bacteria causing the infection include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and group A S aureus: the relative frequencies of the different causative organisms vary by geographical location. Predisposing factors for a child developing a brain abscess include malnutrition, low socioeconomic class, HIV infection, congenital heart disease, and being immunocompromised. Early detection and appropriate surgical intervention—including drainage if possible, as in our case—followed by long-term antibiotic treatment can lead to a successful outcome. Importantly, children who have been treated for the initial infection need long-term follow-up to monitor for sequelae such as hearing and visual loss, epilepsy, and motor and behavioural problems. Age remains an important factor in predicting outcome—the younger the patient, the more likely a successful result.

A space-occupying lesion (SOL) is any abnormal mass within the cranial cavity, such as a tumor, hematoma, or, as in this case, a large abscess. A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall—known as a scaphoid abdomen—was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·9 g/dL (normal range 9·5–14); serum sodium concentration was 138·5 mmol/L (normal range 136·0–145·0) and potassium concentration was 3·7 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries—as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. Clinicians assessing patients after traumatic injury should have a high index of suspicion for diaphragmatic hernia with attention paid to radiographic and chest auscultation findings to avoid complications of delayed diagnosis.
Road traffic crashes are the leading cause of death of children and young adults aged 5–29 years with an estimated 1·19 million deaths each year, according to a recent WHO report. About 92% of these road-related fatalities occur in low-income and middle-income countries, for which African countries take the greatest burden due to the young population. Resulting morbidities and disabilities lead to an average 4–5% loss of gross domestic product due to loss of productivity of those killed or disabled.
Uganda—according to WHO—ranks among those countries with the highest traffic death rates at 29 deaths per 100 000 people compared to 24·1 deaths per 100 000 in the African region and globally to 18·1 deaths per 100 000 people.
According to the Uganda police annual traffic report, mortality from road crashes was as high as 19·4% (4806 deaths of 24 728 casualties of road traffic accidents) in 2023. Collisions with pedestrians—as in our patient—constitute 20% of all traffic crashes and 37% of all those pedestrians die.

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a 1-year history of progressively worsening difficulties with walking, falls, a tremor, and erectile dysfunction. Additionally, he believed he had become more impulsive, anxious, and he reported feeling resentment towards others. The patient had no notable medical or family history.On examination we found him to be generally well; neurological evaluation showed a mixed cerebellar and sensory ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign. In addition, the patient had difficulty standing with both feet together, and walking during the tandem walk test (video).
Dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, as well as a bilateral postural and action tremor—further cerebellar signs—were noted. We also found the patient to have global areflexia and pallhypesthesia in both feet. Notably, during examination and interview, the patient made several out of place comments and jokes and laughed inappropriately. He scored 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment—he had completed 11 years of full-time education—but showed no impairment of daily functional activities.
MRI of his brain showed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with symmetrical middle cerebellar peduncle and periventricular hyperintensities, and diffuse corpus callosum thinning with hyperintensities (figure; appendix). Electrophysiological studies showed a sensory-motor polyneuropathy pattern with predominantly sensory involvement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, thyroid and parathyroid function tests, folate, vitamins B12 and E, cholesterol, ceruloplasmin, C-reactive protein concentration, and autoantibodies were all within typical range.
Considering the findings together, we proceeded to genetic testing for the fragile X syndrome, which showed 111 CGG trinucleotide repeats in the fragile X mental retardation 1 protein (FMR1) gene, confirming a diagnosis of fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
We explained the diagnosis and symptoms of the condition to the patient and he was managed with physiotherapy focusing upon gait and balance training and on prevention of falls; he received advice from an occupational therapist and a clinical geneticist.
Fragile X syndrome and FXTAS are caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide in the FMR1 gene, which is also known as the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) gene. A mutation in the FMR1 gene of more than 200 CGG trinucleotide repeats leads to the absence of the FMR1 mRNA protein and results in developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder—a condition referred to as fragile X syndrome. When a premutation occurs—with between 55 and 200 CGG repeats—the FMR1 gene expresses high levels of mRNA, which results in toxicity and consequently the neurodegenerative condition of FXTAS. Management involves symptomatic therapy: medications, psychological counselling, and rehabilitative treatments. Genetic counselling should be given to all individuals with FXTAS and family members.

A 31-year-old man with Wilson's disease presented with a pruritic rash across the neck of 12 months' duration. His disease had been well controlled on penicillamine (500 mg twice daily) with pyridoxine (25 mg daily) for many years. There had been no new medications, trauma, animal contact, or change in detergents, clothing, or environment before rash onset. Physical examination revealed two annular lesions on the ventral and posterior neck, which were well demarcated with serpiginous, raised borders and central clearing (figure, A and B). There were no other lesions present. Full blood count, liver function tests, and inflammatory markers were within normal limits aside from a chronically increased alkaline phosphatase concentration (179 U/L, reference range 40–130 U/L). Coeliac serology was negative. The rash had not resolved with previous empirical courses of systemic and topical antifungal medication for presumed dermatophyte infection (tinea corporis). A 2-mm punch biopsy of the rash was done and the histology results are shown (figure, C and D).Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is a rare complication of penicillamine therapy for Wilson's disease and might also be seen in association with systemic diseases such as Ehlers Danlos and Down's syndrome. It is a chronic dermatosis characterised by extrusion of elastic fibre aggregates through the epidermis. The exact mechanism of pencillamine-related elastosis perforans serpiginosa is unclear, but has been postulated to occur indirectly as a result of impairment of lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, which has an important role in dermal elastic fibre cross-linking, as well as directly through formation of complexes with elastic fibre precursors, leading to impaired elastic fibre maturation. The diagnosis is made clinically and histologically with the characteristic findings illustrated in the figures.
As seen in our case, this chronic dermatosis is often seen in the second decade of life, following prolonged use of penicillamine. The rash distribution is variable, involving the neck and upper limbs most commonly. Although regression is possible with cessation of penicillamine, scarring and atrophy could persist indefinitely. Misdiagnosis is common and continued use of penicillamine risks progression of rash and permanent scarring. In this case, penicillamine was changed to trientene as an alternative chelating agent to manage the Wilson's disease. Despite its similar mechanism of action to penicillamine, there have been no published case reports of trientene-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa to our knowledge. 4 weeks after cessation of penicillamine, the rash persisted unchanged.

input: A 33-year-old man was referred to our internal medicine department after an ophthalmic examination revealed a bilateral granulomatous anterior and intermediate uveitis with papillitis (figure A) associated with retinal dystrophy features (figure B). The patient had been experiencing decreased vision for several months and had a history of childhood-onset bilateral arthritis, involving proximal and distal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints. His sister, mother, and uncle were previously treated for idiopathic uveitis and papillitis. He reported recurrent headaches and anhidrosis. Physical examination revealed hand deformities (figure C) with nail dystrophy and melanonychia (figure D) and an enlarged spleen (20 cm). X-rays showed erosions of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints (figure E). Laboratory investigations found elevated C-reactive protein (86 mg/L, normal range <5 mg/L), but normal white blood cell counts (normal count, 6.48 g/L). Thorough investigation for infectious diseases and autoimmune biomarkers were negative. Because of the familial context and a recent observation of a similar phenotype, we did targeted sequencing of the ALPK1 gene, which encodes α kinase 1, in the patient and his sister. We found the heterozygous missense variant (p.Thr237Met) in the patient and his sister, which has previously been reported to cause retinal dystrophy, optic nerve oedema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and headache (ROSAH) syndrome. Treatment was started with intravenous tocilizumab at a dose of 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks. ALPK1 is a recently described intracellular pattern-recognition receptor, which senses metabolites of several bacteria. ROSAH syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease with a highly variable phenotype, including (in addition to the ROSAH-defining features) recurrent fever, cytopenias, dental and nail abnormalities, sicca syndrome, and meningeal inflammation on brain MRI. To date, about 60 people have been described as having the syndrome worldwide. The best treatment remains unknown, but biologics targeting tumour necrosis factor, interleukin (IL)-1, and IL-6 have shown efficacy in suppressing systemic inflammation. This large spectrum of inflammatory features can mimic Blau syndrome; however, a rash is common in this disease, whereas it has not been described in ROSAH syndrome.Rheumatologists should consider ROSAH syndrome in patients presenting childhood-onset arthritis with X-ray erosive changes and hand deformities in a context of a family history of eye disease.

A 37-year-old man living in northwest Ohio, USA, presented with a cough, haemoptysis, and weight loss, all observed for 2 months. The patient emigrated from Taiwan at the age of 3 years and now works in a parcel warehouse. He had no history of incarceration or travel outside of the USA.Chest x-ray and contrast-enhanced CT (appendix) showed a left upper lobe lesion with associated mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial biopsy with mycobacterial and fungal stains and cultures was negative, and histopathology showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. A four-drug regimen (daily standard weight-based dosing of rifampicin [600 mg], isoniazid [300 mg], ethambutol [1600 mg], and pyrazinamide [2000 mg]) was started for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis.
After completing 6 months of therapy for tuberculosis, the patient was readmitted to hospital, this time complaining of multiple tender, cutaneous lesions on his face, torso, and extremities; some were verrucous and others nodular (figure). He also had headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Haemogram results showed a white blood cell count of 22 000 cells per μL with 91% segmented neutrophils. An ELISA test for HIV was negative. The chest CT revealed near complete resolution of the lung lesion; however, a CT of the head and neck (appendix) showed numerous white matter ring-enhancing lesions bilaterally in the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and cerebellar hemispheres, as well as a retropharyngeal abscess.
Subcutaneous nodules were drained and histopathology showed broad-based, thick-walled budding yeast suggestive of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Urine antigen testing for B dermatitidis was positive, and fungal cultures from surgical specimens grew B dermatitidis after 1 week.
4 weeks of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day, followed by 12 months of oral voriconazole (300 mg twice daily), led to resolution of skin and brain lesions. Voriconazole has become one of the preferred options for oral stepdown when CNS drug penetration is desired. Disseminated cases of blastomycosis should include CNS imaging even in the absence of CNS-related symptoms. Diagnosis might require multiple testing modalities for improved sensitivity.

The skeleton of a human being buried over 1000 years ago, in the medieval archaeological site of Torre Velha, in north-eastern Portugal, was referred to us for analysis and investigation (appendix).On examination, we found the outstandingly well preserved skeleton of an adult who was likely to have been more than 25 years old at the time of death. The person was approximately 1·80 m tall. Notably, out of the six skeletons examined, where height could be ascertained, this individual was the tallest (appendix). Based on pelvic morphology and metric analysis of the skeleton, we concluded that the individual was a man. However, the bi-iliac width of our person was 289 mm, considerably larger than the average width previously reported for ancient Portuguese men (mean 261·8 mm; SD=13·4; Student's t test: t=22·6944; df=124; p<0·001). Additionally, the individual's teeth were worn asymmetrically, indicating probable malocclusion of the jaw and maxillary prognathism (figure; appendix). Bone densitometry analysis showed normal bone mineral density values (0·792–0·999 g/cm2).
Genetic analysis was undertaken using a variety of different methodologies—including the calculation of X chromosome to Y chromosome autosome ratios (0·902 and 0·298, respectively), X chromosome and Y chromosome dosages (approximately 2 and 1, respectively), and X chromosome heterozygosity (approximately 0·2). We also determined the Y chromosome haplogroup to be R1b-P310 (R1b1a1b1a1), a frequent western-European and pan-European lineage, in accordance with the individual's Iberian genetic ancestry (appendix).
Furthermore, using a novel Bayesian method, allowing us to probabilistically assign individuals to karyotypes based on the number of sequencing reads—or DNA fragments sequenced—mapping to the X, Y, or autosomal chromosomes, we concluded our individual's karyotype to be 47,XXY, and rejected models of contamination of XXY and XX or XY (figure; appendix). The closeness of the observed position of the studied individual and theoretical position for an XXY karyotype (figure) strongly agrees with our posterior probability of approximately 1 for this individual having a Klinefelter's syndrome karyotype. Considering the morphological findings—specifically the height, the bi-iliac width, the possible jaw malocclusion, and the maxillary prognathism—the genetic findings—indicating a karyotype of 47,XXY—we concluded that the studied individual had Klinefelter's syndrome.
The prevalence of Klinefelter's syndrome in the general population has previously been reported to be 0·1–0·2%, but many patients remain undiagnosed.
Typically, people with Klinefelter's syndrome are tall, have broad hips, sparse body hair, small testes, and gynaecomastia; they may have mandibular prognathism. Obesity, low glucose tolerance, and diabetes are observed, as well as osteoporosis because of androgen deficiency. Notably, the absence of osteoporosis in our case does not preclude a diagnosis of Klinefelter's syndrome; osteoporosis is only present in approximately 10–40% of cases. Genetically, about 80% of cases are 47,XXY.
DNA from osteological remains is often scarce, degraded, fragmented, and unsuitable for analysis using commonly available techniques for clinical diagnosis of chromosomal aneuploidies. To overcome these limitations, we have devised a novel Bayesian method, which, we believe, is a potentially efficient statistical way of analysing fragmented DNA from a variety of sources (eg, ancient DNA, cell-free DNA, and DNA from forensic cases).

A 58-year-old man with a 31-month history of seeing peoples’ faces as distorted and, in his words, appearing “demonic” visited our laboratory for assessment. The patient stated that the distortions—severely stretched features of the face, with deep grooves on the forehead, cheeks, and chin—were present on every person's face he encountered, but he reported no distortions when looking at objects, such as houses or cars. The patient said that even though faces were distorted, he was still able to recognise who they were. Notably, he reported no distortions when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper. The distortions were not accompanied by delusional beliefs about the identities of the people he encountered—such as his family or friends.
The patient had a history of bipolar affective disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Additionally, he had a significant head injury at the age of 43 years that led to hospitalisation. He also had possible carbon monoxide poisoning at the age of 55 years, which occurred 4 months prior to the onset of his distortion symptoms. He was not prescribed any medications. He reported no use of illicit substances.
On initial assessment, the patient was well and not distressed; he had some mild low back discomfort. The distortions were very distressing to him initially, he said, but he had become habituated to them. Neuropsychological testing indicated no obvious abnormal general cognitive function; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. He had no deficits of visual acuity (10/10 in both eyes) or colour vision (Ishira plates: 25/25; Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test: average discrimination). Computer-based face perception tests indicated mild impairment in recognition of facial identity but normal recognition of facial expression. No laboratory investigations were done at this stage.
Whole-brain T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI scans showed a round lesion—T1 dark and T2 bright—measuring approximately 1 cm, located on the superior aspect of the head of the left hippocampus, displacing it inferiorly about 3 mm; despite this, the internal anatomy of the left hippocampus was preserved. The impression from the neurologist was that the lesion was probably an arachnoid cyst in the left hippocampal head; other observations included normal ventricle size, unremarkable midline structures, clear paranasal sinuses, and mild cerebral atrophy.
At 1-year follow-up, a repeated MRI showed no change in the size of the cyst.
As the patient reported no distortion when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper, we asked him to compare an in-person face to a photograph of the face taken in the same room under identical lighting conditions. By alternating between observing the in-person face—perceived as distorted—and the photo on a computer screen—perceived as undistorted—he provided real-time feedback on the perceived differences. We then used image-editing software to modify each photo until it matched his in-person perception (figure).Based on the patient's description of his visual perception, the neuropsychological assessment, and the distortion visualisations, we concluded that he had prosopometamorphopsia.
Prosopometamorphopsia is a rare neurological disorder of visual perception in which faces appear distorted in shape, texture, position, or colour. In most cases, the distortions occur all the time, whether the patient sees the face in person, on a screen, or on paper, thus making it difficult for patients to assess the accuracy of illustrations depicting their perceptual abnormalities because the illustration itself will appear distorted.
Prosopometamorphopsia's aetiology is varied and can occur in the context of head trauma, cerebral infarction, epilepsy, migraine, and hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder. The disorder can also manifest without detectable structural brain changes.
Our patient's unusual phenomenology, combined with computer software, enabled us to generate photorealistic visualisations of the distortions he experienced. Such images, we believe, have not been generated before (video).

A 30-year-old white man with no ocular history presented to eye casualty in Sidcup in October, 2012, with bilateral central visual loss, following inhalation of poppers. On examination his visual acuity was 6/12 on the right and 6/18 in the left eye. Slit lamp biomicroscopy showed subtle macular changes in the form of yellow foveal spots (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography showed clear disruption of the foveal cone inner segment–outer segment layer (figure). At follow-up 6 months later, the patient's visual acuity and examination findings remained unchanged, despite cessation of poppers use.
Poppers (slang for various alkyl nitrite compounds) are commonly used in the gay community, for their ability to relax the anal sphincter and known psychoactive effects. Following changes to legislation in 2006, poppers' main ingredient, isobutyl nitrite, was substituted for isopropyl nitrite. Since then, there have been several reports of a new form of visual loss termed poppers maculopathy. The exact mechanism by which poppers cause damage to central photoreceptors is unknown, but there is a clear cause–effect relationship. Despite online warnings outlining the risks of poppers, the number of individuals presenting with associated visual loss is increasing. Fundoscopy findings can be very subtle, with more striking changes seen on optical coherence tomography. A 34-year-old man, from sub-Saharan Africa, was referred to our hospital for short stature, when he came to France, as an actor, to play the part of a child. The patient reported that at birth he required incubator support and that his growth was blunted from early childhood.At our first evaluation, his height was 137 cm, weight was 26·4 kg, and body-mass index 14 kg/m2. He had long extremities compared to his trunk and he had signs of hypogonadism—including small intrascrotal testes (0·5 mL; typical 12–30 in adult males), absent pubic and axillary hair, micro-penis (2 cm), and a high-pitched voice.
Hormone assays showed combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with low serum morning cortisol and undetectable dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphate with low adrenocorticotropin; low thyroxine and triiodothyronine; undetectable testosterone and oestradiol; low inhibin B and low gonadotrophins; low prolactin; and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 were both below detectable limits (appendix).
Brain MRI showed marked pituitary gland hypoplasia, absence of pituitary stalk and ectopic posterior hypophysis, and no extra-pituitary abnormalities.
The patient's bone age was 13 years, and knee MRI showed persistent growth plates at the distal femoral or proximal tibial epiphysis. Genetic testing did not identify pathogenic variants in any of the genes responsible for congenital hypopituitarism.
We commenced treatment with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and recombinant human growth hormone replacement for 2 months before the patient had to return to his country as his visa had expired; he was provided with growth hormone cartridges for an additional 3 months.
Figure Congenital hypopituitarism treated in adulthood
Show full caption
Figure viewer
The patient returned to France 3 years later; his height was 142 cm, but otherwise, his clinical state was unchanged. We commenced stepwise replacement with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, and gonadotropins for the next 4 years. His height increased to 161 cm—an increase of 24 cm—and he achieved normal pubertal development (appendix). During the increase in height, the patient developed scoliosis which necessitated surgical correction and an arthrodesis at T2-L1 (appendix).
At baseline, cardiac MRI showed a small heart—but well-proportioned to the patient's body size—with normal contractile function; hormone treatment resulted in linear, uniform growth of the heart with a progressive increase in ventricular mass and volume. Concomitant decrease in the extracellular space indicated that the cardiac growth resulted from cardiomyocyte correction of hypotrophy; the initial rapid decrease in extracellular space, after levothyroxine and hydrocortisone were started, was mostly attributed to resorption of myxoedematous infiltration, and possibly due to inflammation.
Growth hormone—given prior to puberty induction—transiently increased ventricular contractility to supraphysiologic values, with the ejection fraction reaching 78%; it normalised during gonadotrophin therapy. Left ventricular stroke volume increased proportionally compared to end-diastolic volume, reflecting the heart's ability to enhance its contractile strength in response to increased venous return—Frank-Starling law.
We further observed a uniform increase of the cross-sectional area of the patient's femoral muscles during treatment accompanied by a progressive decrease of intramuscular fat fraction. Growth hormone induced transient glucose intolerance, which resolved during further therapy.
Congenital hypopituitarism is usually diagnosed and treated during childhood or adolescence to correct blunted growth and lack of pubertal development. Rarely is hormone replacement initiated in adulthood, and results of such cases are limited. Regarding the heart, the capacity to generate cardiomyocytes during adult life has been the subject of much debate; cardiomyogenesis is minimal in healthy humans after birth. Metachronous heart growth—as seen in our patient—from size of a child to a normal adult, has not previously been reported. In conclusion, hormone replacement, administered gradually, in an adult patient with congenital hypopituitarism can safely induce heart growth normalisation proportionate to linear growth (video).

A 27-year-old man presented to an emergency department with vomiting and an altered mental state. He had a history of possible Gilbert's syndrome as a child and previous opiate use disorder, but with no evidence of recent use. He gave a family history of a maternal grandfather who had developed seizures during a hospital admission for asthma. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and physically active—including playing hockey. While in the emergency department he became combative and left the hospital against medical advice.Laboratory investigations taken just before he left showed a raised blood ammonia concentration of 155 μmol/L (normal 16–60).
4 days before attending the hospital, he had epidural injections of the corticosteroid triamcinolone at two spinal levels because of chronic back pain. Soon after the procedure, the patient reported a headache and feeling unwell.
The day after his presentation to an emergency department, the patient's father called 911 saying that the patient was behaving strangely and having violent outbursts; he also said that the day before, he and his son had an episode of vomiting after eating a takeaway meal.
When the patient attended the emergency department for the second time, he immediately had a seizure. He was intubated and transferred to our university hospital. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
On examination, the patient had bilateral, fixed, dilated pupils, and he made minimal response to physical stimulation.
Investigations showed that the ammonia concentration had increased further to 591 μmol/L; serum creatinine kinase concentration was 299 units per L (normal 20–200), aspartate aminotransferase 26 units per L (normal <40), alanine aminotransferase 65 units per L (normal <41), alkaline phosphatase 84 units per L (normal 40–129), and total bilirubin concentration was 3 mg/dL (normal <1·2), and screening for paracetamol, salicylates, valproic acid, and serum ethanol was negative.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed diffuse cerebral oedema with effacement of both lateral ventricles (figure).
Despite treatment, including intravenous 3% hypertonic saline, levocarnitine, lactulose, and mannitol, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and 3 days after he arrived at our hospital, he was pronounced brain dead.
Further investigations into the cause of death—including genetic testing for urea cycle disorders—showed a mutation indicative of X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. The patient's family members have been advised to have genetic screening.
The commonest cause of hyperammonaemia in adults is liver disease—specifically cirrhosis. However, congenital disorders—such as urea cycle defects—should also be considered, even later in life.
OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder and it can present at any age; late-onset disease is usually seen in heterozygous females. Adult-onset presentations can be triggered by infection, stress, fasting, surgery, increased protein intake, and medications—including glucocorticoids. Our case emphasises the need for timely recognition of unexplained life-threatening hyperammonaemia and the prompt employment of treatment with ammonia scavengers, arginine and citrulline supplements, and haemodialysis. Liver transplantation is also an option in the management of patients with severe urea cycle disorders.

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age –5·2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353·6 μmol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4–5 red blood cells per high power field).
On diagnostic evaluation, serum antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative and C3 and C4 complement protein concentrations were normal. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac–mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
Therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) was followed by oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks, gradually tapered to 5 mg/day over the next 16 weeks. The day after finishing the three methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg/m2 per dose) were started once a month for 6 months. Vasculitis-induced ischemia resulted in generalised myalgia, anuric acute kidney injury requiring maintenance haemodialysis, stage 2 hypertension that was controlled on concomitant therapy with five oral antihypertensive medications (amlodipine, 0·6 mg/kg per day; prazocin, 0·6 mg/kg per day; enalapril, 0·6 mg/kg per day; metoprolol, 3·0 mg/kg per day; and clonidine, 5·0 mcg/kg per day), and nervous system involvement with seizures requiring two oral antiseizure medications (initially phenytoin, 5·0 mg/kg per day; which was changed to levetiracetam, 20·0 mg/kg per day). During treatment initiation with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and the first cyclophosphamide pulse, mesenteric ischaemia deteriorated into gut perforation, requiring bowel resection and re-anastomosis. Post-operative peritonitis and septicaemia required intravenous broad-spectrum antimicrobials (renal-modified doses; piperacillin–tazobactam, 210 mg/kg per day; teicoplanin, 5 mg/kg per day; metronidazole, 30 mg/kg per day; and caspofungin, 50 mg/m2 per day) and intravenous vasopressors (adrenaline and noradrenaline, titrated to 1 μg/kg per min). The overall disease was severe, reflected by a Factor-Five Score of 3. Discharged under multidisciplinary follow-up, the patient was receiving oral prednisolone (0·5 mg/kg per day, on tapering), oral mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg/m2 per day), and maintenance haemodialysis (done locally) at the last teleconsultation.
Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20·7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves’ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100·0 pmol/L (typical range 12·0–22·0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36·0 pmol/L (typical range 3·1–6·8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3·5–77·0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10·01 μmol/L (typical range 0·35–1·60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0·4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1·2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone—a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis—or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80–100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan—with a density level above 120 HU—should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.

#### 1. Pharmacokinetics of Lipiodised Oil and Latency Period

**Relevant Medical Knowledge:**
Lipiodised oil (also known as ethiodized oil or Lipiodol) is an iodinated ethyl ester of poppyseed oil, containing a very high concentration of iodine (approximately 480 mg/mL). Unlike water-soluble iodinated contrast agents that are rapidly cleared by the kidneys within hours, lipiodised oil is highly lipophilic (fat-soluble). When used for embolization, it is retained locally within the target vessels and surrounding tissues. The oil is slowly broken down by tissue macrophages over a prolonged period, leading to a slow, sustained release of inorganic iodine into the systemic circulation. This creates a long-term "depot" effect, where the body is exposed to a significant iodine load for many months, and in some cases, for years.

This pharmacokinetic profile directly explains the 12-month latency period between the embolization procedure and the onset of thyrotoxicosis. A long delay is not only plausible but characteristic of such a long-acting, oil-based iodine source. The gradual, sustained release of iodine provided the necessary substrate for the patient's thyroid gland to progressively increase hormone production, eventually precipitating overt clinical thyrotoxicosis. This confirms that the embolization procedure is the most probable etiological event.

---

#### 2. Differentiating Thyrotoxicosis with Low Radioiodine Uptake

**Relevant Medical Knowledge:**
Thyrotoxicosis with low or near-absent radioiodine uptake indicates that the hyperthyroidism is not due to de novo hormone synthesis driven by TSH or TSH-receptor antibodies (as in Graves' disease). The main differential diagnoses include:
*   **Subacute de Quervain thyroiditis:** A destructive thyroiditis caused by a viral infection. It is characterized by the release of pre-formed hormone from damaged follicles. The **hallmark clinical features are severe neck pain**, which may radiate to the jaw or ears, fever, and a markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or C-reactive protein (CRP).
*   **Iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow effect):** This is caused by an excess iodine load in a patient with underlying thyroid autonomy (e.g., multinodular goiter). The iodine provides excess substrate for autonomous nodules to overproduce hormone. Patients are typically **euthyroid before exposure, have a non-tender goiter, and have no systemic signs of inflammation (normal CRP/ESR)**. The thyroid gland is saturated with non-radioactive iodine, which competitively blocks the uptake of the radioactive iodine tracer.
*   **Painless (Silent) Thyroiditis:** An autoimmune destructive process, clinically similar to subacute thyroiditis but without pain or inflammation.
*   **Thyrotoxicosis Factitia:** Ingestion of exogenous thyroid hormone.

**How This Helps the Diagnosis:**
This knowledge allows for a systematic exclusion of the other possibilities. The patient's presentation of a non-tender goiter, **complete absence of neck pain, and a normal C-reactive protein level** are fundamentally inconsistent with the diagnosis of Subacute de Quervain thyroiditis. This makes Iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis the most likely diagnosis, as all the clinical features align perfectly.

---

#### 3. Diagnostic Utility of Serum Thyroglobulin (Tg)

**Relevant Medical Knowledge:**
Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced exclusively within the thyroid gland and serves as the matrix for thyroid hormone synthesis. Its level in the blood reflects the functional mass and activity (or injury) of the thyroid gland.
*   **Elevated Tg:** Occurs in conditions where the thyroid is overstimulated (Graves' disease), inflamed/damaged (all forms of thyroiditis), or has an increased mass/turnover (goiter, iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis).
*   **Suppressed/Undetectable Tg:** This is the pathognomonic finding in **thyrotoxicosis factitia**. The ingestion of exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses pituitary TSH production, which in turn shuts down all activity in the patient's own thyroid gland, including the synthesis and release of thyroglobulin.

**How This Helps the Diagnosis:**

A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient gave no history of recent travel, previous abdominal surgery, or adverse reactions to any allergens. She had no past medical problems. However, 2 days before we saw her, the patient had a gastrointestinal endoscopy which found no abnormalities; gastroduodenal and colonic mucosal biopsies had also been reported as healthy.On examination we found the patient to be generally well; heart rate was 92 beats per min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%. She was afebrile. Her abdomen was tender and distended with bulging flanks and shifting dullness: indicative of ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis (19·54 × 109 per L; normal 4·5–11·0) associated with a significant eosinophilia of 8·94 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5), a raised IgE concentration (208 IU/mL; normal 1·5–144), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration (43 mg/L; normal <3·1). CA125 concentration was elevated (83 units/mL; normal 0–35); no other tumour marker was positive. Serum tryptase concentration was normal and tests screening for autoimmune diseases—including antinuclear antibodies for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma—found nothing abnormal.
A CT scan excluded any visceral lesions. A diagnostic paracentesis showed eosinophilic ascites (figure). Blood, stool, and ascites analyses, including specific serological examinations and cultures, excluded viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. That some parasitic infections, such as Strongyloides stercoralis, can be hard to diagnose based on one stool sample, led us to do repeated parasitological examinations of different stool samples, which all showed no positive results.
Lymphocytic and myeloproliferative forms of hypereosinophilic syndrome were excluded: a bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. Using RT-PCR, no FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was found, and T-cell-receptor gene rearrangement testing of the patient's peripheral blood was negative. A QuantiFERON-TB test was also negative.
We suspected a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, but to rule out any intra-abdominal neoplasm and to collect biopsies from the caecum serosa, we did a laparoscopy. Histopathological analysis of biopsy specimens confirmed our suspicions: significant eosinophilic infiltration with greater than 20 eosinophiles per high-power field; the small vessels were not involved, ruling out an associated vasculitis (figure). The patient was started on oral methylprednisolone and her symptoms rapidly improved; the serum eosinophilia returned to a typical level.
Three patterns of eosinophilic gastroenteritis are described: mucosal, mural, and serosal. Diagnosis of the serosal form is often considered a challenge as clinical and radiological presentations can be atypical. Likewise, histological findings can be misleading, as mucosal biopsies in the serosal form of eosinophilic gastroenteritis may appear normal, unlike those of the serosal layers which can confirm the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is usually made based on the combined biological, radiological, and histological findings. Finally, a good response to oral corticosteroids—as happened in our patient—adds weight to making a correct diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

A 28-year-old man was transferred to our hospital after he suddenly lost consciousness in the street. He had an initial diagnosis of opioid overdose. Further, because of respiratory depression, hypoxaemia, miosis, loss of consciousness, and an absence of focal neurological signs and symptoms, the patient was given progressively larger doses of naloxone until he regained consciousness and started breathing normally and spontaneously. He said he had been abusing heroin and so because of this, and the clinical presentation, he was transferred to a clinical toxicology ward for further management. During 12 h of observation, the patient had four further episodes of apnoea despite being given further doses of naloxone. He was initially given a bolus of 0·04 mg intravenously, which was titrated up until his breathing improved. At this point his respiration returned to normal, and he continued treatment with two-thirds of the effective bolus dose infused intravenously every hour. His respiration rate was then monitoried regularly.Recurring periods of apnoea, a need for increasingly larger doses of naloxone, and the history of abuse of unknown amounts of heroin concerned us. Was there an alternative explanation for the patient's presentation? We were specifically worried the patient may have been a so-called heroin body-packer, even though he said he was not. A plain abdominal x-ray showed several foreign bodies (figure). A spiral CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without oral contrast further showed multiple, hyperdense, foreign bodies in the distal section of the oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, and colon (figure). The patient was immediately taken to surgery because of signs of gastrointestinal obstruction, the large number of packets seen on the CT scan, the gradual loss of consciousness, and the risk of packets being broken by a nasogastric tube during a whole bowel irrigation. A total of 82 packets containing heroin—including five that the patient vomited up while being transferred to the operating theatre—were retrieved from the stomach and bowels following total gastrotomy. Each packet weighed 20 g—confirmed by a Drug Enforcement Agency officer—and was encased in two condoms. The patient was later arrested by the police after making a full recovery and being discharged from hospital. We do not know the outcome of any legal proceedings involving the patient. However, under Iranian law, it is illegal to possess, transport, and be involved in the trade of narcotics; punishment can be up to 15 years of imprisonment, and in some cases, the offender is sentenced to death.
In cases of heroin overdose, if respiratory depression is not reversed following repeated intravenous bolus doses of naloxone—a total of 10–12 mg of naloxone can be given as intravenous boluses—then it is not recommended to set up an intravenous infusion.

input: A 14-year-old boy with early-onset guttate psoriasis vulgaris presented at our clinic with several reddish-purple, horizontal streaks on the distal part of his shins. Previously, he had been treated with narrow-band ultraviolet B, topical corticosteroids ranging from mild (hydrocortisone 17-butyrate cream 1 mg/g) to moderate (mometasone furoate cream 1 mg/g and betamethasone valerate ointment 1 mg/g), and tacrolimus ointment 1 mg/g—but the response to treatment was not long lasting. The family consulted a licensed practitioner of traditional Chinese medicine who prescribed a so-called herbal cream (figure). The patient applied the cream topically on the psoriatic lesions twice a day. After 9 months of doing this, he developed a new rash on his shins that was later confirmed to be striae distensae (figure). We suspected that the cause was exposure to a corticosteroid—but the patient had not been using a corticosteroid either topically or systemically during this time. The so-called herbal cream was suspected as a possible source; however, the content label only listed herbal ingredients including Chinese sumac, Sophora flavescens, Stemona tuberosa Lour. Nevertheless, the location of the striae was very unusual, and as a simple test, the herbal cream was applied on the upper arm of the senior physician; after 12 h, a strong vasoconstriction effect was seen (figure), which further raised our suspicion that the cream contained a corticosteroid. We therefore sent it for analysis at the Department of Official Medicines Control Laboratory, Swedish Medical Products Agency, Uppsala, Sweden. The laboratory used liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance, and reported that the cream contained both a potent corticosteroid (0·065% clobetasol propionate) and the antifungals ketoconazole and miconazole. We then reported this herbal product to the Danish Medicines Agency to ensure that it was dealt with appropriately.Prolonged exposure to traditional herbal creams or ointments resulting in cutaneous striae has previously been reported, and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has warned about a so-called natural Chinese herbal remedy—Yiganerjing Cream—containing the same ingredients as in our case. Furthermore, the hazards and adverse effects of herbal products are not confined to dermatology. The under-regulation of medicinal products is widespread, and the consequences of patients using such substances can be seen in clinics from all specialities. Patients who fail to respond adequately to conventional treatments often seek alternative treatment and as a result might expose themselves to potentially harmful agents. The importance of being vigilant when seeing patients taking and using herbal creams and remedies remains key to reaching the correct diagnosis. With such substances being freely available over the internet, the problem is likely to worsen.

A 72-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden onset crampy, generalised abdominal pain. She had a history of peptic ulcer disease, chronic constipation, and heavy smoking. She was tachycardic and febrile, and had generalised peritonism. Her white cell count was 13·6 × 109 cells per L. CT showed pneumoperitoneum in the upper abdomen and pelvic free fluid without oral contrast extravasation (figure A, B). There was faecal loading without features of mechanical obstruction.The patient was thought to have a perforated peptic ulcer and was booked for emergency surgery. Diagnostic laparoscopy, however, revealed faeculent peritonitis and a sigmoid colonic perforation (figure C). Extensive laparoscopic washout, sigmoid colectomy, and colostomy formation were done. Postoperatively, the patient had no major complications. She underwent successful reversal of her stoma 9 months later.
Histopathology assessment showed an 11 mm, full-thickness, rounded antimesenteric defect with no evidence of diverticular disease or a malignant process. The diagnosis was consistent with stercoral perforation. Subsequent colonoscopy confirmed the absence of diverticula and malignancy in the remaining colon and rectum.
Approximately 15% of the population have constipation, although most improve with lifestyle measures and aperients. However, a rare and unusual life-threatening complication of chronic constipation is stercoral perforation. Stercoral perforation is the reported cause of 3·4% of colonic perforations. The pathology is characterised by an antimesenteric, round colonic perforation larger than 10 mm, faecal contamination exuding through the perforation, necrosis, and an inflammatory reaction around the perforation in the absence of tumours, diverticular disease, and trauma. Risk factors for stercoral perforation in patients with chronic constipation include older age (median age 62 years) and smoking. Stercoral perforation has a high mortality of approximately 30–40% and is a devastating sequela of chronic constipation. Many clinicians are sceptical of the diagnosis of stercoral perforation, citing other predisposing bowel pathology, such as diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancy, as the main pathology, with inspissated stool as a disease-modifier. However, this case suggests that stercoral perforation is a true entity independent of other disease processes.
