A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38°C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A–C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11·5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0·5 × 106/L, and platelet count 20 × 109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.

A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0·5–1·0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a previously described macrocytosis—were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF—collected prior to initiation of the treatments—was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations—day 34, 511·5 pg/mL (99·995 percentile); day 233, 25·4 pg/mL (97·20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants—as in our case—causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results—often available only after a significant length of time—should not delay treatment initiation.

A 74-year-old woman with a 3-month history of general malaise and loss of appetite was referred to our unit for investigation of hyperviscosity syndrome. The patient had initially attended her local hospital reporting cyanosis and mild oedema of the toes on both her feet. She also had splenomegaly and polyclonal gammopathy: IgG concentration was 3320 mg/dL (typical range 861–1747), IgA was 508 mg/dL (typical range 93–393), and IgM 1648 mg/dL (typical range 50–269). The progressive hyperviscosity of the patient's blood specimens made further testing difficult, hence the referral to our hospital.
On examination she was generally well; neurologically she had no abnormalities, and a visual examination was within normal limits. The patient reported a 3-month history of episodic bleeding from haemorrhoids.
Laboratory investigations showed complement C3 serum concentration of 68 mg/dL (normal range 80–140), CH50 19·5 U/mL (normal range 30–45), and rheumatoid factor 21480 IU/mL (normal <15).
Plasma exchange was initiated, before which the patient tested positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1b. Before and after plasma exchanges, several Ouchterlony double immunodiffusion assays found no precipitation: negative results. Likewise, a skin biopsy showed inconclusive evidence of vasculitis.
However, based on our clinical suspicion of cryoglobulinemia due to HCV, and after consultation with the laboratory department, we did a visual screening test to see if we could find evidence of cryo-precipitation. We showed the patient's serum formed into a gel when cooled to 4°C; the process reversed upon rewarming (figure). Polyclonal IgG and IgM-λ-type M-proteins were detected from the gel using an immunofixation method.We diagnosed hyperviscosity syndrome caused by type II cryoglobulinemia secondary to HCV; treatment with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir achieved a sustained virological response.
3 months later, the patient developed cryoglobulinemia-induced renal impairment; electron microscopy of a sample of a kidney biopsy showed immune complex deposition in the sub mesangial region. Prednisolone therapy was initiated at 40 mg per day and tapered down following improvement of renal function to 5 mg per day.
Hyperviscosity syndrome is a rare manifestation of HCV-related cryoglobulinemia that can cause a wide spectrum of complications, including purpuric eruptions and renal failure. Cryoglobulinemia should still be considered as a differential diagnosis for unexplained hyperviscosity syndrome for the following reasons: firstly, often there is no correlation between the cryoglobulin level and disease severity; secondly, low concentrations of cryoglobulin may form a gel rather than precipitate; and thirdly, the concentration of cryoglobulin in type I and type II cryoglobulinemia is relatively low.
If cryoglobulinemia is suspected clinically, but not shown through typical laboratory investigations, a visual screening exercise looking for evidence of cryo-precipitation with reversible gel formation upon cooling and rewarming of the patient's serum may be helpful.

A 60-year old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of a painful, swollen left knee and a fever. She had a medical history of osteoarthritis, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia.On examination she looked unwell; she was tachycardic (heart rate 104 beats per min) and febrile (temperature 39·1°C). She had an effusion on her left knee.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 90 × 109 per L and white blood cell count was 5·1 × 109 per L, but with 6% blasts—confirmed on blood smear. 7 months earlier the patient's blood tests had been normal. Analysis of fluid obtained from arthrocentesis was consistent with pseudogout. An infection screen was negative. However, given the fever with functional neutropenia, we decided to commence her on broad spectrum antibiotics.
Bone marrow examination showed 20–25% blasts and morphology consistent with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with myelodysplasia-related changes (figure). Flow cytometry dot plots of the marrow aspirate showed approximately 21% CD34+ and CD117+ myeloblasts (figure). The patient's karyotype was complex—among several abnormalities it included monosomy of chromosome 17 (appendix). Additionally, a pathogenic mutation of the TP53 gene with a variable allele frequency of 64% was detected by next generation DNA sequencing using a 49 gene panel.
Given the patient's comorbidities, her unfit physical state, the complex karyotype, and the TP53 mutation, it was decided, after discussion with her, to try a combination of the hypomethylating agent—azacitidine—and the oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax. The patient developed multiple life-threatening events over subsequent weeks including atrial fibrillation, confusion, and renal failure without tumour lysis. After discussion of options, the family opted for comfort measures and the patient was transferred for care in a hospice and died 6 days later.
Among older patients—especially those with adverse genetic findings—AML is often resistant to chemotherapy and long-term survival rates remain low at 10%. Traditionally, treatment involves intensive chemotherapy followed by allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for fit patients. However, most older AML patients are unfit for curative-intent therapy and receive palliative lower intensity regimens. Oral inhibitors of mutant IDH1, IDH2, and FLT3 proteins—found in approximately half of AML patients—are now approved treatments in some countries. In addition to azacitidine with venetoclax, various other combinations have shown improved survival in subpopulations of older AML patients; none of these strategies, however, have been particularly successful in patients with TP53 mutations (appendix; video).

A 39-year-old woman was transferred to our neurosurgical service following a fall and development of a progressive quadriparesis over the previous 24 h.The patient had a history of uncontrolled type 1 diabetes and chronic pancreatitis associated with alcohol and benzodiazepine dependence.
On examination, we found her to be fully conscious, afebrile, with a low body-mass index (11 kg/m2). She had motor power on the Medical Research Council scale of grade 3 in her left arm and 0 in all other limbs. The patient had a C3 sensory level and all tendon reflexes were absent. She had reduced anal tone and had to be catheterised because of urinary retention. She had no neck stiffness or other signs of meningism.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 31·3 × 109 per L (normal 4·0–10·0) and increased C-reactive protein concentration of 29 mg/L (normal 0–10), serum sodium concentration was 124 mmol/L (normal 133–146), and blood glucose concentration was 31·49 mmol/L (4·0–5·4). We found no ketones in her urine. We corrected the patient's metabolic abnormalities.
CT of the brain and cervical spine showed no abnormalities, but MRI demonstrated a swollen, oedematous spinal cord with T2 hyperintensities from the craniovertebral junction to the conus with patchy enhancement (figure; appendix). T2 sagittal images of the lumbar spine showed a vertical fluid level at the lumbosacral junction: sediment sign (figure).
Shortly after admission, the patient deteriorated: she had respiratory failure and an aspiration pneumonitis requiring endotracheal intubation and prone ventilation. She was started on high dose dexamethasone because the diagnosis was uncertain and the acute swelling of the spinal cord.
The sediment sign on the MRI prompted an urgent lumbar puncture in the prone position—despite her unstable condition. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was cloudy, contained 1530 white blood cells per mm3 (90% polymorphs and no malignant cells), protein was 11·35 g/L (normal 0·18–0·58), glucose was less than 50% of serum glucose levels and lactate concentration was 12·2 mmol/L. The Gram stain was negative, and cultures grew Streptococcus constellatus.
With respiratory support for 2 weeks and intravenous antibiotics for 6 weeks, the patient made satisfactory clinical improvement: her motor power improved to good functional use on her right side, but she remained hemiparetic on her left. She was then transferred for neurorehabilitation at our National Spinal Injuries Unit. T2-weighted MRI at 3 months showed resolution of the swelling of the spinal cord and disappearance of the sediment sign (appendix).
Extensive spinal cord myelitis is uncommon in bacterial meningitis. The lumbar sediment sign has been described in patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage and occurs because of the layering of altered blood products within the CSF at the lumbosacral junction. It has not been described in meningitis—although a similar layering of debris maybe seen in the occipital horns of patients with ventriculitis due to the combination of proteinaceous and necrotic material within the CSF. We postulate that the mechanism of production of lumbar sedimentation in our case is similar: the vertical fluid level was accounted for by the patient's position in the scanner. In the absence of classic features of meningitis—as in our case—the presence of a lumbar sediment sign raised the suspicion of meningitis, and directed specific investigations and appropriate treatment.

On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; microscopy of a sample of fresh urine sediment showed multiple amorphous ovoid crystals (figure). Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, glucose and lipid metabolism, liver function tests, muscle enzymes, parathyroid and thyroid function tests, and inflammatory and immunological markers—found no abnormalities suggestive of primary or secondary glomerular diseases. Additionally, despite renal impairment, the patient had profound hypouricemia (serum uric acid concentration <0·5 mg/dL; typical range in an adult post-menopausal woman is 3·4–7·0).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed two normal kidneys without nephro-urolithiasis.
Urinary excretion of uric acid was abnormally low (<3 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 443–695); urinary excretion of hypoxanthine was slightly elevated (16 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 7–13); and urinary excretion of xanthine was high (135 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 9–14); indicating a possible diagnosis of either type I or type II xanthinuria. Molecular genetic sequencing found two mutations in the XDH gene on chromosome 2, which encodes for the enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase (OMIM 278300: heterozygous mutations c.3847C>T [p.Arg1283*] and c.3520-69_*3432delinsCAGTCGCT); no mutations were found in the MOCOS gene on chromosome 18, which encodes for molybdenum cofactor sulferase, corroborating the diagnosis of hereditary xanthinuria type I.
The patient was informed of the diagnosis and advised to follow a low-purine diet and drink plenty of fluids; she was counselled about possible genetic testing of her siblings.
At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was clinically well and her renal function was stable.
Hereditary xanthinuria is characterised by high levels of xanthine in the urine; uric acid is much reduced in the serum and urine—compared with gout where an increased concentration of serum urate (hyperuricaemia) is the important risk factor. Two clinically similar forms of xanthinuria are found: type I—our patient—where there is an isolated deficiency of xanthine dehydrogenase, and type II, with a deficiency of both xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase (appendix).
Xanthinuria may occur in molybdenum cofactor sulferase deficiency; type II xanthinuria is caused by a mutation in the MOCOS gene. Excess xanthine can accumulate in the kidneys and other tissues; in the kidneys it may lead to stones and in the muscles, pain and cramping. Apart from a low-purine diet and high fluid intake, which prevent xanthine accumulation, no specific therapies are available for this rare autosomal recessive disorder of purine metabolism. Symptoms may occur at any age, with approximately 50% of patients presenting with urinary tract infections, haematuria, renal colic, acute renal failure, crystalluria, or urolithiasis. Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with a poor prognosis. This type of lymphoma is rare outside Africa where is endemic. WHO classifies three variants of Burkitt's lymphoma: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated types. The endemic form develops most frequently in young people in Africa (children, adolescents, and young adults less than 40 years of age) and is associated with Epstein–Barr virus infection. It typically involves the mandible, maxilla, and abdomen. The sporadic form has no geographical predilection and develops most often in adults, most commonly presenting as an abdominal mass and rarely presenting in the orofacial region. Only a small subset of non-endemic Burkitt's lymphomas are Epstein–Barr virus positive. The immunodeficiency-related variant usually is associated with HIV infection and rarely involves the orofacial region.
Because Burkitt's lymphoma grows rapidly. timely diagnosis and treatment are important. A 28-year-old man from the rural area of Tamil Nadu attended our specialist hospital, complaining of multiple, copper-coloured patches on his skin, forehead, arms, and the front and back of his torso (figure). On examination he also had bilateral thickening of his ulnar and median nerves, without any functional impairment; multiple slit skin smear tests were positive for acid-fast bacilli in most of the patches on his body. We made a diagnosis of multibacillary, or lepromatous, leprosy, and started the patient on a 12-month course of multidrug therapy (MDT)—rifampicin 600 mg once a month, dapsone 100 mg daily, and clofazimine 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily. However, within a month, the patient developed raised erythematous lesions over the pre-existing skin patches (figure) as well as general constitutional symptoms including a fever and severe neuritis. A full blood count was normal and serological testing for any additional infections was negative. Biochemical investigations showed abnormal liver function tests (appendix). On the basis of these findings, we made a diagnosis of a severe type 1 leprosy reaction—also known as a reversal reaction—occurring alongside an adverse reaction to dapsone. The patchy, exfoliative dermatitis along with the swollen lips, fever, and hepatitis were key in reaching a diagnosis of an adverse reaction to dapsone. We stopped the MDT regimen, and started the patient on corticosteroids, beginning with a high dose and tapering over subsequent weeks—the hope was that the steroids would help both the adverse reaction to the dapsone and the reversal reaction. At follow-up visits, the patient showed improvement both clinically and biochemically, as indicated by the liver function tests (appendix). We restarted the MDT regimen but this time excluded the dapsone.5 months later the patient again showed signs of a type 1 leprosy reaction. We considered re-starting the dapsone—to see if the patient remained allergic to the drug and because it might have assisted in the treatment of the Mycobacterium leprae—but the patient was unwilling to try this. So he continued the MDT alone—rifampacin and clofazimine—without further treatment with corticosteroids as the neuritis was reasonably controlled by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and regular physiotherapy.
Leprosy has a wide range of presentations, from the lepromatous forms to the borderline forms (borderline-tuberculoid, mid-borderline, and borderline-lepromatous) to the tuberculoid forms. Type 1 or reversal reactions mostly occur in borderline-tuberculoid leprosy with a persistence of cell-mediated immunity. They are diagnosed when raised erythematous patches occur over pre-existing skin lesions in patients undergoing treatment. If the reaction is accompanied by fever, neuritis, or oedema of the hands or feet, it is categorised as a severe reaction and needs treatment with corticosteroids. Dapsone hypersensitivity affects a much smaller—and often unrecognised—population of patients: it is essentially an allergy with clinical features of a fever, skin rashes, mucosal involvement, lymphadenitis, and hepatitis. It carries a mortality of 9·9% and is probably often unrecognised because patients may not have routine blood tests in resource-poor settings. Laboratory findings show an eosinophilia, deranged liver function tests, and, rarely, renal failure. Patients with reversal reactions and hypersensitivity—as in our case—can be managed with the MDT regimen of rifampicin and clofazimine.

Her blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg; and her left radial pulse and left brachial pulse in the dorsalis pedis were absent, with carotid bruits heard on both sides. The patient tested negative for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and inherited thrombophilia. Pathergy and Mantoux tests were negative. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 60 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 91 mg/L. Microbial cultures from the ulcer and blood were negative. CT showed thickening and segmental dilatation of the ascending aorta, aortic arch, descending thoracic and abdominal aorta, and its major branches (figure 1B). Whole body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET showed 18F-FDG avid circumferential wall thickening of the whole aorta and its major branches, without any organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or lung involvement, suggesting active type V Takayasu arteritis. Skin biopsy revealed suppurative necrotising (predominantly neutrophilic) inflammation of the deep dermis (figure 1C), mixed inflammatory infiltrates, secondary vasculitis (lymphocytic), absence of granulomas, and testing for acid-fast bacilli was negative, consistent with a diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum. The patient was started on oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg) with monthly cyclophosphamide pulses (15 mg/kg) for 12 months. A marked improvement in symptoms and complete healing of the skin lesions with some scarring was seen after 6 months of therapy (figure 1D).Pyoderma gangrenosum is an uncommon manifestation of Takayasu arteritis reported in 1–30% of patients in various studies. The treatment of pyoderma consists primarily of corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy in severe or refractory cases. A man aged 57 years, who had had herpes zoster 10 years previously, visited our emergency room with a tingling ache in his right lower back. Physical examination revealed neither eruption nor trauma on the body surface. However, an abdominal wall protrusion was observed on his right side, especially while he was standing (figure). Abdominal imaging using contrasted computer tomography did not reveal any abnormalities.Abdominal muscle paralysis was considered as the possible diagnosis and 60 mg loxoprofen, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, was administered for his back pain once daily for 5 days. 5 days after the initial visit, dome-shaped papules with overlying small, dark-coloured vesicles appeared on his trunk and extremities, suggesting disseminated herpes zoster. The patient was treated with 1000 mg oral valacyclovir three times daily for 7 days, along with the same regimen of loxoprofen as already described. The vesicular papules dried up after 5 days and became brown scabs within a week. The protruding abdominal wall flattened within a month, and the patient's lower back pain gradually abated within a couple of months.
Herpes zoster is characterised by the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus, which causes a vesicular rash, typically restricted to a single dermatome. However, some patients develop disseminated herpes zoster; these patients are more likely to be immunosuppressed. It is rare for this condition to occur in an immunocompetent host, as it did in this case.
Post-herpetic abdominal pseudohernia is uncommon, occurring in 2% of patients with herpes zoster. Although pseudohernia should be suspected when a patient develops abdominal paresis coincident with or after a herpetic rash, abdominal paresis can also very rarely precede a rash. Awareness of this clinical condition might help physicians anticipate herpes zoster, allowing prompt treatment.

A 31-year-old HIV-positive man presented to the hospital on June 30, 2022, with a vesicular rash (figure A), perianal lesions, swollen inguinal lymph nodes, and arthralgia of the right knee. Under antiretroviral therapy, the HIV viral load was below the limit of detection, and his CD4+ T-cell count was 802 cells per μL. Given the rising number of monkeypox cases in Europe at that time and the patient's history of unprotected sexual contact with a man 1 week before symptom onset, an infection with monkeypox virus was suspected. Specimens from two different skin lesions yielded a positive PCR result (cycle threshold values of 20 and 21) for monkeypox virus. The patient was discharged and self-isolated.11 days later a follow-up examination was scheduled, the rash and lymphadenopathy had completely resolved, but a marked swelling of the right knee was noted (figure B). Arthrocentesis was performed, resulting in aspiration of 60 mL of cloudy synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count of 16 127 cells per μL with 88·5% mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and 11·5% neutrophil granulocytes. The synovial fluid PCR yielded a positive result for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 27). Laboratory test results were unremarkable apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein of 18 mg/L.
Bacterial cultures and broad-range PCR of synovial fluid, serological testing for rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and antinuclear antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, and PCR for Lyme disease were all negative. A second arthrocentesis was needed 8 days later due to reoccurrence of effusion. PCR of synovial fluid was again positive for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 33), whereas PCR of whole-blood was negative for monkeypox virus. MRI showed synovitis, joint effusion, and a marked oedema of the medial femoral condyle with a subchondral demarcation zone of 1 cm, compatible with the diagnosis of arthritis and osteomyelitis (figure C–E). Treatment with non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs led to improvement of arthralgia and swelling within 3 weeks.
Viruses are common triggers of arthritis, but viral bone infection has only rarely been reported. However, viral osteomyelitis was a typical complication of smallpox. Referred to as osteomyelitis variolosa, it affected 2–5% of children and 0·25–0·50% of all patients infected with smallpox. No cases of monkeypox-related arthritis or osteomyelitis have been described in the literature so far. Considering that variola virus and monkeypox virus are closely related, we believe that monkeypox virus might lead to arthritis and potentially osteomyelitis.

A 50-year-old woman attended our clinic reporting a slow-growing mass over the bridge of her nose; she said it had been present for approximately 6 months. She had earlier been prescribed antibiotics for a suspected complicated sinusitis.5 years before this presentation, the patient had been found to have mantle-cell lymphoma; she had received multiple systemic treatments—including rituximab-ibrutinib, rituximab-hyperfractionated cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and dexamethasone, and zanubrutinib for stage IV disease with known bone marrow and colon involvement, at the time of diagnosis.
On examination, we found the patient to have a firm, fixed, and painless soft tissue mass on her forehead; she had no pustules or fistulae or splenomegaly. She had small bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed a normal complete blood count and a normal lactate dehydrogenase concentration.
An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed widespread, albeit non-bulky, lymphomatous involvement with small lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm—including increased activity in the soft tissue inferior to the frontal bone of the skull and extending to the medial periorbital regions bilaterally (appendix). A cervical node biopsy confirmed relapsed CD20+, CD5+, CD10-, CD19+, and CyclinD1+ mantle-cell lymphoma with a Ki-67 of 40–50% (Ki-67s of greater than 30% predict a worse outcome) and indicated actively proliferating cells.
A brain MRI showed no evidence of intracranial lymphoma; nevertheless, it did show a homogeneously enhancing mass over the glabella (figure). We did not biopsy the glabellar mass—the patient did not give her consent for this procedure—but a bone marrow biopsy showed mantle-cell lymphoma involving approximately 20% of the biopsy without any aberrations of the TP53 gene. Flow cytometry confirmed a CD5+ monotypic B-cell population was present in approximately 17% of total events. Otherwise, the bone marrow was normocellular (40–50%) with trilineage haematopoiesis; chromosomal of the bone marrow showed normal karyotype (46XX). The patient underwent apheresis of T cells which, as expected, had no effect upon the glabellar mass as it continued to grow insidiously (figure). We therefore decided to give low-dose bridging radiation to the glabella while chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells were prepared; she then received anti-CD19 CAR T-cells which resulted in complete metabolic remission witnessed by no activity on 18F-FDG PET/CT staging 3 months after treatment.
On review more than 1 year after the CAR T-cell infusion, the glabellar mass was no longer visible, and the lymphoma was in remission (appendix).
Mantle-cell lymphoma—a subcategory of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma—usually presents in elderly men in an advanced stage with extra nodal disease. Recently mantle-cell lymphoma has been classified into nodal and leukaemic non-nodal; nevertheless, extra nodal soft tissue involvement may occur as the disease progresses—even if it is not found at the time of initial diagnosis. Extra nodal involvement typically affects the bone marrow and gastrointestinal tract—involvement of the glabellar area has not been clearly delineated before. Treatment regimens for mantle-cell lymphoma are changing with the development of CAR T-cells, bispecific antibodies, and novel Bruton tyrosine-kinase inhibitors. As outcomes improve and patients’ survivals are prolonged, we need to remain cognisant of atypical presentations of recurrence.

A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our department with gradual onset of pain in her hands, hips, and knees, which had progressively limited her mobility over the past 6 years. She also reported feeling tired and feverish.On examination we found the patient to have skin sclerosis, microstomia, and reduced mobility in most of her joints. She also had white papules with ulcerations on the skin over her trunk, arms, and legs, but predominantly they were grouped around the large joints—hips, knees, and elbows (figure). We noted a palpable tendon friction rub on the joints of the patient's hands; there was no swelling or tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 33 mg/L (normal 0–5), anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 8·2 g/dL, and a moderately elevated creatine kinase of 480 U/L (normal <200).
Tests for autoantibodies found increased titres for antinuclear antibodies (1:2560; normal <1:160) and highly elevated antibodies against double-stranded DNA (>200 U/L; normal <100). Anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies were raised and antibodies against PM/Scl-75 and PM/Scl-100 were strongly positive on immunofluorescence. Autoantibodies to rheumatoid factor (30 U/mL; normal <14) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (19 U/mL; normal <5) were positive.
An x-ray of the patient's pelvis showed generalised massive multilocular calcinosis (figure) and an x-ray of her hands showed calcification around the tips of her fingers and thumbs (figure). MRI of the patient's thighs showed myositis and fasciitis. A CT scan of the patient's chest showed interstitial lung disease. Ultrasound scans of the patient's joints—specifically her hands and fingers—showed polyarthritis.
Taking these findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis together with polymyositis and polyarthritis. We started the patient on a combination of methotrexate, baricitinib, and intravenous immunoglobulins to modulate the immune response, and prostaglandins to cause vasodilation. Within 8 months, the ulcerative calcinosis of the patient's skin, her myositis, and her fasciitis had improved substantially; her pain had also substantially reduced.
Although calcinosis cutis is described in many diseases—including metastatic diseases, lymphomas, and metabolic diseases—it may occur secondary to medical treatments and trauma. Massive infiltrations—as in our patient—are rare and we were fortunate that our multimodal, disease-targeted pharmacological therapy combination was effective. Clinicians using such combined therapies for prolonged periods of time should remain mindful of the risk of infection (video).

12 years earlier, the patient had a right colectomy with resection of liver metastases for a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon, stage pT3N2aM1; the tumour was of a hypermutant phenotype referred to as microsatellite instability high (MSI-H) and deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). At the time, the patient had been diagnosed with Lynch syndrome after DNA sequencing showed a pathogenic variant in MSH2. After the patient had the surgery, he was treated with adjuvant chemotherapy—folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin, also known as FOLFOX. 3 months later, the disease had progressed in the liver and coeliac and periaortic lymph nodes; he was treated with folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and cetuximab.
Notably, a family history showed the patient's mother had carcinoma of the uterus and colon, and his sister had malignancy in the uterus.
5 years after his initial diagnosis, the patient was enrolled in a clinical trial and given combined treatment with the immune-checkpoint inhibitors—including nivolumab for 24 months and 4 injections for induction therapy of ipilumumab; the disease went into remission.
9 years after the initial presentation, a CT scan showed a new metastatic lesion in the left adrenal gland which was treated by stereotaxic radiotherapy.
When we first assessed the patient, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a mass extending from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium causing obstruction of the tricuspid valve (appendix); contrast-enhancement showed some opacification of the mass (appendix). A 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed no metabolic activity in the right atrium nor in the inferior vena cava.
After assessment and discussion with the patient—considering firstly his generally good physical state, secondly the response of the disease to immune-checkpoint inhibitors, and thirdly, the obstruction of the tricuspid valve—we excised the right atrial mass during beating-heart surgery with partial cardiopulmonary bypass (appendix).
Gross macroscopic evaluation of the excised mass showed a small amount of thrombus with mostly tissue consistent with a metastatic process (appendix); histopathological analysis of a sample of the lesion confirmed mucinous adenocarcinoma. The patient continued solely on nivolumab, and his general condition improved.
5 months after the heart surgery, the patient was well; a transthoracic echocardiogram and a cardiac CT scan showed no residual or recurrence of the right atrium metastatic mass (appendix). A CT scan confirmed partial response of the metastases in the lymph nodes.
Lynch syndrome, with a pathogenic germline variant in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM, is the most common hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition syndrome. Diagnosis—necessitating input from both oncology and genetics—as well as follow-up involving colonoscopy surveillance is key. In addition, the efficacy of immune checkpoint immunotherapy, specifically anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA4 antibodies, has resulted in an unprecedented improvement in the number of patients with Lynch syndrome-associated cancers having a successful outcome. The benefits of a multidisciplinary management approach—illustrated by the different teams involved in the treatment of our patient—are clearly apparent.

A 4-year old girl was admitted to our hospital after she collapsed at home while having dinner. She had a history of recurrent upper airway infections and wheezing, which were being treated with inhaled β2-adrenoceptor agonist, as an outpatient.On examination in our emergency department, the patient was tachycardic and tachypnoeic with subcostal recession and fine bilateral crackles; oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry was 85% at an oxygen flow rate of 2 L/min. Her abdomen was distended, but non-tender; her fingers were clubbed, and she had peripheral oedema in both legs.
A chest x-ray showed both cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions—the right being greater than the left—and a small amount of ascitic fluid (figure). An echocardiogram showed a large circumferential pericardial effusion and reduced cardiac contractility with a shortening fraction of 20%. The patient required immediate intubation and the insertion of a pleural drain on her right side and a pericardial drain (figure) as well as inotropic support.
Once the patient was clinically stable, we carried out a comprehensive diagnostic work-up—with coeliac disease included in the list of diagnoses because of the abdominal distension; other diagnoses considered were cardiomyopathy, infections, autoimmune disorders, cystic fibrosis, and malignancies.
Anti-transglutaminase IgG concentration was 600 U/mL (reference range <7), and anti-gliadin IgG concentration was 302 U/mL (reference range <7).
Notably, the patient's IgA antibodies (<5 mg/dL; reference range 27–195) and serum albumin concentration (23 g/L; reference range 38–54) were low; aspartate aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 10–45) and alanine aminotransferase (78 U/L; reference range 5–25) were raised.
Upper endoscopy showed a reduction and fissuring of duodenal folds—confirming coeliac disease. Histopathology identified intraepithelial lymphocytosis, marked villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia: modified Marsh classification type 3b, Corazza grade B1.
The patient was started on a gluten-free diet and her abdominal distension resolved and there was no recurrence of the pericardial effusion. She was allowed home after 3 weeks when she had made a full clinical recovery. At outpatient follow-up 3 months later, she was seriously considering a career in medicine (figure).
For coeliac disease to manifest itself with cardiopulmonary symptoms at a young age—as in our patient—is unusual and while pericardial effusion is a rare presentation of the illness, it is important to consider it as a differential diagnosis. IgA deficiency is observed in approximately 2% of patients with coeliac disease, further complicating the process of establishing the correct diagnosis (video).

A 10-year-old girl with an antenatal diagnosis of Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome was referred to our institution with a 1-day history of rectal bleeding. She had stools of normal consistency and frequency, had not been on any medication recently, and had no abdominal pain or other accompanying symptoms.Her physical examination revealed extensive red–purple masses on her right lower leg. These masses on the right lower quadrant felt like a paste when palpated. Laboratory tests revealed that her haemoglobin concentration was 10·6 g/dL, white blood cell count was 9000 cells per μL, and platelet count was 221 000 cells per μL; coagulation tests were normal. D-dimer was high and thromboelastogram results were normal.
An intravenous dose of tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg was started, and colonoscopy was done, which showed continuous submucosal involvement of the rectum and sigmoid, with areas of erythema and whitish zones suggestive of lymphatic lesions, without mucosal erosions (figure, A). Large varices were observed with extensive involvement through the descending, transverse colon, hepatic angle, and ascending colon (figure, B). They extended towards the lumen, in the shape of grape clusters, leaving only a small segment towards the caecum free of disease. The ileum could not be visualised. No mucosal lesions were evident. MRI enteroclysis showed concentric mural thickening of the rectum and proximal sigmoid of the right colon, especially at the level of the caecum and the proximal aspect of the ascending colon. Concentric thickening and hyperaemia of the adjacent rectum wall were also observed. Compared with an examination done 3 years previously, there was evidence of increased involvement of the intestinal wall and adjacent tissues. Given the impossibility of surgical resection, the patient has been treated with oral rapamycin 1·5 mg per day for the past 10 months. She has presented with two episodes of self-limiting rectal bleeding since she started rapamycin, and has been undergoing strict follow-up with a paediatric multidisciplinary team (including surgery, haematology, traumatology, and endocrinology).
Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome is a congenital vascular malformation, with a pathogenesis that is not completely understood. Alteration in the fetal mesoderm has been postulated, as a result of intrauterine damage causing dilation of the arteriovenous anastomosis, deep vein obstruction with varices, or hypertrophy of the lymphatic vessels. Gastrointestinal tract involvement is observed in up to 20% of cases, usually in the rectum and sigmoid, which can manifest as gastrointestinal bleeding, usually during the first decade of life. Since most of the time the bleeding is self-limiting and the involvement of the colon is distal, the patient should be followed up and treated for anaemia if necessary. Angiographic intervention such as embolisation of the bleeding vessel can sometimes be successful. Endoscopic therapy is usually preferred for localised lesions or postoperative residual disease. Endorectal resection extending to the transverse colon has been reported in cases of more extensive disease. Involvement of the ascending colon is very unusual, and the extensive involvement of the bowel makes this particular case unique and challenging.

On physical examination, auscultation of both lower lungs revealed fine crackles. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed mediastinal lymphadenopathy and diffuse ground-glass opacities (left, axial view). Also visible were areas of superimposed interlobular and intralobular septal thickening, a pattern known as crazy paving (left, box). A subsequent transbronchial lung biopsy showed multiple noncaseating granulomas (middle, inset showing granuloma; hematoxylin and eosin stain). Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures, histopathological analysis, and molecular testing were negative for infectious organisms, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A 51-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of blackouts occurring in the context of worsening breathlessness (New York Heart Association [NYHA] class IV) and swelling of her legs. 14 months earlier she had a gastric banding operation.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus for which she had been taking oral azathioprine 50 mg twice a day, prednisolone 5 mg daily, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day for 5 days a week for the past 19 years; she had no significant family history.
On examination, the patient's body-mass index had fallen from 46 kg/m2 pre-gastric bypass to 25 kg/m2; her jugular venous pressure was elevated, heart sounds were normal, and her chest was clear. She had bilateral peripheral oedema to her ankles and abdominal distension. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed right bundle branch block with evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy.
Laboratory investigations showed renal impairment with creatinine 99 μmol/L and estimated glomerular filtration rate 51 mL/min per 1·73 m2. High-sensitivity troponin I was 251 ng/L (normal <32) and plasma concentration of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was raised at 32 208 ng/L (normal <400).
Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with small cavity, normal ejection fraction, and impaired longitudinal function; and right ventricular dysfunction and bi-atrial dilatation. A cardiac MRI (figure) confirmed LVH with 16 mm maximal wall thickness and non-coronary late gadolinium enhancement. Myocardial T1 relaxation time was normal; a high-resolution CT showed fibrotic changes in the lungs.
Considering the findings in the round, we suspected hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy and stopped this medication. Right heart catheterisation confirmed pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease. Right ventricular biopsy demonstrated marked vacuolation—shown on electron microscopy to be an excess of lysosomes (figure) containing electron-dense, phospholipid-rich lamellar bodies: features that are common to Fabry's disease and hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy. A normal α-galactosidase A level, a normal T1 relaxation time on MRI, and negative genetic tests for abnormalities of the GLA gene excluded the former.
We decided that the patient was not eligible for cardiac transplantation due to her frailty and comorbidities. However, within 12 months after stopping the hydroxychloroquine, her condition was much better: the breathlessness had improved—NYHA class III—and the concentration of NT-proBNP had reduced to 5337 ng/L. In retrospect, we found evidence of LVH and ECG changes before gastric surgery, but we believe that the rapid weight loss may have accelerated the damage to the heart by altering the absorption of the hydroxychloroquine.
Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy is rare—although the true prevalence is unknown—and related to perturbed lysosomal autophagy. Risk factors—relevant to our case—include older age, female sex, and a high cumulative dose of hydroxychloroquine; we calculated the dose to have been greater than or equal to 2774 g over 19 years. Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy should be considered in patients with LVH and restrictive cardiomyopathy, as it may be partially reversible after medication withdrawal (video).
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy, Lupus myocarditis, Fabry’s disease

An 85-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of fever. At another hospital, treatment with cefditoren had been ineffective. 55 years earlier, she had been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and given a 2-year course of antituberculosis drugs, including isoniazid, streptomycin, and paraaminosalicylic acid. On physical examination, ulcerative inflammation involved the left auricle and completely spared the left earlobe (figure), which suggested chondritis rather than dermatitis. Tender left cervical lymphadenopathy was noticed (figure). Whole-body CT showed enlarged left cervical lymph nodes, stippled and nodular calcification in both lungs, and lymph node calcification in the mediastinum, which suggested old healed pulmonary tuberculosis. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation in the left auricle and left cervical lymph nodes (figure) with no arthritis or vasculitis. Incisional biopsy specimens of the affected cervical lymph nodes showed epithelioid granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis on haematoxylin and eosin stain, which were consistent with tuberculosis. Biopsy specimens of the cartilage and skin in the inflamed auricle identified chondritis with no granulomatous inflammation on haematoxylin and eosin stain. In both specimens, Ziehl Neelsen stain results, mycobacterial culture result, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were negative. Treatment with antituberculous drugs, including 2-month course of isoniazid (200 mg/day), rifampicin (450 mg/day), and ethambutol (500 mg/day), and 7-month course of isoniazid (200 mg/day) and rifampicin (450 mg/day), resolved fever, auricular chondritis, and cervical lymphadenitis. At the 2-year follow-up, the patient did not have recurrence of lymphadenitis and auricular chondritis, and chest x-ray showed no recurrence of pulmonary tuberculosis.M tuberculosis can be an immunological trigger for onset of various connective tissue diseases. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, and cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa have been reported to develop concomitantly with tuberculous infection and respond to antituberculosis drugs.
Auricular chondritis is a typical sign of relapsing polychondlitis, but is rarely seen in patients with various connective tissue diseases, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome, Behcet's disease, and ulcerative colitis. In this case, tuberculous lymphadenitis, with no other sites of active tuberculous involvement, was diagnosed on the basis of the specific pathophysiological findings because the sensitivity of mycobacterial culture and M tuberculosis PCR for tuberculous lymphadenitis is low and biopsy is the most reliable method. Auricular chondritis is probably not a tuberculous infection on grounds of the non-contiguousness, pathophysiological findings, and microbiological examination results. Therefore, cervical tuberculous lymphadenopathy is considered to induce autoimmune inflammation of the auricular cartilage based on the coincidence and response to antituberculosis drugs.
target: Auricular chondritis associated with tuberculous lymphadenopathy
options: Relapsing polychondritis, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Systemic lupus erythematosus, Auricular chondritis associated with tuberculous lymphadenopathy

A 95-year-old woman attended our oral medicine department reporting a painful white plaque on the left margin of her tongue. The patient had been seen by her dentist 8 months earlier, who concluded that the small, nodular, white patch (figure), opposite a broken tooth, had been caused by trauma; he polished the broken tooth and arranged no follow-up appointments. However, 8 months later, the patient went back to her dentist because of persistent pain; the white patch had progressed, and the dentist referred her to us.The patient had a history of hypertension treated with candesartan; she reported no tobacco use or alcohol consumption.
On examination, she was generally well; in her mouth the original white plaque had developed an ulcerated lichenoid appearance, and three new plaques were present on her tongue (figure). Regional lymph nodes in the neck were not palpable. Two biopsies were taken and each examined at three levels: the first showed squamous cell carcinomatous proliferation—essentially in situ, locally ulcerated, with focal budding of the basal layer and micro-infiltrative subepithelial small clumps or squamous epithelial cells (figure); the second biopsy found an acanthotic leukokeratotic mucosa with sparse subepithelial lymphocytic inflammation, and a few apoptotic bodies (figure). Well differentiated micro-invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue was diagnosed. The second biopsy also showed lichenoid inflammation.
The patient had a partial glossectomy and a sentinel lymph node biopsy which showed no signs of metastasis; no adjuvant treatment was indicated. At her last follow-up 1 year after surgery, the patient was in clinical remission.
Late diagnosis of oral cancers—as with many malignancies—results in poorer prognosis. Notably, oral traumatic lesions typically resolve within 4 weeks once the causative agent is removed.
All new oral white and red patches, whether they appear malignant or not, should be monitored and investigated. Importantly, any plaque, patch, ulcer, lump, or anything that appears atypical needs to be explored and the aetiology found; many head and neck cancers present initially with lesions in the oral cavity. The persistence of pain and any persistent or progressive lesion should be biopsied to avoid missing an oral squamous cell carcinoma or misdiagnosing a lesion that appears to be benign. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), in the UK, guidelines recommend that any non-healing oral ulcer or a lump on the tongue should be referred to a specialist so that patients with a suspected cancer are seen within 2 weeks.
Contributors
We were all involved with the patient's care. EV, DM, and SW devised the article. EV and DM gathered the data. EV, DM, and BHB did the investigations. EV and DM wrote the original draft. SW reviewed and edited the paper. Written consent for publication was obtained from the patient.
options: Traumatic granuloma, Oral Crohn's disease, Oral squamous cell carcinoma, Oral lichenoid lesion

A 2-year-old boy presented for severe frostbite after being outside on a cold day (mean temperature –18°C). The child had reportedly spent 20–30 minutes outside and was found without gloves. Eight fingers (1–5 on the right hand, and 1, 2, and 5 on the left hand) first appeared pale, then developed severe blisters. He was admitted for wound care, surgical debridement of necrotic skin, and pain control. At first, radiographs of the hands were typical (appendix). The patient was discharged home after 2 weeks, following a favourable evolution. 1 year later, he presented with widened interphalangeal joints in the eight fingers affected by frostbite. On x-ray, there was substantial damage to the metaphyses and epiphyses (figure A). Conservative treatment (occupational therapy and splinting) was started. During follow up, joint damage progressed to deformity and growth restrictions in the affected fingers (appendix). At the age of 17 years, there is substantial joint and bone damage, finger shortening, and nail dystrophy in the eight fingers affected by frostbite (figure B and C). The patient does not report any joint pain or stiffness and has a near-typical functional status.
Frostbite is cold-induced tissue damage, with lack of supervision and alcohol and drug use as common risk factors in children and adolescents. Short-term complications include severe pain, infections, and tissue necrosis (ranging from skin blisters to extensive gangrene). Long-term sequelae include neuropathic pain, vasospasm, nails dystrophy, and risk for squamous cell-carcinoma. Additionally, frostbite arthropathy can appear months to years after the acute episode. In an immature skeleton, frostbite arthropathy can exceptionally result in physeal, growth plate, and epiphyseal destruction of affected phalanges. The frequency of this complication is unknown, with only a few historical cases published. Physicians should be aware of this rare complication of severe paediatric frostbite, which can occur even after an initially favourable evolution. In the absence of curative treatment, prevention of cold-induced injuries (especially in at-risk familial and environmental contexts) remains crucial.
options: Genetic bone dysplasia (such as progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia), Frostbite arthropathy of childhood, Inborn error of immunity (such as monogenic type 1 interferonopathy), Severe juvenile idiopathic arthritis

A 40-year-old-woman presented to our outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of pain in her throat and a feeling that she had a foreign body in the submandibular region. She said the pain was pricking, intermittent, bilateral, non-radiating, aggravated by eating solid food, and moderate to severe in intensity. She reported no history of trauma or previous operations—specifically a tonsillectomy. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.At examination, on bimanual palpation—tolerated by the patient without the use of any anaesthetic spray—we found tender bony prominences in both tonsillar fossa; bilateral grade 1 tonsillar hypertrophy was also present. We found no other physical abnormalities and all laboratory investigations were normal. CT showed bilaterally elongated styloid processes; with three-dimensional reconstruction the abnormalities were clearly seen, and the enlarged styloid processes measured—3·9 cm on the left side and 3·5 cm on the right side (reference range 2·5–3 cm; figure).
Initially, we decided to treat the patient conservatively with analgesics and neuropathic pain medications; this had no effect. We then carried out a bilateral transoral tonsillectomy with styloidectomy; both the elongated styloid processes were visualised during surgery and about 1 cm and 2 cm of the elongated styloid processes were resected from right and left sides respectively, bringing their lengths down to within the reference range.
Notably, the foreign body sensation resolved following surgery. At 3 months' follow-up, the patient was symptom-free.
Eagle syndrome, also known as styloid or stylohyoid syndrome, is a very rare entity which was first described in 1937. Watt Weems Eagle, born in Statesville, North Carolina, was the first chief of the ear, nose and throat division at Duke Medical Center. Classically, the syndrome is characterised by orofacial pain, dysphagia, and the sensation of a foreign body in the throat. The condition is usually seen in women older than 30 years and can be confused with a wide array of head and neck disorders—including trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, temporal arteritis, migraine, and cervical arthritis—hence its presentation to dentists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. The exact pathophysiology behind this syndrome is still unknown. However, it is associated with a history of neck trauma, tonsillectomy, and the presence of an arcuate foramen. Most cases can be managed conservatively but surgery may be indicated in unresponsive cases (video).

input: A 58-year-old woman presented with fever and fatigue for the past 4 weeks. She reported hyperpigmented lesions on her arms and face on a background of mostly hypopigmented skin, creating a leopard-like appearance (figure A). The lesions first appeared 9 months earlier, and the dark pigment intensified over time. Her history included vitiligo and primary adrenal insufficiency, for which she received glucocorticoid replacement therapy with delayed-release hydrocortisone (10 mg orally per day; 0·11 mg per kg body weight [87 kg]) and fludrocortisone (0·1 mg orally per day). Serum electrolytes were normal; C-reactive protein was raised to 40 mg/L (reference: <5 mg/L); and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 46 mm/h (reference: <30 mm/h after 1 h), while complete blood count was within the normal range. Serum cortisol was 17 nmol/L (reference: 124–662 nmol/L) and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was 274 pmol/L (reference: 2·6–10·1 pmol/L). Based on her presentation, we suspected inadequate glucocorticoid replacement because of enhanced glucocorticoid demand. Hydrocortisone was increased to 40 mg per day. A CT scan showed splenomegaly and diffuse lymphadenopathy (figure B). Surgical extirpation and histopathological analysis of an axillary lymph node revealed follicular lymphoma (stage 3B). The insidious development of lymphoma might have enhanced the patient's glucocorticoid requirement, as reflected by her symptoms and elevated concentrations of ACTH. Cosecretion of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone with ACTH, both from the common precursor POMC, enhanced the contrast of hyperpigmented islands on vitiligous skin. After treatment with bendamustine and rituximab (R-Bendamustine protocol: 3 cycles, cumulative dose of bendamustine at 1080 mg [IV], cumulative dose of rituximab at 2250 mg [IV]), lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly had disappeared and the patient was free of symptoms when on hydrocortisone (20 mg per day).Patients with inadequate glucocorticoid replacement generally present with fatigue, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea, as well as hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. In severe cases, adrenal crisis might occur and rapid intravenous replacement of glucocorticoids is required. As for the patient described here, cutaneous hyperpigmentation might also indicate an increased glucocorticoid demand compared with the replacement dose. Thus, inspection of the skin might be a useful diagnostic tool in patients with primary adrenal insufficiency, including mucosal membranes, scars, and skin creases. However, in patients with underlying skin conditions, the presentation of the characteristic hyperpigmentation might vary and could be misinterpreted as part of the skin disease if not carefully examined. If a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency who is on glucocorticoid-replacement therapy develops hyperpigmentation, possible causes of the increased glucocorticoid demand need to be investigated, including malignancies, infection, or autoimmune disease. Here, we were able to diagnose lymphoma as the underlying cause of the increased glucocorticoid requirement.

input: A 40-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 4-year history of recurrent central chest pain. The pain was unrelated to food or exertion, and occurred intermittently during both day and night. The patient had no medical history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia or hypothyroidism. She did, however, give a history of having a prolonged fever for about 3 months accompanied by arthralgia at the age of 13 years. She said that at the time she had extensive investigations for infections and possible malignancies—but the fever resolved gradually without any cause being identified. She said that she had had no further problems until the current complaint began 4 years ago. On clinical examination, her blood pressure was 130/90 mm Hg in both upper limbs, pulses were easily palpable, and there were no bruits or murmurs heard on auscultation. A chest x-ray showed calcification of the wall of the aortic arch and descending thoracic aorta, with narrowing at the level of the diaphragmatic hiatus (figure). Full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, lipid profile, and parathyroid hormone levels were normal. MRI angiograms showed narrowing of the aorta in the post-subclavian area, in the descending thoracic aorta at the level of the diaphragm, and at the level just above the origin of the left renal artery (figure); T2-weighted images showed a thickened and oedematous thoracic aorta, suggesting active inflammation (figure), and a CT angiogram showed extensive calcification (figure). Taken together these findings led us to making a diagnosis of aorta arteritis type III with active disease. Takayasu arteritis or aorto-arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches. The disease may manifest itself with only non-specific features like fever, myalgia, arthritis, and malaise during the acute phase, which can last for several months. In the chronic phase, in the absence of clinical features secondary to vessel occlusion or ischaemia, the diagnosis maybe further delayed. However, disease activity may persist in the aortic wall despite the patient being asymptomatic and all inflammatory markers remaining within normal limits. A high index of suspicion is required to make the diagnosis during the acute phase, and regular monitoring is necessary to avoid serious long-term complications. The disease takes its name from Mikito Takayasu, who described the first case in 1908 at the Annual Meeting of the Japan Ophthalmology Society.

A 69-year old man, from Lombardy, Italy, was admitted to our unit because of acute respiratory distress syndrome that required mechanical ventilation; he was in Nice, France, on holiday. He had previously been fit and well; he had a history of hypertension controlled with bisoprolol 2·5 mg/day. He initially reported vomiting and diarrhoea, and 7 days afterwards, he came to our emergency department with a cough, fever of 39°C, and dyspnoea. He was immediately transferred to our intensive care unit (ICU) because of the respiratory distress syndrome and severe hypoxia. Investigations found a haemoglobin concentration of 15·4 g/dL, a platelet count of 187 × 109 per L, and a leucocyte count of 14·9 × 109 per L (neutrophils 89%, lymphocytes 7%, monocytes 4%, and no eosinophils or basophils 0%). His blood pH was 7·27, partial pressure of carbon dioxide was 45·3 mm Hg, partial pressure of oxygen was 146 mm Hg, and peripheral oxygen saturation was 98·2%.A CT of his chest showed bilateral ground-glass opacities and condensations (figure; video). PCR of swabs taken from his upper respiratory tract showed severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-Cov-2) confirming a diagnosis of coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19). Multiplex PCR was negative for other viruses using BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2 plus (bioMérieux, Marcy l'Etoile, France) and no bacterial infections were found. An electrocardiogram (ECG), done on admission to the ICU, showed signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diffuse inverted T waves (figure)—a previous ECG showed inverted T waves in anterior leads only. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I concentration was raised at 9002 ng/L (normal <40). Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild LVH; the left ventricular ejection fraction and wall motion were within normal limits (figure; video). The patient was known to have LVH which was probably caused by his chronic hypertension.
Antiplatelet therapy—aspirin—and anticoagulation therapy—fondaparinux—were started because we suspected a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction: his Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) score was greater than 140. However, coronary angiography showed no disease, but cardiovascular magnetic resonance scanning showed subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the apex and inferolateral wall—suggestive of myocarditis (figure; video). We decided not to do an endomyocardial biopsy because the patient showed no signs of heart failure or arrhythmias. Additional tests for common causes of myocarditis—including parvovirus B19, human herpes virus, Epstein-Barr virus, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, HIV, and hepatitis C virus—were negative. We therefore concluded that SARS-CoV-2 infection was the most likely cause of our patient's myocarditis. We gave the patient hydrocortisone at day 11 for 9 days with the aim of reducing inflammation—particularly of the myocardium. The patient was weaned off mechanical ventilation and discharged from the ICU after 3 weeks.
We believe this comprehensive description of myocarditis associated with COVID-19 confirms the importance of recent data reporting acute cardiac injury in almost a fifth of patients, with a 50% survival rate. It is recommended that troponin is not routinely measured in patients with COVID-19. However, physicians need to pay heed to the possibility of myocarditis in cases of COVID-19: in cases with high GRACE scores and dynamic ECG changes, usual guidelines to exclude the possibility of an acute myocardial infarction, including measuring troponin and doing an angiogram within 24 h, need to be followed (video).

A 68-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) was referred to our specialised team. The patient had noticed increasing difficulty speaking and swallowing, followed by excessive weight loss and sialorrhoea, for 1 year before the diagnosis. A feeding tube had been inserted to support nutritional intake 2 weeks after the patient had first been diagnosed.During the following months, treatment was delivered by our multidisciplinary team composed of a rehabilitation physician, occupational therapist, physiotherapist, speech therapist, dietitian, psychologist, social worker, and spiritual counsellor, according to international ALS care guidelines. The aim was to optimise quality of life through symptom management and psychological support. Particularly important for the patient was his ability to communicate and the management of the sialorrhoea—both relevant for continued social interaction. The sialorrhoea was initially managed with glycopyrronium and dextromethorphan combined quinidine, and then with botulin toxin A injections into the salivary glands. As the disease progressed, a second round of botulinum injections failed to adequately relieve his symptoms; the patient decided against radiotherapy of the salivary glands—the next line of treatment.
The ALS-care team provided support—including psychological—to reduce both the patient's and his partner's struggle with the impact of ALS on their lives.
6 months after being diagnosed, his general practitioner started regular conversations with the patient about his values in life, his needs, and goals—considering the progressive course of his disease: advance care planning. End-of-life practices were explored.
9 months after being diagnosed, the patient developed progressive weakness in his hands; he reported that the symptom burden of dysphagia, excessive sialorrhoea, and uncontrollable coughing was exhausting.
10 months after being diagnosed, the patient's respiratory function had decreased to a point where options for respiratory support had to be discussed; he agreed to nocturnal non-invasive ventilation (NIV) to reduce symptom burden. Continuous, invasive ventilation—through a tracheostoma—had been discussed before starting NIV, but the patient felt that this would not allow him to continue being, and wanting to remain, an autonomous, independent person.
13 months after being diagnosed, the patient started to contemplate how his life would end; both he and his wife attended sessions with the spiritual counsellor to assist him in coming to terms with the last phase of his life.
14 months after being diagnosed, the patient spoke to his general practitioner and requested euthanasia. An independent physician was consulted to confirm that the patient's request was voluntary and well considered, and to substantiate that there was unbearable suffering without the prospect of improvement. The request was also discussed between the general practitioner and the ALS-care team. The patient died peacefully, in the presence of his family and general practitioner, 15 months after being diagnosed with ALS.

A 28-year-old man presented to our rheumatology department with a 10-year history of progressive facial and truncal rash and mild muscle weakness. He had previously presented with these symptoms at a local dermatology clinic at age 18 years. After this initial examination, the patient was diagnosed with dermatomyositis and given combined treatment with prednisone, methotrexate, and hydroxychloroquine. This treatment resulted in improved muscle weakness after a few months; however, the patient had mild hepatotoxicity and so methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine were discontinued. He also reported recurrence of cutaneous involvement, which prompted re-referral and re-evaluation at our department 10 years later.
On re-examination, physical examination revealed a violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids and malar area, accompanied by a striking reticular erythematous eruption on the neck and back (figure 1A). Muscle involvement was assessed by use of the Manual Muscle Testing-8 scale, yielding a score of 150 (ie, normal muscle strength).
Histopathological evaluation of the reticular rash biopsy sample revealed interface dermatitis on haematoxylin and eosin staining (figure 1B), along with basement membrane thickening highlighted by periodic acid-Schiff staining (figure 1C). Laboratory investigations showed creatine kinase concentrations within the normal range (64 U/L; reference range 50–310 U/L) and exclusive anti-transcriptional intermediary factor 1-γ (anti-TIF1-γ) antibody positivity, detected by immunoblot, with negative results for other myositis-specific autoantibodies. In China, there are currently no commercially available ELISA kits for anti-TIF1-γ antibody detection that have been approved by the China Food and Drug Administration. Muscle MRI showed no inflammation or oedema, and high-resolution pulmonary CT revealed no interstitial lung disease. Extensive malignancy screening, including whole-body PET–CT and gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed no occult neoplasms. Peripheral blood PCR revealed elevated interferon-stimulated genes (MX1 and IFI44), confirming a type I interferon signature. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analysis revealed MX1 expression in the basal epidermis and perivascular regions.
When the patient was first diagnosed at his local dermatology clinic at age 18 years, his clinical manifestations were characterised by prominent cutaneous features without evidence of calcinosis, which is suggestive of cancer-associated adult dermatomyositis. However, detection of myositis-specific autoantibodies, including anti-TIF1-γ, was unavailable at the time. Upon re-evaluation 10 years later, and taking into account the patient's history, symptoms, laboratory examination, and cutaneous biopsy findings, the diagnosis of dermatomyositis was confirmed. Baricitinib (4 mg per day) combined with prednisone (0·8 mg/kg per day) were initiated. At 24 weeks follow-up at our department, Cutaneous Disease Area and Severity Index scores improved by 60% (scores reduced from 25 to 10), with reduced erythema intensity and extent of rash. As there was no progression of muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, or malignancy after 24 weeks, prednisone was tapered to 7·5 mg per day.
Anti-TIF1-γ antibodies are strongly associated with malignancy, with peak risk 3–5 years before and after disease onset. Characteristic cutaneous findings of anti-TIF1-γ positive dermatomyositis, including facial rash, V-neck and back rash, periungual telangiectasias, heliotrope rash, Gottron's sign, palatal patch, and diffuse photoerythema, are well documented. However, reticular rash, a rare manifestation as seen in this patient, expands the spectrum of cutaneous manifestations. Emerging evidence implicates type I interferon dysregulation in pathogenesis, and Janus kinase inhibitors might be of benefit to patients with refractory cutaneous dermatomyositis.
