A 62-year-old man was admitted to our hospital after a fall; he had been found by his sister, lying on the floor and somnolent.
The patient had a history of unexplained profound visual impairment, which began in his childhood; he had not been able to do military service because of it. He also had sensorineural hearing loss, for which he had a cochlear implant when he was 58 years old. Additionally, the patient, who was intellectually impaired, was wheelchair-bound because of ataxia, spasticity, and the visual difficulties; he had no children.
The patient's sister, aged 52 years, had a similar phenotype with pes cavus, hearing loss, visual impairment, and loss of safe ambulation. The parents were well and reported no difficulties—although a first cousin was reported to have a presentation like the patient and his sister. On examination, the patient was not distressed; blood pressure was 135/60 mm Hg, pulse 87 beats per min, and oxygen saturation 93%. He was unable to walk independently and was markedly ataxic. He had bilateral pes cavus (figure) with atrophy of the distal muscles of both legs; bilateral Babinski signs were noted. The patient had pseudophakia and a bone-spicule pattern retinitis pigmentosa (figure); he could detect hand movements from 50 cm, with crescentic-sparing of the temporal visual field. He did not report anosmia.Laboratory investigations showed normal plasma lactate, no acanthocytes were seen in a peripheral blood smear, and he did not have abetalipoproteinemia. Phytanic acid concentration was 0·42 μg/mL (typical range 0·02–1·93). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed an elevated protein concentration, but no indications of inflammation.
Cerebellar atrophy was seen on a CT scan of the patient's brain; electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed long-term neurogenic changes, but—importantly—slowing of nerve conduction velocities (22–40 m/sec) and prolonged F-wave latencies, indicative of a chronic polyneuropathy with pronounced demyelinating features. Histopathological examination of samples of a biopsy of the sural nerve corroborated a demyelinating neuropathy with onion bulb formations.
Genetic testing, using Sanger sequencing, showed a mutation in the ABHD12 gene, which was a nonsense homozygous variant (NM 015600.4: c.784C>T, p.Arg262*) causing a substitution of the arginine 262 for a stop codon. A diagnosis of PHARC—an acronym formed from polyneuropathy, hearing loss, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, and cataract—syndrome was made. Previously, no mutations had been found on sequencing the patient's mitochondrial DNA.
The patient was able to return home to the care of a nurse and a dedicated family doctor. Physiotherapy was arranged and both the patient and his sister will continue to be followed up.
PHARC syndrome is a rare, autosomal recessive, neurodegenerative disease resulting from mutations in the α/β-hydrolase domain-containing 12 (ABHD12) serine hydrolase encoding gene. The differential diagnosis includes other rare diseases—specifically Refsum disease, abetalipoproteinemia, mitochondrial disorders, and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
In Refsum disease, which has retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia, and chronic polyneuropathy as its cardinal features, an elevated plasma phytanic acid level is a key indicator of the diagnosis. Abetalipoproteinemia causes marked steatorrhoea, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy, pes cavus, and acanthocytosis.
Mitochondrial disorders can affect most organ systems—importantly the brain and the heart—and can present at any age with eye problems, proximal myopathy, sensorineural deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and diabetes. Measurement of plasma or CSF lactate concentration may help in the diagnosis, but it is not pathognomonic.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a slowly progressive distal motor neuropathy of the arms and legs, often associated with mild to moderate distal sensory loss. Sensorineural hearing loss may also occur. Presentations of PHARC syndrome—and similar disorders—vary greatly. Mild cases, or patients without the full spectrum of abnormalities, may be missed; variation in presentations is due, at least in part, to the severity of the mutations.
options: Refsum disease, Abetalipoproteinemia, Mitochondrial disorders, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

A 7-year-old girl, with early-onset sarcoidosis, attended our clinic for a routine follow-up eye examination. She had reported no recent visual problems.The patient had been diagnosed with sarcoidosis 3 years earlier, after she developed problems walking, red eyes, rashes on her face and arms, and a fever. She had an elevated angiotensin converting enzyme concentration and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 52 mm/h. Synovial biopsy showed a non-necrotising granuloma and genetic testing found a novel mutation of unknown significance in the NOD2 gene. The patient was treated with methotrexate and adalimumab.
On examination, we found that she had reduced visual acuity in both eyes: 20/40 in the right and 20/60 in the left (typical 20/20). A slit-lamp examination showed bilateral anterior chamber inflammation and large off-white deposits on the inner corneal surface known as mutton-fat keratic precipitates (figure). Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showed inflammatory cells in both eyes and the keratic precipitates (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a raised ESR of 41 mm/h.
We started the patient on topical corticosteroids (dexamethasone eye drops) and provided the family with advice about concordance. At follow-up 4 weeks later, both the patient's vision and the anterior chamber inflammation had improved. The patient's concordance with the methotrexate and adalimumab had also improved: previously doses had been omitted based on the assumption that a long period without symptoms was due to remission rather than simply control of the disease process.
Sarcoidosis is a rare, multisystem, chronic inflammatory disorder most commonly affecting the lungs (in adults) and skin (in children). Early onset, defined as before the age of 4 years, typically presents with a triad of skin, joint, and eye problems, and may be caused by mutations of the NOD2 gene. Eye signs in both early and later presentations in childhood include anterior uveitis, vitritis, choroiditis, and retinal vasculitis.
Anterior uveitis may be asymptomatic in children up until the development of irreversible sight-threatening complications. Although anterior chamber inflammation is often difficult to detect, mutton-fat keratic precipitates can be seen with the naked eye. The presence of these large deposits—aggregates of polymorphonuclear cells, lymphocytes, and epithelioid cells—suggests granulomatous disease indicating differential diagnoses and investigations.
Clinical features are key to identifying the underlying granulomatous disorder when mutton-fat keratic precipitates are seen. Prompt diagnosis and management of the associated systemic disease, with coordinated care involving specialists, affords the best opportunity of disease control, and reduced burden of avoidable later-life morbidity and disability.

After 3 months of therapy, in May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department and complained of a worsening of his dyspnoea, leading us to suppose that disease progression had occurred. However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis—as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib—of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

A 32-year-old woman with a long history of Raynaud's phenomenon presented to the rheumatology clinic for assessment of severe fatigue and a mottled, purplish discolouration of the skin of her lower extremities. In 2014, she was diagnosed with chronic idiopathic dysautonomia, which leads to orthostatic hypotension and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Tilt-table testing resulted in a progressive drop in systolic blood pressure by 30–35 mm Hg and diastolic blood pressure by 15–20 mm Hg when tested at a tilt angle of 70 degrees for 18 min. During this test, she also developed progressive sinus tachycardia, with her heart rate increasing from 117 beats per min to 170 beats per min.The appearance of the patient's legs during assessment was suggestive of livedo reticularis (figure A). However, her legs did not show marked patterns of discolouration after waking up in the morning (figure B). The patient also noted that the mottled skin would go away if she were outside in warm weather or after a hot shower. Tests for lupus anticoagulant, cryoglobulins, and cold agglutinins were negative.
The patient was advised to increase her salt intake to 3–5 g/day for treatment of POTS and to use custom-made compression stockings; she also started treatment with pyridostigmine bromide (one 60 mg tablet four times daily) and ivabradine hydrochloride (half 5 mg tablet twice daily). However, her livedo reticularis persisted.
Livedo reticularis is a violaceous reticular discolouration of the skin, with connecting rings forming a network-like pattern, more commonly involving the extremities. This discolouration appears when peripheral venous plexuses of the skin become visible, resulting from venodilation, venous pooling, and deoxygenation of blood. The primary form of livedo reticularis is transient, whereas the idiopathic form tends to be persistent. Both forms are more common in women than in men, are generally asymptomatic, and do not require pharmacological intervention. However, avoiding exposure to cold temperatures and use of vasoconstrictors (eg, sympathomimetic drugs, triptans, amphetamines, amantadine, and nicotine) is helpful. In addition, a secondary form of livedo reticularis can be congenital, such as with cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, or acquired. This form is associated with various underlying conditions such as multiple haematological and hypercoagulable disorders, cutaneous vasculitides, embolic phenomena, autoimmune rheumatic diseases, chronic dysautonomia leading to POTS, medications, infections, and several neoplastic, neurological, and endocrine disorders. POTS is an unusual cause of livedo reticularis, in which an abnormal response by the autonomic nervous system causes cutaneous vasospasm, leading to decreased arteriolar inflow, and increased resistance to venous outflow, causing venous vasodilation. Consequently, affected patients typically have venous pooling, deoxygenation of blood, and the appearance of livedo reticularis.

An 80-year-old Japanese man attended our hospital with a 3-day history of stiffness in his jaw and difficulty moving his right arm. He had no history of ever travelling abroad, but he did have a medical history of hypertension, osteoporosis, and total gastrectomy due to gastric carcinoma. He told us that he had hurt his right hand while working in his garden 10 days ago. On physical examination, we found him to have a stiff neck, trismus, and a fixed sardonic-type smile (figure). Additionally, his abdomen was board-like rigid, and there was muscle rigidity and increased tone in his arms and legs. His temperature was 36·7°C. On the dorsum of his right hand there was a contused, yellowish-coloured, necrotic wound, approximately 2 cm in diameter. He gave no history of tetanus toxoid inoculation, and a blood test showed a white blood cell count of 5·8 × 109 per L and a haemoglobin concentration of 13·0 g/dL. He had no IgG antibodies against tetanus: the ELISA recorded 0·00 IU/mL. Therefore, based on the clinical findings on admission and the laboratory result, we made a diagnosis of generalised tetanus and gave him tetanus immuno-globulin, 3000 units intravenously, and tetanus toxoid, 0·5 mL intramuscularly, and we started him on metronidazole, 500 mg intravenously every 6 h. We surgically debrided the wound on his right hand. An assessment with the Ablett classification of tetanus showed that his condition deteriorated soon after admission—he moved from grade 2 to grade 3 within 24 h—and we decided to put him on a ventilator. Further, because he was at risk of laryngeal spasm, he was given a continuous intravenous infusion of midazolam and dexmedetomidine. He remained on the ventilator for 21 days. He was finally discharged from hospital after an admission of 60 days, which included a 28-day stay on the respiratory step-down unit. He made a full recovery apart from a persistent rigidity in his right hand.Tetanus is caused by a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani, a Gram-positive, obligate anaerobic rod-shaped bacterium that forms spores. C tetani spores occur worldwide as constituents of soil. Tetanus affects an estimated 1 million people worldwide every year, leading to between 48 199 and 80 042 deaths annually, in 2015. The yearly incidence of tetanus in Japan (0·09 per 100 000 population) is higher than that in the USA (0·01 per 100 000), and the EU (0·02 per 100 000). Japan has the world's largest ageing population and tetanus has been included in the routine childhood vaccination schedule since 1968, resulting in 47% of the country's inhabitants—ie, those born before 1968—being vaccine-naive with regards to tetanus. Further, 85% of notified cases are people aged 55 years and over.
Tetanus toxoid as post-exposure prophylaxis is available under the universal public health-care system; however, unfortunately, few people—including clinicians—recognise the importance of pre-exposure prophylaxis because there is no national catch-up vaccination programme. We advocate that administrators and clinicians should promote education on both pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis for tetanus. Tetanus is a vaccine-preventable disease; therefore prophylaxis should be provided for people in developing countries and developed countries with ageing populations.

A 64-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic, erythematosus papulopustular facial lesions (figure, A). The patient had been diagnosed with rosacea, and received oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks as first-line therapy by her family doctor. Because of the poor response to therapy, she had been referred to our dermatology clinic for further evaluation. On clinical examination, the eruptions, which were practically asymptomatic, had a rosacea-like appearance. They had emerged and gradually worsened over a period of 5 weeks. There were no pathological findings on physical examination and routine laboratory test results were normal. Microscopic examination of specimens collected from the patient's skin by epidermal scraping showed many Demodex folliculorum mites (figure, B, magnification ×100). The patient showed substantial improvement after treatment with oral metronidazole (250 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) and subsequent weekly topical permethrin (cream 5%).
Demodex spp are common saprophytic vermiform mites, which asymptomatically parasitise the hair follicles and the pilosebaceous glands of mammals. In human beings, two species of acarid mite have been identified: Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis. Sites favoured by Demodex spp mites include the scalp, forehead, and chin, and areas around the orbit, nose, and mouth. Demodex spp have been implicated in the development of various facial conditions, including pityriasis folliculorum, rosacea-like demodicidosis (also known as demodicosis), pustular folliculitis, demodectic blepharitis, and so-called “demodicidosis gravis”. Clinical features of Demodex spp infestation include erythematopapulous and pustulous skin lesions together with erythematodesquamative changes of the face. Furthermore, demodicidosis should also be considered in any patient with rosacea-like dermatitis resistant to conventional rosacea therapies.
Although there is no consensus to how and what degree infestation with Demodex spp mites contributes to skin pathology, there is evidence that demodicidosis is a condition distinct from common rosacea. The prevalence of Demodex spp carriers increases with age. It is possible that large numbers of demodex mites can stimulate inflammatory or allergic reactions by mechanical blockage of follicles, or by acting as vectors for microorganisms, which ultimately results in connective tissue damage and telangiectasia. Another interesting hypothesis is that inflammatory response may be stimulated by antigenic proteins related to a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from D folliculorum.

A 51-year-old woman with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and low-grade fever presented to our rheumatology clinic. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension, and had mechanic's hands (scaly, hyperkeratoic rash) and 3 out of 5 according to the Oxford scale for strength in deltoids and biceps.
Laboratory investigations found a creatine kinase concentration of 3193 IU/L (normal range 26–200 IU/L) and creatinine concentration of 90·2 μmol/L (normal range 35–106 μmol/L). Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a cytoplasmic pattern, anti-EJ antibody was positive (identified through immunoblotting), and a chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure A).
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of anti-synthetase syndrome was made. She was treated with methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) and cyclosporine (50 mg twice per day) for five days, and monitored at regular intervals as an inpatient. Over 2 weeks after the initial treatment the patient's creatine kinase concentration decreased gradually; however, she began to show decreased urine output, her creatinine concentration increased to 600·3 μmol/L, her haemoglobin concentration dropped from 87 g/L to 73 g/L, and her platelet count gradually decreased from 266 × 109 per L to 78 × 109 per L. Furthermore, the patient developed abdominal pain with bloody stools 3 weeks after the initial treatment. Abdominal enhanced CT showed swelling of the small intestine wall, suggesting ischemic bowel disease (figure B). Meanwhile, continuous renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin infusion were performed, and rituximab was tried (2 × 500 mg intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days) to treat both thrombotic microangiopathy and anti-synthetase syndrome. The patient's symptoms of ischemic bowel disease and changes in the blood system were improved; however, her impaired renal function did not recover and regular haemodialysis was performed during follow-up for 3 months.

Thrombotic microangiopathy rarely accompanies anti-synthetase syndrome; only about six cases of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy have been reported, of which two cases had no or only mild kidney injury. Other studies have suggested that, under certain circumstances, circulating autoantibodies in patients with autoimmune inflammatory muscle diseases (including anti-synthetase syndrome) might inhibit plasma von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity, which is another pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy. Patients could need combination therapy to treat anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy, including plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressive drugs. Initial neurological examination was consistent with a right-sided hemiplegia. A CT scan of her head confirmed infarction of the left basal ganglia and left paraventricular regions of the brain. A non-contrast chest CT scan showed a 6 cm diameter, high attenuation circle in the left atrium (figure). Further investigation using transthoracic echocardiography (figure) revealed a mobile left atrial mass with concentric circles around the periphery, consistent with a free-floating thrombus; it also showed severe mitral stenosis with a dilated left atrium filled with dense spontaneous echo contrast and no left atrial appendage thrombus.The woman, who was first diagnosed with rheumatic heart disease 10 years ago, was taken to surgery, where the free-floating mass was removed and the mitral valve replaced. Subsequent pathological examination confirmed a giant thrombus with a smooth outer shell, and an area below the surface containing multiple haemorrhagic regions. The variable consistency of this subsurface area may have been the cause of the concentric circles seen on CT scan and transthoracic echocardiography.
Left atrial ball thrombi almost always form in the setting of mitral valve disease and are linked to high rates of embolism. Prompt surgical removal is the recommended and appropriate therapeutic intervention.

An 86-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis—reporting progressive dyspnoea, rated as Class II on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification, for the previous few months—had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in our unit. The patient's valve was replaced with an aortic valve bio prosthesis (Evolut PRO/PRO+ 29 mm [Medtronic Evolut™]).
Immediately after the valve had been replaced, continuous electrocardiogram monitoring showed ST-segment elevation in all antero-septal leads. A coronary angiogram showed complete occlusion of the distal part of the left anterior descending artery (figure 1).We then did a mechanical embolectomy—using a stent retriever (enVast 4·5 × 37 mm [enVast™]) combined with vacuum-assisted aspiration—which resulted in the immediate restoration of blood flow in the blocked artery; no residual material was seen in the vessel on repeat angiography (figure 1).
The extracted material was amber-coloured, calcified, and 2 mm in size; histopathological examination showed that it was mostly composed of collagen, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix—compatible with a fragment of a leaflet from the patient's original aortic valve (figure 2). Additionally, substrates appeared non-birefringent under polarised light, confirming the absence of polymer-coated device fragments.The patient's chest pain promptly resolved; concentration of high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 24 h (202 ng/L; normal value <14). The patient remained asymptomatic for 1 day after the operation.
On day 2 postoperatively, she developed severe abdominal pain; an abdominal CT scan showed patency of both the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries with radiological signs of intestinal ischaemia. The patient had abdominal surgery which was complicated by multiple-organ failure; she died 4 days after the index TAVR.
Embolisation of aortic valve debris is a feared complication during TAVR, typically resulting in cerebrovascular accidents, and mesenteric or peripheral ischaemia. Histological analysis of captured material from cerebral protective devices has previously been done.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report showing that embolisation of aortic valve debris—confirmed by histological examination—into coronary circulation can be extracted with a stent retriever. Coronary embolisation during TAVR is unpredictable and no effective preventive measures exist; conventional angioplasty is often unsuccessful because of the presence of the calcified, non-friable material inside the vessel.

A 53-year-old man presented to our emergency department with a 2-week history of increasing dyspnoea and a dry cough.
The patient had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease recently diagnosed in the outpatient department; he was not concordant with prescribed bronchodilator treatment because the symptoms were mild. He was a smoker of 9 pack-years and continued to smoke. He reported no environmental or occupational exposures to fumes, gas, or dusts. He had no previous history of chest trauma.
On examination the patient was alert and breathless at rest; he showed no signs of respiratory failure, cyanosis, or clubbing. Pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 145/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 85%, and respiratory rate was 24 breaths per min. On auscultation, breath sounds were diminished in the right lung.
Laboratory investigations showed no abnormalities: no anaemia or erythrocytosis. An electrocardiogram showed no signs of ischaemia, infarction, or ventricular hypertrophy, or abnormalities of rhythm.
A chest x-ray showed a right hydropneumothorax (figure). A right chest thoracostomy with a negative pressure suction system was inserted. 1 h later, a repeated chest x-ray showed complete lung expansion with right lower lobe consolidation, and subcutaneous emphysema around the chest tube (figure). In the next 24 h, the patient developed worsening dyspnoea with hypoxaemia; arterial blood gases showed hypocapnia with a pCO2 of 26·1 mm Hg (normal range 28·3–38·7) and hypoxaemia with oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. CT pulmonary angiography ruled out a pulmonary embolism and chest tube malposition but showed right lower lobe consolidation and upper lobe bullae and centrilobular emphysema (appendix).3 days after admission, an additional chest x-ray showed that the consolidation had resolved, with complete lung expansion (figure).
The rapid clearance of the consolidation affecting the collapsed lung led us to a diagnosis of lobar re-expansion pulmonary oedema in the context of a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
The patient improved and required no specific therapy. He was allowed home after 7 days; he was well and showed no signs of respiratory distress. He was prescribed tiotropium and brief smoking cessation intervention. He was given an appointment with the stop-smoking service and a test for alpha-1 antitrypsin was booked.
Re-expansion pulmonary oedema (REPE) is a rare complication, likely to occur in less than 1% of all pleural drainage procedures—including pneumothorax, haemothorax, and pleural effusion. The mechanism behind REPE is not completely understood but involves an increase in negative intrapleural pressure after rapid draining, which causes a rise in hydrostatic vascular pressure, reperfusion damage, and pulmonary capillary permeability in the atelectatic lung. Pre-existing parenchymal lung illness, or lobar, or segmental bronchial obstruction, prior to pleural drainage, may cause REPE; thus, it is reasonable to postulate that—in our patient—pre-existing bullae in the upper lobe may have prevented parenchymal collapse and conditioned localised REPE of the lower lobe.

A 37-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of partial loss of vision and diplopia while driving home 2 h earlier. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.On examination we found him to be alert and oriented. Temperature was 37·6°C, pulse was 93 beats per min, and blood pressure was 130/89 mm Hg supine and 120/75 mm Hg erect. Neurological examination showed the patient to have decreased visual acuity in both eyes with a bitemporal hemianopia; we observed no oculomotor palsies and no sensory or motor deficits.
Laboratory investigations showed no abnormalities.
Brain MRI showed a partially cystic sellar and suprasellar mass that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images without clear contrast enhancement. The optic chiasm was compressed and displaced by the lesion (figure).
Endocrinological work-up showed a slightly elevated serum prolactin concentration of 30 ng/mL (normal <20 in men); all other pituitary function studies—including thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, insulin-like growth factor 1, testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinising hormone—were within normal ranges.
We then embarked upon a transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of what we thought was a pituitary adenoma in a patient with pituitary apoplexy. However, on removal of the sella floor, the classic white-greyish discolouration of the dura was not evident: the sella had a more purplish appearance—and although this might have been attributable to intrasellar haemorrhage, a small scratch of this layer produced a mass with yellow crystalline-like fluid. Progressive resection was performed using sharp dissection and curettes, and no evidence of haemorrhage was found; after near complete resection, a dural layer came, surprisingly, into view. A 4 mm 45° endoscope was inserted for verification and this confirmed that the dural layer was intact with no intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Further, we observed no cavernous sinus invasion or mass remnant. Postoperatively, the patient had complete resolution of his diplopia and visual deficit and no evidence of diabetes insipidus.
Histopathological examination showed the tumour consisted of fibrous tissue with cholesterol clefts, lympho-plasma-cellular infiltrates, marked haemosiderin deposits, multinucleated giant cells, granular necrotic debris, and accumulations of foamy macrophages; no epithelial cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen or cytokeratin were observed in any part of the tumour. A xanthogranuloma was therefore confirmed.
The patient was well with no neurological deficits or evidence of disease recurrence 12 months postoperatively.
Pituitary apoplexy—a clinical syndrome secondary to sudden haemorrhage or infarction—occurs in approximately 7% of pituitary adenomas; a severe headache, often accompanied by visual disturbances, is commonly the presenting complaint. Xanthogranulomas of the sellar region are extremely rare and might be misdiagnosed as macroadenomas presenting with pituitary apoplexy if—as in our case—the lesion is an intrasellar, extradural xanthogranuloma with suprasellar extension (video).

A 78-year-old gardener presented to our hospital with a fever and a painful swollen right hand. She had started to feel pain in both her ring and little finger 4 days earlier, which spread to her wrist. She also said she had been feverish but did not report having rigors. Notably, she said she frequently handled manure and had puncture wounds from repeatedly pricking herself on the thorns on her rosebushes. She had a history of temporal arteritis and was being treated with prednisolone 40 mg daily.On examination, she was febrile (39°C) but haemodynamically stable. Both the ring finger and little finger on her right hand were swollen and tender; pain and the tenderness spread to her forearm when she flexed all her fingers. However, no signs of any abnormality were seen on her skin or other systems—specifically the respiratory system. Full blood count showed raised white blood cell count 14·5 × 109 per L (normal range 4·3–10·8) and C-reactive protein (39 mg/L).
We did an extensive debridement of the patient's hand and forearm, which showed purulent material in all the tendon sheaths; these, along with the carpel tunnel, were opened and washed (figure). We started the patient on amoxicillin–clavulanate, after taking samples for microbiological analysis. A 38-year-old primigravid woman presented to our hospital at 31 weeks of gestation with severe abdominal pain. She had no uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, or trauma. She was hypotensive, her abdomen was peritonitic and a fetal heart rate tracing showed fetal distress with bradycardia (60 beats per min [normal range 110–160 beats per min]). We performed a laparotomy within minutes of admission, which revealed that the uterus had split open along its entire length, as well as 1·5 L of haemoperitoneum. We delivered the baby, repaired the rupture, and transfused blood products to prevent consumptive coagulopathy in the mother. Unfortunately, the neonate's Apgar scores were 2 points at 1 min and 4 points at 5 mins, and blood gases within the umbilical cord showed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 6·84, bicarbonate 10·5 mmol/L, partial CO2 pressure 61·6 mm Hg, base excess −23 mmol/L). He died despite resuscitation.As obstetricians, we were perturbed; a spontaneous uterine rupture before the onset of labour in women without a caesarean scar or myomectomy scar is extremely uncommon. However, when we examined our patient following the surgery, we noticed a unilateral Z thumb deformity of her left hand, which we confirmed on x-ray, and thin skin with multiple haemosiderin scars on her left foot (figure). We learned that she had a history of easy bruising in childhood and had sustained an open ankle fracture 6 years earlier while skipping, with rupture of the anterior talofibular ligament, peroneous tertius, and extensor digitorum brevis muscle tendons. Following orthopaedic surgery, she consulted three specialists, all of whom felt that the probability of a connective tissue disorder was low and that she did not require further investigation, given that she had no skin elasticity and her Beighton score was only 2 points.
However, considering the history of unprovoked uterine rupture, the low energy mechanism of the ankle injury, and our clinical findings, we reasoned that her a priori risk of connective tissue disorder was high. Therefore, with the patient's consent, we proceeded with genetic tests using next-generation sequencing of whole blood. The results confirmed a pathogenic, heterozygous variant (c.951+5G→A [p.Gly300_Ala317del]) in the COL3A1 gene, consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. This variant disrupts a splice donor site shown to cause exon skipping and in-frame deletion within the collagen helical domain. Subsequent echocardiography and whole-body magnetic resonance angiography of the patient excluded valvular disease, aortic root dilation, and vascular aneurysms (figure).
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder arising from deleterious missense, splicing, and haploinsufficiency variations in the COL3A1 gene, affects the synthesis of type III collagen, the foundation of the connective tissue in hollow viscera (eg, uterus), vessels, and skin. The physical features are subtle and the Beighton score (which includes the large joints in its calculation) can be misleadingly normal, given that large joint hypermobility and hyperextensibility of the skin—characteristic of the more common forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome—are unusual in the vascular form of the disease.
A history of recurrent, atraumatic bruising with haemosiderin pigmentation of the skin (as seen in our patient) suggests pathological soft-tissue fragility and should prompt genetic testing to avoid missing the diagnosis. Pregnant women are especially vulnerable, given that catastrophic complications from peripartum arterial and uterine rupture occur in 5% of women with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Adverse obstetric outcomes are potentially preventable through pre-pregnancy genetic counselling and targeted antenatal surveillance, but only if the syndrome is suspected sooner.

input:
A baby girl delivered vaginally at full-term at a local hospital was found to have a global decrease in tone which was predominately in her arms. She had been born after an induction of labour because of decreased movements and oligohydramnios seen at 39 weeks of gestation on ultrasound.An ultrasound of the baby's head soon after birth demonstrated no obvious abnormalities. However, a T1-gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine showed an enhancing, intramedullary lesion extending from the medulla down to the upper thoracic spinal cord—indicating a possible high-grade neoplasm (figure). The patient was transferred to our quaternary referral hospital and comprehensive cancer centre.
On examination, the baby was awake and alert, with a flat fontanelle, normal head circumference, and global hypotonia. Over the next 2 weeks, her quadriparesis became progressively worse—the cervical spine showed signs of compression because of the expansile tumour in the spinal canal. We decompressed the cervical spine by doing a laminoplasty; we used electrostimulation, neuromonitoring, and intraoperative ultrasound to locate a safe midline entry point to obtain a biopsy and partially debulk the tumour. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample confirmed the suspected diagnosis of congenital spinal cord glioblastoma WHO grade IV.
Next generation sequencing showed a gene fusion involving the neurotrophin tropomyosin receptor kinase (NTRK) 1 gene: an inversion on chromosome 1q. No other pathogenic mutations, amplifications, deletions, or rearrangements were identified. Additionally, the tumour showed diffuse tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) positivity; she was treated with induction chemotherapy and the oral TRK inhibitor, larotrectinib, starting at a 50% dose of 50 mg/m2 twice a day for the first week to monitor for possible signs of toxicity because of the concurrent chemotherapy. The full dose of 100 mg/m2 twice a day was started in week 2 and continued. The patient tolerated the treatment well, and following cycle 1 of only conventional chemotherapy, a small reduction in size of the spinal cord tumour was seen.
2 weeks after the addition of larotrectinib, we observed a significant decrease in the size and enhancement on MRI of the lesion, with improvement in the patient's quadriparesis.
8 weeks into treatment with the oral TRK inhibitor and 4 cycles of carboplatin and etoposide, the tumour had completely regressed and was no longer visible with imaging (figure). 17 months after starting treatment, the patient was crawling and progressing toward walking; she continues treatment on the oral TRK inhibitor only, and there was no evidence of recurrence of the tumour.
The NTRK genes—NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3 which produce TRK proteins—are affected by oncogenic fusions leading to a wide range of both paediatric and adult neoplasms. Small molecule TRK inhibitors have shown efficacy in treating a diverse array of TRK-positive tumours. In clinical trials of TRK inhibitors for tumours—in both adult and paediatric patients with a variety of different primary tumour types with NTRK gene fusions—response rates ranged from 75–93%. The first generation TRK inhibitors appear, on the whole, to be well tolerated in terms of adverse events: most are low grade—including neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, anaemia and neutropenia, and nausea and vomiting.
Aided by histopathological examination findings, next generation sequencing can uncover NTRK fusions that may change the clinical course for patients with many primary tumours. While we could not entirely rule out a response to chemotherapy alone resulting in the improvement seen in our patient, the prognosis for congenital glioblastomas treated with chemotherapy alone remains very poor (video).

A 43-year-old man was consulted for acute, inflammatory, cervical and low-back pain, associated with a swollen left elbow, wrist, and knee. He had a 38·5°C fever and elevated C-reactive protein concentration (265 mg/L). Knee aspiration showed an inflammatory synovial fluid (73 000 white blood cells per mm3; 80% neutrophils) without bacteria or microcrystals on direct examination. A disseminated infection of both the axial and peripheral joints was suspected and an empirical antibiotic therapy targeting Staphylococcus aureus was initiated, including cefazolin and gentamicin. Spinal MRI revealed a C3–C4 posterior facet joint inflammatory arthritis and a L3–L4 interspinous bursitis. Repeated lumbar CT showed the development of an erosion within the spinous process of L4 (figure). Cultures of the knee synovial fluid were positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Nucleic acid amplification tests for N gonorrhoeae were also positive in the synovial fluid and at the oropharyngeal site. The patient reported previous unprotected sexual behaviours, but did not have any urogenital, rectal, or pharyngeal symptoms. Cefazolin was switched to a 2 g daily dose of ceftriaxone for a total duration of 21 days because of the axial involvement, resulting in a clinical and biological improvement. Endocarditis was ruled out by a transthoracic heart ultrasound and repeated blood cultures. Altogether, radiological findings suggested an axial location of the N gonorrhoeae infection, which was supported by the improvement of back pain with antibiotic therapy. Screening was negative for other sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV, syphilis, and Chlamydia trachomatis. Beyond HIV, we also investigated other causes of immunosuppression, including diabetes and hypogammaglobulinaemia, which were negative. However, the patient was not screened for complement deficiencies.
Disseminated gonococcal infection is a re-emerging disease that usually affects peripheral joints. It rarely involves axial joints, with only two previously reported cases. Disseminated gonococcal infection should be suspected in patients having unprotected sex behaviours with peripheral or axial inflammatory arthritis. Because culture of N gonorrhoeae is difficult, synovial fluid aspiration should be repeated, including detection by nucleic acid amplification tests. Multisite testing of N gonorrhoeae should also be encouraged in patients who are at risk of sexually transmitted diseases, even if asymptomatic.

A 62-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-h history of abrupt-onset of right flank pain and vomiting.
The patient had a history of vertigo and recent unintentional weight loss with migrating lymphadenopathy. She was prescribed meclizine and loratadine. She reported no history of trauma.
On examination the patient was distressed and pale; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure 96/53 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 95%; her temperature was 36·6oC. She had tenderness in the right periumbilical region of her abdomen, with no rebound or guarding. Urine analysis showed 1+ protein, positive leukocyte esterase; microscopic examination showed 12 white blood cells, and 8 red blood cells.
Laboratory investigations found the patient to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 6·8 g/dL (reference range 11·7–15·7); she was given an emergency transfusion of packed red blood cells. Further tests showed a white blood cell count of 49 × 103 per μL (reference range 4·0–11·0), platelets 380 × 103 per μL (reference range 150–450), and serum creatinine concentration of 0·9 mg/dL (reference range 0·51–0·95).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a large right perinephric haematoma. A renal angiogram showed no signs of active bleeding.
The patient was stabilised with further medical management involving intravenous crystalloid fluid and an additional transfusion of packed red blood cells. Given the profound leukocytosis and absence of signs of infection, oncology colleagues were consulted, and an outpatient bone marrow biopsy was planned.
However, 2 days later, the patient presented to our hospital again with acute onset pain in the flank, but this time on the left side; her haemoglobin concentration was 6·0 g/dL and she was thrombocytopenic—nadir of the platelet count was 7 × 103 per μL. She received a transfusion of platelets and further packed red blood cells.
An abdominal CT scan showed a new left perinephric haematoma; the right sided haematoma appeared stable (figure 1). A renal angiogram showed active bleeding from a left upper pole segmental arterial branch and a right upper pole peripheral arterial branch; these were then both successfully embolised. A previously well 54-year-old woman with no history of trauma presented to Kimitsu Chuo Hospital (Kisarazu, Japan) in February, 2017, with a 1-year history of coccydynia during sitting. Digital rectal examination revealed a hard mass in the retrorectal area. Pelvic radiograph indicated disseminated calcification in front of the coccyx (figure, A) and pelvic CT scan showed a large retrorectal solid tumour containing calcific particles without destruction of the coccyx. Lumbosacral spine MRI showed that the retrorectal tumour was multilocular (figure, B). Colonoscopy was normal. Percutaneous biopsy of the tumour identified a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, abdominal and vaginal ultrasonography, whole-body CT scat, pelvic MRI, and PET/CT detected no primary tumour. A diagnosis of isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult cancer was made.
In compliance with the patient's wishes, radiotherapy—not chemotherapy—was initiated while surgical resection was considered. However, at 6 months after her first visit, radiotherapy resulted in no improvement and a repeat CT scan detected a tumour in the pancreatic head. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the tumour identified a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma, which was considered to be the primary lesion.
Retrorectal tumours are rare and many cases are asymptomatic and are only found incidentally because of their subtle clinical symptoms (eg, rectal discomfort, change in bowel habit, and chronic pain in the perineum). They are broadly categorised as benign versus malignant and congenital versus acquired. Most of them are benign developmental cysts resulting from abnormal closure of the ectodermal tube, such as epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, enteric cysts, or neurenteric cysts. Other benign retrorectal masses include teratomas, meningoceles, and neurilemmomas. Malignant retrotectal tumours that have been reported are chordoma, chondrosarcoma, and osteosarcoma. Although sacral metastases might be observed in patients with various malignancies, isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult cancer is a very rare phenomenon.
Intratumoural calcification in malignancies derives from three factors: metastatic calcification caused by hypercalcaemia, dystrophic calcification occurring as a reaction to tissue necrosis, or ontogenic calcification in which cancer-producing mucin glycoproteins accelerate bonding of calcium and phosphorus. In this case, we believe that the low degree of differentiation and the mucin formation of mucinous adenocarcinoma, which is rare in pancreatic cancers, led to dystrophic and ontogenic calcification of the isolated retrorectal metastasis, respectively, since the patient did not have hypercalcaemia.
Although the patient was scheduled to receive pancreaticoduodenectomy and resection of the isolated retrorectal metastasis, liver metastases were subsequently found on pre-operative CT scan and the surgery was cancelled. She opted not to receive chemotherapy and was transferred to a hospice for end-of-life care.

A 16-year-old girl attended our outpatient clinic complaining about a hard lump on the second toe of her left foot. She said it had been present for 6 years, but that in the past 3 months it had become moderately painful and that the pain was aggravated by walking. She said that the lump had not increased in size. She reported no history of trauma and no relevant medical history.On examination, the patient was fit and well, and all vital signs were within normal limits. The lump was firm and round and located on the proximal phalanx of her second toe of her left foot; there were no overlying skin changes. The lesion was hard, fixed to the bone, and non-tender on palpation; there were no signs of local inflammation. Neuromuscular examination of the lower limbs was unremarkable: we found no other palpable masses.
x-ray showed a 1–1·8 cm well circumscribed, lucent, central medullary lesion within the diaphysis of the proximal phalanx. Cortical expansion and thinning were also present (figure). We saw no fractures on the x-ray.
Laboratory investigations—including inflammatory markers, a full blood count, and calcium and phosphate concentrations—were all within normal limits.
We decided to surgically excise the lesion with intramedullary curettage and subsequent bone grafting because the lesion was painful, and no fracture was seen on the x-rays.
Histological examination of the lesion undertaken postoperatively showed lobules of hyaline cartilage encased by normal bone and fibrous tissue, consistent with a diagnosis of an enchondroma. Cellularity was within normal limits and without atypical cells or mitotic figures (figure).
At follow-up 3 weeks later, the surgical incision had healed well and the patient said the pain had gone.
Enchondromas are benign cartilage-forming tumours that usually develop in the medulla—marrow cavity—of long bones. They typically present during the second decade of life, but they can present at any age. Enchondromas are often an incidental finding because they are usually asymptomatic. However, when pain is the presenting symptom, a chondrosarcoma should be at the top of the differential diagnosis list—especially if the lesion is on the hands or feet. Additionally, fractures should be excluded first. Treatment depends upon the presence of symptoms and size of the lesion: localised asymptomatic enchondromas which are small enough not to provoke pathological fractures and show no signs of increasing in size can be kept under regular observation with repeated radiographical check-ups—usually annually. Symptomatic, large, or rapidly growing enchondromas can be managed surgically (video).

input:
A 25-year-old man presented to our department with a 5-year history of an insidious, progressive weakness in his right hand. Despite being right-handed, he had recently become reliant on his left hand to carry out tasks needing manual dexterity. Clinical examination showed muscular atrophy without fasciculations of the first dorsal interosseous muscle and weakness of both the thenar and hypothenar muscles of the right hand; he also had atrophy but no fasciculation of the lumbrical and interosseous muscles. He complained of bilateral, electric shock-like sensations throughout his body when we examined the range of movements of his neck—Lhermitte's sign. Laboratory investigations showed a serum B12 concentration of 648 pg/mL (normal range 174–878) and the serum panel for heavy metal toxicity—including arsenic, mercury, and lead—was negative. Investigations for rheumatoid arthritis—including antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor (less than 14 IU/mL)—were within the normal ranges and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal at 2 mm/h.An MRI of the patient's brain showed no abnormalities; however, an MRI of his cervical spine showed myelomalacia of the spinal cord but no other features that might give a clue as to the underlying cause of his problems (figure). The association of the patient's electric shock-like sensations prompted us to do a dynamic cervical spine MRI study with the neck in positions of flexion and extension: MRI showed that the spinal cord was being compressed—most noticeably at the level of the fifth cervical vertebral body—and that the dorsal epidural space was abnormally expanding while in a flexed position (figure). Such radiographic findings are pathognomonic of Hirayama disease and so clinched the diagnosis.
To prevent further neurological injury, we did a two-level anterior cervical spine fusion at C4/C5 and C5/C6 using synthetic interbody grafts between the vertebral bodies after removal of the intervertebral disc material; these were secured with a titanium plate from C4 to C6. A further dynamic cervical spine MRI done 6 weeks after the operation showed that the spinal cord was no longer being compressed when the patient flexed his neck (figure). Dexterity in his right hand had subjectively improved at follow-up 6 months later.
Hirayama disease—first described by Keizo Hirayama in 1959 as a juvenile, unilateral, muscular atrophy of the upper limb—predominantly affects adolescent men and is thought to be caused by dynamic mechanical or ischaemic injury to the ventral cervical motor neurons. Our case shows the importance of doing a dynamic flexion and extension MRI in young patients with otherwise unexplained progressive neuronal dysfunction. The imaging findings are key to differentiating the disease from more common disorders—such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, tabes dorsalis, spinal muscular atrophy, or syringomyelia—and allowing for appropriate surgical action, as in our patient.

input:
A 40-year-old woman was referred to our clinic by her optometrist because she had lesions on her retina suggestive of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). She was otherwise well: with no systemic or visual symptoms.In her medical history, the patient had no previous problems with her eyesight. However, at the age of 10 years, she had developed end-stage renal disease—initially diagnosed as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis—which eventually resulted in her having a right kidney transplant when she was 22 years old. 6 years later, aged 28 years, she developed signs of rejection and required hospitalisation. At that stage, a kidney biopsy led to a diagnosis of dense deposit disease (DDD). She received a second kidney transplant at age 39 years.
She had been prescribed a combination of immunosuppressive drugs—prednisolone, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus—for the past 2 years, and her blood pressure had remained stable without pharmacotherapy.
On examination, we found her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Fundus examination showed drusen-like deposits in the macula and numerous lesions in the peripheral retina of both eyes (figure). Optical coherence tomography showed subretinal dome-shaped deposits—known as drusen—in the peripheral retina, with some encroaching in the macular region of both eyes (figure). Drusen is the plural form of druse, a German word meaning node or geode.
Considering the situation in the round, including the patient's age and medical history, and the appearance and distribution of the fundus lesions, we concluded that the drusen were a feature of DDD rather than AMD. The patient continues to be followed up by both her nephrologist and ophthalmologist.
DDD, which was previously known as type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, is classified as either complement or immune complex mediated; DDD is considered a subtype of complement C3-mediated glomerulopathy. Patients with DDD have diffuse, dense deposits in the glomerular basement membrane, and unlike other forms of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, they also typically have drusen deposits in Bruch's membrane of the eye. It is a rare disease that usually presents in children aged 5–15 years old and eventually leads to end-stage renal disease.
Drusen in patients with DDD typically develop after more than 20 years, and although the retinal lesions do not directly cause visual impairment, vision can deteriorate, most commonly due to macular detachment, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal neovascularisation similar to patients with AMD.
Anyone under the age of 50 years found to have retinal drusen should therefore be assessed for renal disease at the time of presentation, and should have regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor for the development of potential vision-threatening changes (video).

A 20-year-old daycare teacher presented to our hospital reporting a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash. The patient also had a fever, myalgia, nausea, reduced urine output, peripheral oedema, and dyspnoea on exertion. She reported that the rash had rapidly increased in size over the past 72 h—coinciding with a doubling of the dose of her lamotrigine which she was prescribed for bipolar affective disorder.Apart from her mental health condition, she had no other significant medical history.
On examination, we found the patient to be feverish with a temperature of 40·3°C and bradycardic with a heart rate of 42 beats per min. She had a morbilliform rash—prominently seen over her trunk and extremities; there was no mucosal or genital involvement (figure). Hepatosplenomegaly and mild oedema of both the patient's legs were also noted.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a leukocytosis of 14·03 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11) with an eosinophilia of 1·08 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 24 mm/h (normal 0–29).
The patient's aspartate aminotransferase was 42 units per L (normal 8–33) and alanine aminotransferase was 79 units per L (normal 7–55): indicating a transaminitis. The blood urea nitrogen concentration was 50 mg/dL (normal 6–21) and creatine concentration was 5·6 mg/dL (normal 0·5–1·2).
Screening for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses was reactive only for hepatitis A virus IgG. An autoimmune panel was negative for antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. However, a Monospot test was positive; a cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG test was also positive.
Considering the findings in the round—the transaminitis and acute renal failure showed multiorgan involvement, the positive Monospot test indicated active Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, and the positive IgG test suggested previous CMV infection—we made a diagnosis of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome induced by lamotrigine with a concomitant infection. We considered that the EBV was either a new infection or a reactivation of a previous infection with the virus.
We stopped the lamotrigine and gave the patient a course of pulse steroids which gradually led to an improvement in her symptoms and renal function.
DRESS syndrome is an idiosyncratic drug-induced delayed type IV hypersensitivity severe multisystemic reaction that typically develops within 2–8 weeks of exposure. The proposed pathogenesis is a reactivation of latent herpesviruses which can be triggered by certain medications—including lamotrigine; a cross-reaction is thought to occur between the virus-specific T lymphocytes and the medications. In our case, the underlying cause of DRESS syndrome could be explained two ways: firstly, the concurrent lamotrigine use and a primary EBV infection or, secondly, lamotrigine-induced reactivation of EBV which then caused DRESS syndrome. Whatever the sequence of events, the treatment remains the same: immediate cessation of the drug causing the problem, systemic corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressants—including intravenous immuno-globulin in steroid-resistant cases (video).

A 50-year-old woman reporting chest discomfort and found to have ventricular tachycardia (VT) on electrocardiogram (ECG) with a reduced ejection fraction on echocardiogram was transferred to our hospital (figure). The patient had no significant medical history.On examination in our emergency department, she appeared well: her blood pressure was 114/79 mm Hg and her oxygen saturation was 97% breathing room air. She was afebrile.
We repeated the echocardiogram which showed a 20% ejection fraction, global hypokinesis of the left ventricle, and biventricular dilation—notably the patient was not in VT during the procedure (figure). Coronary artery angiography showed no significant stenosis and a repeat ECG demonstrated right bundle branch block and features suggestive of an acute anteroseptal infarct (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 2922 pg/mL (normal 0–125) and a troponin T concentration of 0·17 ng/mL (normal 0·01–0·03).
The patient returned to normal sinus rhythm after intravenous amiodarone and oral metoprolol; a cardioverter defibrillator was implanted for secondary prevention.
Cardiac MRI after cardioversion showed features of a transmural myocardial infarction of the anterior aspect of the interventricular septum and basal anterior wall (figure).
Our differential diagnosis at this time included inflammatory conditions—infectious or autoimmune—and ischaemic cardiomyopathies. No definitive clinical, laboratory, or radiographic findings entirely supported any specific aetiology. An endomyocardial biopsy provided little clarification of the diagnosis as it did not include any myocardium. The patient was then allowed home.
One month later, she presented in respiratory distress; she was hypoxic, had acute kidney injury, and worsening of her reduced ejection fraction. The patient required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and an intra-aortic balloon pump; 2 weeks later she had a heart transplant.
Pathological examination of the explanted native heart showed giant cell myocarditis centred around the interventricular septum; the relatively localised lesion had both active inflammation and cardiomyocyte injury, as well as chronic features of interstitial fibrosis (figure).
Approximately 5 months after transplantation, the patient's postoperative course was complicated by Klebsiella aerogenes pneumonia and transient evidence of acute cellular and active antibody-mediated rejection with donor specific antibodies—although recent biopsies showed no evidence of rejection and donor specific antibodies were undetectable. Endomyocardial biopsies since have shown no recurrence of giant cell myocarditis.
The finding of giant cell myocarditis was unexpected in our case: very few cases present with acute ischaemia and heart block. Most patients present with congestive heart failure and a small percentage with ventricular arrhythmias. Various immunosuppression regimens, albeit without consensus recommendations, have been shown to prolong time before transplantation or death, compared to patients receiving no immunosuppression. In cases that proceeded to cardiac transplantation, mortality is the same as patients having transplants for both dilated and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (video).

A 41-year-old woman presented to our clinic because of the sudden appearance of erosions on and swelling of her lips. On clinical examination, diffuse erythema of the labial mucosae with small vesicles and crusted erosions on both the superior and inferior vermillion borders were noted (figure). Further inspection of her mouth showed erythema and erosions on the inner cheek and mild focal desquamated gingivitis. The patient was otherwise healthy, with good oral hygiene. No other lesions were seen on the rest of her body. She had been taking paracetamol and amoxicillin for 3 days for a sore throat and fever. Based on the clinical symptoms and medical history, we diagnosed erythema multiforme (EM) major. She was treated with prednisolone 60 mg/day, with dramatic improvement of her symptoms.EM is an inflammatory condition that can affect the skin, the mucosa, or both. It is characterised by acute onset of symptoms and is divided into major or minor depending on the presence or absence of mucosal involvement, respectively. Infections with herpes simplex viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M pneumoniae-induced rash mucositis) have been thought to be pathogenetic factors—along with several drugs, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, allopurinol, and some antibiotics. EM is no longer considered to be on the spectrum of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, which include Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and SJS/TEN overlap. It differs in that it occurs in younger people and is associated with frequent recurrences. Also, patients tend to be free of comorbidities such as HIV infection or cancer, and when they have systemic symptoms, they are usually mild.
In our patient, herpes simplex virus infection was excluded, both as a primary phenomenon in the mouth and as a secondary phenomenon causing EM. The exclusive involvement of the oral mucosa in EM is uncommon and may be challenging diagnostically in the differentiation from various inflammatory and autoimmune disorders—including lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, and herpetic gingivostomatitis.

A 34-year-old woman, 22 weeks pregnant, attended the National University Hospital, Singapore, reporting asymptomatic hypertension on home blood pressure monitoring.She had a prior diagnosis of lupus membranous nephropathy and antiphospholipid syndrome with anti-cardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant, and had a deep vein thrombosis diagnosed 3 years earlier. She had been taking hydroxychloroquine, prednisolone, ciclosporin (due to azathioprine intolerance), low-dose aspirin, and therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from the first trimester of pregnancy, and had been normotensive.
On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 160/87 mm Hg; there were no neurological abnormalities or signs of fetal distress. Her serum creatinine concentration (69 μmol/L) and total urinary protein (6·4 g/day) were raised from her preadmission baseline (taken 3 months before the current presentation) of 52 μmol/L and 0·7 g/day, respectively. Her anti-double stranded DNA antibody titre was more than 800 IU/L, C3 protein concentration was 55 mg/dL (baseline 71 mg/dL), and C4 protein concentration was less than 8 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed 166 red blood cells per high power field, with casts and 25% dysmorphic red blood cells on phase-contrast microscopy. Her complete blood count was unremarkable (haemoglobin concentration 11·0 g/dL and platelet count 201 × 109/L).
Taken together, the findings suggested a lupus flare with proliferative glomerulonephritis. We started intravenous pulsed methylprednisolone (500 mg daily) and oral labetalol (200 mg thrice per day), withheld ciclosporin to avoid worsening hypertension and renal function, and continued aspirin (100 mg daily) and enoxaparin (60 mg twice per day).
48 h later, the patient developed an abrupt onset of cough and dyspnoea at rest. Her blood pressure was 175/85 mm Hg, there were coarse crackles in the lung bases, and she required supplemental oxygen with a Venturi mask with an FiO2 of 40%. Arterial blood gas measurements showed hypoxaemia and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 237 mm Hg. Tests showed new-onset anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 126 × 109/L), an NT-proBNP concentration of 4077 pg/mL, and widespread opacities on chest x-ray (figure). We suspected superimposed pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome and acute pulmonary oedema, and gave furosemide, but the dyspnoea did not improve despite diuresis. Venous thromboembolism was unlikely as she had been adequately anticoagulated with enoxaparin (anti-factor Xa activity 0·78 IU/mL [target 0·6–1·0]), and her electrocardiogram did not show abnormalities.
We intubated the patient for mechanical ventilation due to worsening respiratory distress and did a flexible bronchoscopy; sequential bronchoalveolar lavage showed fresh blood and haemosiderin-containing macrophages (figure). We diagnosed diffuse alveolar haemorrhage due to systemic lupus erythematosus. Our principal differential diagnoses were evolving catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome and antiphospholipid syndrome with microvascular features: diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, diffuse ischaemic myocarditis, and antiphospholipid antibody-associated nephropathy.
Tests for infectious pulmonary triggers of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative. We gave further pulsed methylprednisolone (1000 mg daily for 2 days) and commenced plasma exchange, but the hypoxaemia remained refractory, and we were concerned that the patient was at immediate risk of death. The pregnancy was terminated to offset competing haemodynamic demands from the gravid uterus, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and rituximab (two 1-g infusions given 14 days apart) were started urgently.
The patient stabilised, and after several weeks she was extubated and transitioned to mycophenolate mofetil (1·5 g daily). She was discharged after 9 weeks in hospital with tapering doses of prednisolone for sustained immunosuppression.
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage is a rare but potentially fatal pulmonary manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus; patients with active lupus nephritis, positive lupus anticoagulant, C3 hypocomplementemia, and thrombocytopenia have an increased risk of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage can also occur with the microvascular phenotype of antiphospholipid syndrome, which typically presents with renal, cardiac, and pulmonary features. Antibody and immune complex-driven disruption of the alveolar–capillary basement membrane causes bleeding, dyspnoea, and a drop in haemoglobin (by at least 1·5 g/dL). Haemoptysis can be absent in a third of cases.
Pregnant patients with lupus nephritis and antiphospholipid syndrome have at least a 25% risk of pre-eclampsia. Pulmonary oedema and HELLP syndrome are subtypes of pre-eclampsia with severe features. Given the overlapping signs between diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pre-eclampsia—anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and diffuse lung infiltrates on imaging—diffuse alveolar haemorrhage should be considered in the differential diagnosis of dyspnoea during a HELLP-like presentation in a patient with active lupus nephritis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Notably, in pre-eclampsia, complement concentrations are usually normal or elevated. Prompt bronchoscopy and multidisciplinary care, including plasmapheresis, might avoid maternal death in cases of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, although maternal survival might require termination of the pregnancy.

A dilated fundus examination (figure B) and optical coherence tomography (appendix p 2) revealed bilateral subhyaloid and intraretinal haemorrhages, Roth spots, and macular oedema. The patient completed four cycles of CHOP and intrathecal chemotherapy prophylaxis and obtained a complete morphological and radiographic remission on bone marrow biopsy and PET scan.
Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm is an aggressive and uncommon haematological neoplasm, typically presenting with concurrent bone marrow (90% of cases), lymph node (50%), and spleen or liver (40%) involvement. Dissemination to non-lymphatic organs occurs in 20% of patients, but rarely includes CNS tissue. However, one report describes monocular vision loss due to optic nerve involvement. The case reported here highlights how systemic involvement of the bone marrow can lead to clinically significant cytopenias with end-organ complications. Furthermore, his chemotherapy-induced DIC probably also contributed to his risk of bleeding diatheses. Ophthalmological consultation is necessary, because pancytopenia and DIC can trigger intraocular haemorrhages that might lead to severe eye pain and blindness and require ocular surgery.

input:
A 40-year-old man presented to our emergency department with acute upper abdominal pain 8 h after ingestion of sushi. During physical examination, he was found to have tenderness in the epigastric region. Abdominal CT showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the gastric body with surrounding fat stranding. Emergency gastroscopy identified a 15 mm long larva of the nematode Anisakis simplex penetrating the inflamed body of the stomach (figure). Disinfestation rapidly resolved the patient's symptoms.Anisakiasis is a gastrointestinal infection caused in human beings by nematode larvae belonging to the family Anisakidae. The disease is caused by Anisakis spp and Pseudoterranova decipiens, which are present in both raw fish and raw squid. When the host animal dies, the larvae migrate from the viscera to the muscle. Human infestation results from accidental ingestion of the larvae. Sources of human infections differ between countries. The larvae penetrate the gastrointestinal mucosa—leading to an inflammatory response with a generalised immunoglobulin E (IgE)—mediated allergic reaction—and this results in an ulcer, an eosinophilic granuloma, or even gastrointestinal perforation. Depending on the site affected, anisakiasis is divided into gastric, intestinal, and ectopic. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhoea, which may be complicated with urticaria or anaphylaxis. Involvement of the small intestine occasionally produces intestinal obstruction. Gastric anisakiasis and intestinal anisakiasis typically occur 1–12 h and 12–48 h after ingestion, respectively. Although patients may have no awareness of the relationship between symptoms and foods, a history of recent consumption of raw seafood is an important clue to the diagnosis. Eosinophilia may develop a few weeks after disease onset, and the specific IgE antibody test is useful when endoscopic diagnosis is not possible. Endoscopic disinfestation is the only definitive treatment, though conservative management usually resolves symptoms within a few weeks due to the death of the larvae that occurs after a few days.
Early evisceration, thorough cooking, and deep freezing of seafood are recommended to prevent the disease. Many cases of anisakiasis are reported in Japan because the raw flesh of fish and squid is commonly sold without evisceration or deep freezing; keeping the guts in situ supposedly helps maintain a good appearance of the produce, and deep freezing leads to a deterioration in taste. Anisakiasis should always be considered as a differential diagnosis in patients with acute gastrointestinal symptoms because of the continuing and growing worldwide trend of eating raw seafood.
